text: Empirical tuning procedures were conducted with AGM-1 and AGM-3 for NSGA-II and PAES according to [42] aiming at defining the population size, mutation rate and crossover rate. The tuning results were compared using the indicator HV. Firstly, the population size was tested and configurations with populations formed by 100 individuals covered configurations using 50 and 70 individuals for both algorithms. So, the population size for the NSGA- II versions and the external archive size for PAES were set as 100. Secondly, the mutation rate was tuned using three configurations: {0.8, 0.9, 1.0}. Solutions achieved with the rate 0.9 outperformed solutions found by the other configurations for both MOEAs. Finally, the crossover rate was empirically adjusted for NSGA-II. The value 0.1 outper- formed the other tested values: {0.2, 0.04}. The values tested in the parameters tuning were extracted from experiments conducted in [12], [14], [18], [19]. The maximum number of generations was set as 300 and it was used as stop criterion for all algorithms. Each experiment was executed 30 times for each PLA in order to know the behavior of each algorithm to solve the problem [43].
paraphrases: We performed empirical tuning for NSGA-II and PAES using AGM-1 and AGM-3, as outlined in [42], to establish optimal population size, mutation rate, and crossover rate. The Hypervolume (HV) indicator was used to compare tuning results. Initial tests on population size showed that 100 individuals encompassed the performance of 50 and 70 individuals for both algorithms; thus, NSGA-II versions used a population size of 100, and PAES used an external archive size of 100. Next, the mutation rate was optimized across configurations {0.8, 0.9, 1.0}, with 0.9 yielding superior solutions for both MOEAs. Finally, the NSGA-II crossover rate was empirically set to 0.1, which outperformed {0.2, 0.04}. Parameter values for tuning were derived from previous experiments [12, 14, 18, 19]. All algorithms ran for a maximum of 300 generations, serving as the stopping criterion. Each experiment was repeated 30 times per PLA to understand algorithmic behavior [43].

Following the methodology in [42], empirical tuning was conducted for NSGA-II and PAES using AGM-1 and AGM-3 to determine optimal population size, mutation rate, and crossover rate. The Hypervolume (HV) metric was employed for comparing tuning outcomes. Initial population size tests indicated that a population of 100 individuals performed as well as or better than populations of 50 or 70 for both algorithms. Consequently, NSGA-II versions and PAES's external archive were set to 100 individuals. Subsequently, mutation rates of {0.8, 0.9, 1.0} were evaluated, with 0.9 proving superior for both MOEAs. Lastly, NSGA-II's crossover rate was empirically adjusted, with 0.1 demonstrating better performance than {0.2, 0.04}. These parameter values were based on prior research [12, 14, 18, 19]. A maximum of 300 generations served as the universal stopping criterion. To assess each algorithm's performance for each problem, every experiment was run 30 times per PLA [43].

text: Solution approach ⇒ genetic feature selection optimization algorithms. In this paper, we introduce an approach, based on genetic algorithms (GAs), to SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints. A GA is a stochastic and global search heuristic that mimics natural evolution (Mitchell, 1996). GAs can quickly scan a vast population of possible solutions. These algorithms often work well for highly constrained problems, such as the Traveling Salesman (Muhlenbein, 1989) and satisfiability problems (De Jong and Spears, 1989). Our approach, called Genetic Algorithms for optimized FEature Selection (GAFES), adapts GAs for SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints. GAFES can quickly derive an optimized feature selection by evaluating different configurations that both optimize product capabilities and honor resource limitations. GAFES combines a novel feature selection repair operator and a penalty function for resource constraints to obtain fast feature selection times. Our empirical results show that GAFES can produce feature selections with objective function scores that are within 86–97% of the feature selections produced by prior feature selection techniques, such as FCF (White et al., 2009) and CSP/SAT-based approaches (Benavides et al., 2005; Batory, 2005; Czarnecki and Wasowski, 2007), for feature models whose size ranges from 10 to 10,000 features. Moreover, in our experiments, GAFES derives feature selections 45–99% faster than these existing heuristic and exact feature selection optimization techniques.

In order to create a feature selection optimization problem, values for the resource consumption and value of each feature must be generated. text: The optimality and the time consumption of a solution are measured as dependent variables. ... Optimality is defined as (Approximation Answer/Optimal Answer) to measure how close an algorithm can get to the optimal answer. Here, the Approximation Answer represents the total value of a solution produced by an approximation algorithm such as GAFES or FCF + M-HEU. Since BBLP is an exact technique, we use the total value of a solution produced by FCF + BBLP as the Optimal Answer. For example, for the same optimization problem (the same feature model, the same resource constraints, and the same optimization target), if GAFES obtains an approximate solution with the total value of 90 and FCF + BBLP obtains an optimal solution with the total value of 100, then the optimality of the GAFES solution is 90%. But finding exact solutions is NP-hard, which means that it is not feasible to apply FCF+BBLP to large feature models (e.g., number of features ≥ 500). Therefore, for large feature models (number of features ≥ 500), we used the test pattern generation technique devised by Akbar et al. (2001) to generate random optimization problem instances that we knew the optimal answer to (Section 7.1.2). The time consumption of a solution is measured by purely computing the running time of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) to generate the solution. The startup time of the JVM and the time to generate the input feature model and the optimization problem instance are not considered. For example, the time consumption of a GAFES solution only comprises the running time of all steps described in Algorithm 1, i.e., the running time of population initialization and genetic iterations. Each genetic iteration is composed of chromosome selection, crossover, mutation, replacement, fitness evaluation, and our repair operator called FesTransform. To guarantee precision, we used Java’s System.nanoTime() to capture the start and stop time of GAFES and the other algorithms. The scalability of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) was evaluated by measuring how the time consumption of each algorithm increased as the feature models increased in size. Based on a statistical analysis of the time consumption of each algorithm to solve for feature selections on different size feature models, we evaluated and compared the scalability of the three algorithms. An algorithm was considered more scalable if the rate of increase in solving time as it was fed larger and larger feature models was lower than another algorithm.

We used solution optimality and time consumption as our dependent variables. ... Optimality is defined as the ratio of (Approximation Answer/Optimal Answer), reflecting how close an algorithm's solution is to the true optimum. Here, the "Approximation Answer" represents the total value of a solution generated by an approximation algorithm (e.g., GAFES or FCF + M-HEU). The "Optimal Answer" is derived from the total value of a solution produced by FCF + BBLP, as it is an exact technique. For example, if for the same optimization problem (identical feature model, resource constraints, and optimization target), GAFES achieves an approximate solution with a total value of 90, and FCF + BBLP yields an optimal solution with a total value of 100, then the GAFES solution's optimality is 90%. However, since finding exact solutions is NP-hard, applying FCF+BBLP to large feature models (e.g., 500 or more features) is not practical. Thus, for large feature models (number of features ≥ 500), we adopted the test pattern generation technique by Akbar et al. (2001) to create random optimization problem instances where the optimal answer was known (Section 7.1.2). This measurement excludes the JVM startup time and the time spent generating the input feature model and the optimization problem instance. Each genetic iteration comprises chromosome selection, crossover, mutation, replacement, fitness evaluation, and our FesTransform repair operator. For precise timing, we used Java’s System.nanoTime() to record the start and stop times for GAFES and the other algorithms. The scalability of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) was evaluated by observing how their time consumption increased as the feature models grew in size. Based on a statistical analysis of each algorithm's time to solve for feature selections across different size feature models, we compared their scalability. text: Software product line (SPL) development is a new approach to software engineering which aims at the development of a whole range of products. However, as long as SPL can be useful, there are many challenges regarding the use of that approach. One of the main problems which hinders the adoption of software product line (SPL) is the complexity regarding product management. In that context, we can remark the scoping problem. One of the existent ways to deal with scoping is the product portfolio scoping (PPS). PPS aims to define the products that should be developed as well as their key features. In general, that approach is driven by marketing aspects, like cost of the product and customer satisfaction. Defining a product portfolio by using the many different available aspects is a NP-hard problem.

text: In our previous work [11], we presented an initial proposal to solve the feature model selection problem – and thus supporting PPS – by combining NSGA-II algorithm [12] with Mamdani fuzzy inference systems [13] (hybrid approach). The proposal in our previous work had three main drawbacks: (i) The previous proposal has a severe associated construct validity threat, which is due to the difficulty to obtain from SPLs the required data to run our approach; (ii) We only used a “toy” example to validate our approach and only class level correlation between features and assets was used; (iii) We did not conducted any statistical analysis of the results returned by the NSGA-II algorithm, as suggested by Arcuri and Briand [14]. Therefore, herein we put forward an extension of our previous work, which focused on improving the aforementioned issues.

text: The study consisted of three different IVM tasks: identification of variability (Task 1), instantiation of variability (Task 2) and change of variability (Task 3). Task 1 and 2 were performed in Phase 1 and Task 3 was addressed in Phase 2. In the following we describe these three tasks. _Task 1: Identification of variability. Each team received as an input three specifications from the domestic appliances product family (e.g. microwave ovens). These specifications differed across teams, that is, variability models were managed in the project across teams. Initially, the participants in each team were asked to review the specifications and identify variation points and variants. The identification of variability had to be issue-based, that is, the students had to create issues for the variants (see Section 2.1.4). Afterwards the students had to construct a variability model, that is, variation points, variants and their relationships. Additionally, the students were asked to add the captured rationale. From each team, we expected the output of a variability model (similar to Fig. 3) enriched with rationale containing one to two variation points and 5–10 variants. In current SPLE practice, when transitioning from single system development to SPL-based development, domain experts identify variability by analyzing legacy specifications (John and Dorr, 2003). In particular, a domain expert decides on variability after discussing possible variations with the relevant stakeholders. Based on the decisions, the domain expert then constructs the variability model. Task 1 was based on this practice: We asked the subjects to elicit variability by reviewing the specifications, creating issues on variability, making decisions and constructing the variability model. _Task 2: Instantiation of variability model. The students were asked to instantiate their variability models developed in Task 1. For each team, we assigned six different product instantiations. As input for each product instantiation, teams were given additional criteria specifications consisting of textual description of product criteria. The students were required to add criteria by reviewing the specification and create a justification matrix (similar to Table 2) for each product instantiation. In practice, an application engineer would evaluate variants against product specific quality concerns (or criteria) in order to instantiate a variation point. Task 2 is based on this practice, because the students are asked to instantiate variation points by creating justification matrices. _Task 3: Change variability model. Each team was provided with a change request specification to add or deleting a variant to the variation points obtained from Task 1. An example of such a change request was: “Change the variability model by assuming that you have new variant XXX (e.g. Sensor Cooking for the Cooking model in Fig. 3). Also justify your changes”. Students were also provided with the rationale captured in Task 1. As Phase 1 and Phase 2 used different teams, students in Task 3 did not get the variability model created by them in Task 1. Moreover, they obtained a different variability model created by other students in Task 1. The students were asked to evaluate the change requests using a justification matrix and change variability models by updating rationale (see Section 2.1.5). In current SPLE practice, domain engineers change variability models to address the change requests from customers, application engineers and other domain engineers. Here, a domain engineer together with relevant stakeholders would decide on the changes in variability by evaluating various alternatives (similar to Task 3). Additionally, the engineer should be able to reason about these changes with his manager. The three tasks were performed by all the 258 students participating in the experiment. The participation of the students was voluntary and they were informed that they would be observed. During the sample selection we considered ethical issues (in the context of student projects described by Singer and Vinson (2002)). The participation of the students was voluntary. The students did not get any special credit points. The participants were informed that they would be observed.

This research involved three distinct Issue-based Variability Management (IVM) tasks: Task 1 focused on identifying variability, Task 2 on instantiating variability, and Task 3 on changing variability. The initial two tasks were executed during Phase 1, while Task 3 was conducted during Phase 2. Detailed descriptions of these tasks follow:

*   **Task 1: Variability Identification.** Each team was provided with three unique specifications from a domestic appliance product family (e.g., microwave ovens). These specifications varied between teams, signifying that different teams managed distinct variability models within the project. Initially, team members were required to analyze the specifications to pinpoint variation points and their associated variants. This identification process was issue-based, meaning students had to create issues for each variant. Following this, participants constructed a variability model, outlining variation points, variants, and their interrelationships, and also incorporated the underlying rationale. The expected deliverable from each team was a variability model (similar to Fig. 3), enhanced with rationale and containing 1-2 variation points and 5-10 variants. This task simulated the industrial practice in SPLE where domain experts analyze existing specifications and consult with stakeholders to define variability, subsequently building the variability model.

*   **Task 2: Variability Model Instantiation.** Students were tasked with instantiating the variability models they had developed in Task 1. Each team was given six different product instantiations. For each instantiation, additional specifications detailing product criteria textually were provided. Students needed to incorporate these criteria by reviewing the specifications and then create a justification matrix (akin to Table 2) for each product instantiation. This task replicated the real-world function of an application engineer who assesses variants against specific quality criteria to instantiate a variation point.

*   **Task 3: Variability Model Change.** Each team received a change request to either add or remove a variant from the variation points established in Task 1. An example of such a request was: "Modify the variability model by adding a new variant XXX (e.g., Sensor Cooking for the Cooking model in Fig. 3). Also, provide justification for your changes." Students were also given access to the rationale previously captured in Task 1. As separate teams were involved in Phase 1 and Phase 2, students in Task 3 did not work with their own previously created variability model; instead, they received a variability model from another team from Task 1. Their assignment involved evaluating the change requests using a justification matrix and then modifying the variability models by updating the rationale. This task mirrored the role of domain engineers in SPLE, who modify variability models based on change requests from customers or other engineers, evaluating alternatives and justifying decisions to management.

All 258 students participating in the experiment completed these three tasks. Their participation was voluntary, and they were informed that their activities would be observed. Ethical considerations relevant to student projects, as detailed by Singer and Vinson (2002), were taken into account during sample selection. No special academic credit was awarded for participation.

All 258 students participating in the experiment performed these three tasks. Their participation was voluntary, and they were informed that they would be observed. During the sample selection process, ethical considerations, as described by Singer and Vinson (2002) in the context of student projects, were observed. No special credit points were awarded to the students for their participation.

5. This study involved three distinct Issue-based Variability Management (IVM) tasks: variability identification (Task 1), variability instantiation (Task 2), and variability change (Task 3). Tasks 1 and 2 were conducted in Phase 1, and Task 3 in Phase 2. These tasks are described in detail below:

*   **Task 1: Variability Identification.** Each team was given three differing specifications from the domestic appliance product family (e.g., microwave ovens) as input, with specifications varying across teams, indicating distributed variability model management. Participants first reviewed the specifications to identify variation points and variants. This identification was issue-based, requiring students to create issues for each variant. Following this, students constructed a variability model, including variation points, variants, and their relationships, and appended the captured rationale. Each team was expected to deliver a rationale-enriched variability model (akin to Fig. 3) containing 1-2 variation points and 5-10 variants. This task mirrored common SPLE practice where domain experts identify variability from legacy specifications and stakeholder discussions, subsequently building the variability model.

*   **Task 2: Variability Model Instantiation.** Students were directed to instantiate the variability models they had developed in Task 1. Each team was assigned six different product instantiations, and for each, received additional textual specifications describing the product criteria. Students were required to incorporate these criteria by reviewing the specifications and creating a justification matrix (similar to Table 2) for each product instantiation. This task simulated the practical role of an application engineer who evaluates variants against product-specific quality concerns to instantiate a variation point.

*   **Task 3: Variability Model Change.** Each team received a change request specification to either add or remove a variant from the variation points established in Task 1. An example was: “Change the variability model by assuming a new variant XXX (e.g., Sensor Cooking for the Cooking model in Fig. 3). Also, justify your changes.” Students also had access to the rationale captured in Task 1. Since Phase 1 and Phase 2 utilized different teams, students in Task 3 did not use their own variability model from Task 1; instead, they were given a variability model created by another team. They were asked to evaluate the change requests using a justification matrix and modify the variability models by updating the rationale. This task reflected the real-world practice of domain engineers modifying variability models in response to change requests from various stakeholders, evaluating alternatives, and justifying the decisions to managers.

All 258 students participating in the experiment completed these three tasks. Their participation was voluntary, and they were informed that they would be observed. During the sample selection, ethical considerations in the context of student projects, as described by Singer and Vinson (2002), were taken into account. No special credit points were awarded for student participation.

6. The study incorporated three distinct IVM tasks: identifying variability (Task 1), instantiating variability (Task 2), and changing variability (Task 3). Phase 1 covered Tasks 1 and 2, while Task 3 was addressed in Phase 2. These tasks are detailed below:

*   **Task 1: Identification of variability.** Each team was provided with three unique specifications from the domestic appliances product family (e.g., microwave ovens) as input. These specifications varied across teams, meaning variability models were managed individually by teams within the project. Initially, participants in each team were asked to review the specifications and identify variation points and variants. This identification had to be issue-based, requiring students to generate issues for each variant. Subsequently, students constructed a variability model, detailing variation points, variants, and their relationships, and added the captured rationale. Each team was expected to produce a rationale-enriched variability model (similar to Fig. 3) containing 1-2 variation points and 5-10 variants. This task was designed to emulate current SPLE practice where domain experts identify variability from legacy specifications and through discussions with stakeholders, then construct the variability model.

*   **Task 2: Instantiation of variability model.** Students were instructed to instantiate the variability models they had developed in Task 1. Six different product instantiations were assigned to each team. For each product instantiation, teams received additional textual criteria specifications. Students were required to incorporate these criteria by reviewing the specification and creating a justification matrix (similar to Table 2) for each product instantiation. This task reflected the practical scenario of an application engineer evaluating variants against product-specific quality concerns (or criteria) to instantiate a variation point.

*   **Task 3: Change variability model.** Each team received a change request specification to add or delete a variant from the variation points obtained from Task 1. An example of such a change request was: “Modify the variability model by assuming a new variant XXX (e.g., Sensor Cooking for the Cooking model in Fig. 3). Also, justify your changes.” Students were also provided with the rationale captured in Task 1. As Phase 1 and Phase 2 involved different teams, students in Task 3 did not work with their own variability model from Task 1; instead, they received a different variability model created by other students in Task 1. They were asked to evaluate the change requests using a justification matrix and modify the variability models by updating the rationale. This task was based on the current SPLE practice where domain engineers modify variability models to address change requests from customers, application engineers, and other domain engineers. Here, a domain engineer, along with relevant stakeholders, would decide on the changes in variability by evaluating various alternatives (similar to Task 3). Additionally, the engineer should be able to justify these changes to their manager.

All 258 students participating in the experiment performed these three tasks. Their participation was voluntary, and they were informed that they would be observed. During the sample selection process, ethical issues (in the context of student projects described by Singer and Vinson (2002)) were considered. The participation of the students was voluntary, and they did not receive any special credit points. The participants were informed that they would be observed.

text: D1: Neutral mentors. In order to perform the study, four neutral mentors were selected by the faculty teaching the course. The mentors had one-year teaching experience in software engineering. These mentors were trained in IVM by two colleagues of the author. The rationale behind the usage of mentors is to avoid interaction of the authors with the participants of the study (this prevented the authors to manipulate the participants of the study). Yin (2003) and Lee (1989) also emphasize the use of neutral mentors. D2: Assignment of participants to mentors. The 258 participants were divided randomly into four training groups consisting of about 60–70 participants. This was our high-level team creation. A trainer was assigned to each of the training groups, thus creating a one-to-one mapping between trainer and training group. The use of random sampling ensured a heterogeneous distribution of participants in each of the training groups (see SQ2). Each of the training group was decomposed into smaller groups to obtain fine granular teams (see D5). Issue-based variability management was taught to participants by the individual trainers. Overall, nineteen sessions were conducted to teach the rationale modeling approach to the participants. D3: Setting and unit of analysis with embedded design. Fig. 5 shows the organizational setup used for the quasi-experiment. To study the interaction of participants with IVM we considered a team of participants performing issue-based variability management as a unit of analysis. As the study included several instances of unit of analysis, our setting has an embedded design. The sample performing variability management in the project is the Setting. The setting consists of several objects of Unit of Analysis (which is a team performing issue-based variability management). These Units are observed by the Mentors. The participants are Actors (between 2 and 22) that perform issue-based variability management which is the unit of analysis of the experiment (see Fig. 6). The top-level Issue-based variability management is decomposed into three sub use cases Variability identification, Variability instantiation and Variability evolution. The first two optional sub use cases were included in Phase 1 and third optional sub use case was included in Phase 2. Both unit of analysis and embedded design are often used in case studies. Embedding a unit of analysis in the quasi-experimental setting: (i) enabled us to focus on the individual points of interests and (ii) additionally helped us to perform observations for collecting qualitative evidence. D4: The two phase approach. As instantiation and evolution of variability models are two different activities, we planned to analyze these activities separately in two phases (Phase 1 and Phase 2), which were performed chronologically one after the other. The two phase separation also helps us to study the reuse of rationale during the evaluation of ERP, that is, rationale captured during variability identification within a team in Phase 1 was used by a different team in Phase 2. The tasks for the two phases were already specified in Section 4.2. The students worked within the TU Munich campus. The participants worked on dedicated workstations throughout the project. This allows the mentors to observe the teams personally. In Phase 2, the participants did not have dedicated workstations; in fact, they worked at various distributed locations throughout campus. As a result, the mentors were not able to observe the students personally. D5: Creating teams. We replicated the unit of analysis several times with different team sizes and participants. Replications are considered to be critical for obtaining strong empirical evidence (Amir and Sharon, 1990). To realize a unit of analysis in Phase 1, we spitted the four high-level groups into low-level teams using convenience sampling. We provided nineteen time slots, with a mentor assigned to each slot. Each participant was asked to register for a slot that corresponds to their mentor from the training session. The number of participants in a slot was fixed (15–22 participants). In some slots, mentors further divided the participants randomly into smaller teams (team size < 6). In some other slots, mentors sampled large teams (8 ≤ team size ≤ 13). Due to problems with room availability, in some situations all students registered for a slot were used as a team (team size ≥ 15). Here, team size was very large. To ensure the heterogeneity of the participants in the various teams we used so called exercise teams in Phase 2. An exercise team was randomly created at the beginning of the software engineering course for performing the assignments of the software engineering lecture. In the following, we summarize teams that were created in the two phases (see Table 4): • In Phase 1, 42 teams were created with a team size between 2 and 22. The reason for the large number of teams was to study the impact of team size on the quality of instantiation. • In Phase 2, we defined 50 teams consisting of 2–6 students. Having smaller team sizes compared with Phase 1 enabled us to study the reuse of rationale closely. Domain and application engineering were separated in each of the team. All decisions were made using the issue-based communication. D6: Variables measured. The independent and dependent variables, the corresponding study question and the variability management activity are summarized in Table 5. No variables were defined for measuring SQ2, because it was evaluated based on qualitative data. We validated how the rationale captured by a team in Phase 1 is reused (ERP) in a different team of Phase 2. Therefore, Quality of rationale is measured during variability identification and Reuse of rationale is measured during variability evolution. Other variables such as Motivation of participants, Team size and Quality of instantiation were measured Phase 1.

2. **4.4. Data Collection and Coding**
This section describes the methods for collecting and encoding data in this study.
**4.4.1. Direct Observations by Mentors**

Mentors personally observed all participants throughout Phase 1, ensuring continuous observation of each team by at least one mentor. Their primary role was to record qualitative data concerning participant interactions with IVM. Specifically, mentors monitored how issue-based argumentation structures were developed, how decisions were reached, and to what extent rationale was reused. Mentors used a five-point linear scale (from Q7, where 1 denoted highest motivation and 5 lowest) to rate individual participant motivation. Motivation assessments occurred in two stages: during training sessions and throughout Phase 1. A student's total motivation score was derived by averaging their motivation levels from both phases. This approach to motivation assessment is a modified version of Briand's technique (Briand et al., 2001), which also uses a five-point linear scale but directly queries students about their motivation post-experiment. Our modification involved utilizing tutors for the assessment and employing a two-stage evaluation process. Mentors assessed individual motivation during both training and experimentation (Phase 1), and the mean of these assessments was computed. Recognizing the complexity of verbalizing motivation, factors such as participant enthusiasm, proactive questioning during training, focus during tasks, and active teamwork were considered. Before the training sessions, the four mentors received brief instruction on maintaining consistent motivation assessment. Practically, all mentors shared a unified understanding of motivation. Motivation was not measured in Phase 2 due as direct observations by mentors were not conducted.
**4.4.2. Analysis of Artifacts**

Collected artifacts were analyzed to quantify the quality of instantiation, the quality of rationale, and the reuse of rationale. A five-point linear scale, ranging from 1 (best quality) to 5 (worst quality) (refer to Q8 in Appendix A), was used for these measurements. To conduct these measurements, we gathered the rationales from each team and compared them against a reference baseline. This baseline, provided by our industrial partner, contained variability models, including justification matrices for identification, instantiation, and evolution (e.g., Tables 1–3). Essentially, the reference baseline comprised expert-derived justification matrices. The terms "quality of instantiation," "quality of rationale," and "reuse of rationale" refer to the overall quality of the justification matrices created or reused by a team. Each team in Phase 1 underwent an assessment for its quality of instantiation. Similarly, each team in Phase 2 was assessed for the quality of rationale and the reuse of rationale. Unlike Phase 2, rationale in Phase 1 was captured and reused within the same team during variability model instantiation, thus we did not quantify rationale reuse in Phase 1. Furthermore, qualitative evidence regarding rationale reuse during product instantiation was gathered (see R4).

*   **Assessing Rationale Quality and Instantiation Quality:** To evaluate rationale quality, we first verified the realism and logic of stakeholder assessments and their arguments (using ++, +, 0, −, and −−). We then confirmed the logical consistency of decisions, for instance, checking if a decision incorporated the assessments from the justification matrix. Rationale that passed these initial checks received a "Fair" (level 3) assessment. If a justification matrix failed these checks, the rationale was graded "Low" or "Very low" depending on the documented information. A positive assessment required the justification matrix to contain information closely aligning with the reference baseline. To determine a team's overall assessment, the mean was calculated. For example, if a team documented three justification matrices during variability instantiation (as shown in Table 3), their overall quality of instantiation was the average of the individual quality scores for those three matrices.

*   **Measuring Reuse of Rationale:** Consider two versions of a justification matrix: an "old" one from variability identification and a "new" one from variability evolution. Reuse of rationale is defined as the direct re-employment of information common to both matrices (e.g., shared assessments or criteria). Our measurement process for reuse of rationale was as follows: First, reused rationale information was identified by extracting commonalities between the old (captured during Phase 1 variability identification) and new (Phase 2 variability evolution) justification matrices. Subsequently, we evaluated if the reuse was sensible (by considering participants' arguments for reusing assessments). A pair of justification matrices passing this check received an assessment of at least "Fair." Pairs failing the test were graded "Low" or "Very low." "High" and "Very high" assessments were assigned when the reuse was consistent with the reference justification matrices provided by our industrial partners.
**4.4.3. Questionnaire for the Sample**

At the conclusion of Phase 2, participants were given a set of questions (Q1–Q6 in Appendix A) and asked to complete the questionnaire. The questions were predominantly open-ended, allowing respondents to express their views verbally. Consequently, data collection via the questionnaire was primarily qualitative. Q6 was structured as a closed question.

Specifically, they focused on how issue-based argumentation structures were built, how decisions were made, and whether and how rationale was reused. Individual participant motivation was assessed by mentors using a five-point linear scale (Q7), where 1 indicated highest and 5 (worst) lowest motivation. Motivation assessment occurred in two stages: during training sessions and during Phase 1. A student's overall motivation was calculated as the mean of these two assessments. This approach to motivation assessment is a modified version of Briand's technique (Briand et al., 2001), which also uses a five-point linear scale but directly asks students for self-assessment post-experiment. Our modification involved using tutors for assessment and employing a two-stage evaluation process. Mentors evaluated individual motivation during both training and Phase 1 experimentation, and the mean of these assessments constituted the final score. Recognizing the challenge of verbalizing motivation, several aspects were considered: participant enthusiasm, willingness to ask insightful questions during training, focus during training/project work, and teamwork (active interaction with others). Prior to training sessions, the four mentors received brief instruction on consistent motivation assessment. Pragmatically, mentors shared a common understanding of motivation. Motivation was not measured in Phase 2 due to the absence of direct mentor observations.

"Quality of instantiation," "quality of rationale," and "reuse of rationale" refer to the overall quality of justification matrices developed or reused by a team. Each team in Phase 1 was assessed for its quality of instantiation. Similarly, each team in Phase 2 received an assessment for the quality of rationale and reuse of rationale. Unlike Phase 2, rationale was captured and reused within the same team during variability model instantiation in Phase 1, thus rationale reuse was not quantitatively measured in Phase 1. text: This paper provides three contributions to the study of multi-step configuration for SPLs. First, we present a formal model of multi-step SPL configuration and map this model to constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). Second, we show how solutions to these SPL configuration problems can be automati- cally derived with a constraint solver by mapping them to CSPs. Moreover, we show how feature model changes can be mapped to our approach in a multi-step scenario by using feature model drift. Third, we present empirical results demonstrating that our CSP-based reasoning technique can scale to SPL models with hundreds of features and multiple configuration steps.
paraphrases: This paper offers three key contributions to the field of multi-step configuration for Software Product Lines (SPLs). Firstly, it introduces a formal model for multi-step SPL configuration, which is then mapped to Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs). Secondly, the paper illustrates how solutions to these SPL configuration challenges can be automatically generated using a constraint solver by framing them as CSPs, and additionally, it demonstrates how changes in feature models can be incorporated into our multi-step framework via feature model drift. Lastly, empirical findings are presented, confirming the scalability of our CSP-based reasoning technique for SPL models encompassing hundreds of features and multiple configuration stages.

The paper makes three significant contributions to the understanding of multi-step configuration in SPLs. Our initial contribution is a formal model for multi-step SPL configuration, which we translate into Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs). Our second contribution demonstrates how to automatically solve these SPL configuration problems using a constraint solver by transforming them into CSPs; furthermore, we illustrate how feature model modifications can be integrated into our multi-step approach through the concept of feature model drift. Finally, the third contribution consists of empirical evidence showcasing that our CSP-based reasoning method is scalable for SPL models featuring hundreds of features and numerous configuration steps.

text: In this paper, we propose similarity-based prioritization to prioritize the products. The goal is to increase the inter- action coverage of the SPL under test as fast as possible over time. With our algorithm, we hope to reduce the time re- quired to find defects, and thus to reduce the overall testing e↵ort. In our approach, we select the product with maxi- mum number of features to be the first one to test (a.k.a. allyesconfig [10]). We select the following product that has the minimum similarity with the previous product. Then, we select the next product that has the minimum similar- ity with the previous two products. The process continues until all products are ordered. The general idea of similarity- based testing is not new, Henard et al. combine the sampling with prioritization [15], but we adopt it by calculating the similarity between the products di↵erently. In addition, the input of our approach can be all the valid configurations if the size of SPL is small, a set of configurations has been sampled using sampling algorithms, or a set of configura- tions has been given by domain experts.
paraphrases: This paper presents a similarity-based prioritization method for products, aiming to rapidly increase the interaction coverage of the Software Product Line (SPL) under test. Our algorithm seeks to decrease the time spent on defect discovery and, consequently, the overall testing effort. The process begins by selecting the product with the most features (referred to as allyesconfig [10]) as the initial test case. Subsequent products are chosen based on having the least similarity to the previously selected product(s), continuing until all products are ordered. While the concept of similarity-based testing isn't novel (e.g., Henard et al. combined sampling with prioritization [15]), our method distinguishes itself through a unique approach to calculating product similarity. Furthermore, our approach can utilize various inputs: all valid configurations for small SPLs, a sample of configurations generated by sampling algorithms, or a set of configurations provided by domain experts.

We introduce a similarity-based prioritization technique for products in this paper, with the objective of maximizing the interaction coverage of the Software Product Line (SPL) under examination in the shortest possible time. Our algorithm is designed to expedite defect detection and, by extension, minimize the total testing effort. Our method involves first testing the product with the highest number of features (known as allyesconfig [10]). The next product chosen for testing is the one that exhibits the lowest similarity to the preceding product. This pattern continues, with each subsequent product selected having the least similarity to all previously chosen products, until all products are prioritized. While the core concept of similarity-based testing is not new, and works like Henard et al. [15] have integrated sampling with prioritization, our innovation lies in our distinct method for calculating product similarity. Additionally, our approach is flexible regarding input, accepting either all valid configurations (for smaller SPLs), configurations derived from sampling algorithms, or expert-provided configurations.

To encompass and replicate these scenarios, our experimental approach was as follows: during test execution, if a tester needed to investigate a potential product defect, they would halt the test using the Test-Watcher and consult the experiment conductor, who possessed prior knowledge of the test suite's issues. This particular scope was chosen because participants were allocated two hours to complete two test suites, one for each product, resulting in a total of 12 test cases. Previous experimental runs had demonstrated that this number of tests was appropriate for the given time. ... The TestWatcher allowed us to simulate a simplified test environment. As mentioned in Section 2, when a tester pauses a test case to investigate whether an observed behavior is a product defect or a test problem, their subsequent actions vary based on the environment's setup. To account for and simulate these diverse situations, we implemented the following strategy in both experiments: during test execution, if a tester needed to ascertain if a product defect was present, they would use the Test-Watcher to pause the execution and seek guidance from the experiment conductor, who was already familiar with the issues in the test suites. text: Task 1 - Methodological approach: The members of group 1 had to design a building automation system with a Timer component, a light sensor and a roller shutter controller that resolves conflicting behaviors between the timer component and the light sensor component. Task 1 - Clone and own approach: The Matlab/Simulink group had to perform the same task and created an initial model from given diagrams. - Task 2 - Methodological approach: Task 2 introduced variability to the base model and therefore started the actual creation of the product family. The Timer component should become an optional component and had to be replaced by a wind sensor for the second variant. Moreover a second light sensor had to be added and both products had to be instantiated. Here the main difficulty lied in creating the initial decision model and the corresponding constraints. - Task 2 - Clone and own approach: Group 2 had to follow the clone and own approach in that the participants copied the initial Matlab/Simulink model and created the new instance through adapting that model for the second variant. - Task 3 - Methodological approach: The third product had to support a timer component and two light sensors. Therefore the Matlab model was similar to the initial product and reused existing elements. It included minor changes to the conflict resolution between Timer and light sensors. All products had to be instantiated. This task focused on reusing product line infrastructure artifacts, so the effort could be compared to the clone and own approach. - Task 3 - Clone and own approach: Group 2 copied one of the existing models and manually derived a third variant. - Task 4 - Methodological approach: In this task a temperature dependent roof light had to be added to all existing products as a common feature. The task implied a change in the Matlab model, the Decision model was largely left unchanged. Again all instances of the model had to be created. This task mainly focused on maintenance issues for an existing product family. - Task 4 - Clone and own approach: The members of group two had to update all models of the product line.

text: We provide a task of each kind for each product line, for a total of four distinct tasks, as discussed next. Task 1 - New requirement for Best Lap. The new requirement for Best Lap is similar to our motivating Scenario 1: There are two methods of feature ARENA that contain conditional statements forbidding negative scores. So, to accomplish the task, besides changing the totalScore assignment, participants should remove or rewrite these conditional statements (see one of them in method setScore of Figure 1). To reach them, participants need to consider interprocedural dependencies. That is, there are cross-feature depen- dencies from the maintenance point to two conditional statements, each one in a different method. In case Emergo is available, the participant should use it to identify the cross-feature dependencies between totalScore and the rest of the code. Otherwise, the partic- ipant is free to use standard tools like find/replace and highlighting. This setup also holds for the subsequent tasks. Task 2 - New requirement for MobileMedia. The task for MobileMedia is conceptually similar in the sense that participants should change a variable assignment, follow cross-feature depen- dencies, and update conditional statements (here, only one if state- ment). However, in contrast to Task 1, where the method call depth to reach the two conditional statements is 1, here the call depth is 2. That is, from the maintenance point, we need to follow two method calls to reach the if statement. Task 3 - Unused variable in Best Lap. In Best Lap, we asked participants to fix unused-variable warnings for two variables: tires and xP. We introduced the bugs ourself by removing correct #ifdef directives around the variable declarations. We can solve all unused- variable tasks by following intraprocedural dependencies only, but they typically require investigating code of different features. To accomplish the tasks, we ask participants to put a correct #ifdef around the variable declarations. The variables tires and xP are inside methods with 147 and 216 source lines of code, respectively. Task 4 - Unused variable in MobileMedia. Again the Mobile- Media task is conceptually similar to the Best Lap task. Participants should fix the unused-variable warning of numberOfViews and albumMusic. The two variables are placed in shorter methods when compared to Task 3: they have 49 and 71 lines of code. Overall, the tasks for both product lines have similarities, but they are not equivalent. Actually, these differences—methods size, method call depths to reach the impacted feature, and number of conditionals to change—between tasks for both product lines help us to better analyze the effects of our two treatments and is properly controlled by our experiment design, as we shall see in Section 4.5. Finally, we designed warmup tasks on a toy product line so that participants could learn how to use Emergo at the start of the experi- ment. We performed warmup tasks together in a class context but did not evaluate their results.

Participants could use Emergo to identify cross-feature dependencies if available; otherwise, standard tools like find/replace were permitted. This framework applied to all subsequent tasks. Task 2, a new requirement for MobileMedia, involved similar modifications to a variable assignment, cross-feature dependency tracing, and updating a conditional statement, but with a deeper call depth of two compared to Task 1's one. Task 4, another unused variable task for MobileMedia, was conceptually similar to Task 3, requiring participants to fix warnings for 'numberOfViews' and 'albumMusic,' but these variables were in shorter methods (49 and 71 lines). While the tasks across both product lines shared similarities, their differences—method size, call depth to affected features, and number of conditionals—were intentionally designed and controlled to better analyze the impact of our experimental treatments. Before the main experiment, participants completed un-evaluated warmup tasks on a toy product line to familiarize themselves with Emergo.

text: The tasks were embedded within an online questionnaire. On each model ten questions were asked, examining whether specific configurations of Skoda Yeti are allowed according to the model. These questions can be described as surface-level tasks which measure comprehension of models more directly than deep-level tasks, which require participants to work with the models in a usage context [23]. For our research goal of checking the comprehensibility of a relatively new language, surface-level model comprehension tasks are most appropriate. The participants were presented with the model and one question at a time. They had to choose between the following answers: Correct, Wrong, Cannot be answered from model, I don’t know. After answering a question, the participant proceeded to the next question, but could not return to previous questions. This way we could measure the time needed to answer an individual question. The questions used in the experiment appear in the appendix.

Given our objective of evaluating the comprehensibility of a new language, surface-level comprehension tasks were ideal. Participants viewed one model and one question at a time, selecting from "Correct," "Wrong," "Cannot be answered from model," or "I don’t know." Progressing to the next question was mandatory after answering, with no option to revisit previous ones, which allowed us to measure the time taken for each individual response. The complete list of questions is available in the appendix.

These questions represented surface-level tasks, which assess direct model understanding, unlike deep-level tasks that demand interaction with models in a usage scenario [23]. Once an answer was submitted, they moved to the next question without the ability to return, enabling us to record the time spent on each question. The full set of experimental questions can be found in the appendix.

text: During the experiment, subjects have to update logistic systems derived from the Egemin’s SPL. The goal of an update is to bring a system from its current (as-is) state to the expected new state (to-be). To update the system a subject has to stop and start relevant services, and remove, replace and add resources (.Net assemblies and executables). During an update, either the architecture-centric approach or the baseline approach is used. The updates are performed on variants of the Kimberly Clark (KC) logistic system. The system is installed in the standard location (Program Files/Egemin) and is operational. The KC logistic system consists of an E’tricc service, an E’wms service, an E’pia service (logistic platform), and the associated clients (see Figure 1). For the purpose of the experiments we have defined three kinds of the update scenarios: - S0 Learning scenario kind - these are easy scenarios which require simple changes that affect one of the subsystems. The aim of the learning scenarios is to familiarize subjects with the system under update and the usage of our tool. - SA Simple scenario kind - in these scenarios, the E’wms or E’tricc services and corresponding client screens are object of the update. The number of changes is limited. To perform the correct update two processes must be restarted. - SB Complex scenario kind - in these scenarios, the whole logistic system is affected by the update. Most of the running processes have to be restarted to perform the update correctly. The concrete scenarios were prepared by Egemin’s senior architect, who did not participate in the experiment as a subject. The proposed scenarios are similar to the updates Egemin integrators perform in practice. We asked the subjects to perform two updates for each scenario kind, one with the architecture-centric approach, the other with the baseline approach. We prepared pairs of similar scenarios to ensure objectivity and avoid interference between treatments.
paraphrases: In this experiment, participants were tasked with updating logistic systems originating from Egemin's SPL, aiming to transition them from their current "as-is" state to a desired "to-be" state. This process involved stopping and starting services, as well as managing resources like .Net assemblies and executables. Updates were conducted using either an architecture-centric or a baseline approach on variants of the operational Kimberly Clark (KC) logistic system, which is installed in a standard location and comprises E’tricc, E’wms, and E’pia services, along with their clients. We designed three types of update scenarios: S0 (Learning) for familiarization with simple, subsystem-specific changes and tool usage; SA (Simple) involving limited changes to E’wms or E’tricc services and their clients, requiring two process restarts; and SB (Complex) affecting the entire logistic system and necessitating most running processes to be restarted. These scenarios, crafted by an Egemin senior architect not involved as a subject, mirrored real-world updates. To maintain objectivity and prevent treatment interference, subjects performed two updates per scenario type—one with each approach—using paired, similar scenarios.

The experiment required subjects to upgrade logistic systems derived from Egemin's SPL, moving them from their current configuration to a specified new one. This upgrade process entailed stopping and restarting necessary services, along with adding, removing, or replacing resources such as .Net assemblies and executables. Updates utilized either an architecture-centric or a baseline methodology and were applied to different versions of the operational Kimberly Clark (KC) logistic system, installed in its default location and consisting of E’tricc, E’wms, and E’pia services, plus their respective clients. For the experiment, three update scenario types were developed: S0 (Learning), which were easy scenarios with minor subsystem changes, intended to acquaint subjects with the system and tool; SA (Simple), focusing on E’wms or E’tricc services and client screens, with limited changes and requiring two process restarts; and SB (Complex), impacting the entire logistic system and necessitating most process restarts. Egemin's senior architect, who did not participate as a subject, created these scenarios to reflect typical updates performed in practice. To ensure impartiality and avoid confounding factors, participants completed two updates for each scenario type—one using the architecture-centric approach and the other with the baseline approach—using carefully matched pairs of scenarios.

text: The family-based mutant-detection methodology introduced in Sect. 3.3 allows for measuring the effectiveness of different kinds of PL analysis strategies in general, and sample-based PL testing in particular. To this end, we first derive a set of mutants from a PL implementation (cf. Sect. 3.2) using code- mutation operators and mapping-mutation operators . To measure effectiveness for a given sample, we investigate how many of the generated mutants are detectable by at least one test configuration in the sample. As outlined in Algorithm 1, we generate an (abstract) test suite for each mutant contain- ing a set of test cases detecting the mutant. Those test cases are equipped with presence conditions over features denot- ing the set of product configurations on which the test case is able to detect the mutant. After successful termination, our algorithm guarantees that for every product configuration on which a mutant is detectable, at least one respective test case is generated. Hence, this additional information can be used for precisely measuring the mutation-detection score of a given sample.
paraphrases: The family-based mutant-detection methodology, detailed in Section 3.3, enables the evaluation of various Product Line (PL) analysis strategies, especially sample-based PL testing. Our process begins by generating a set of mutants from a PL implementation (as described in Section 3.2) using both code-mutation and mapping-mutation operators. To gauge effectiveness for a specific sample, we determine the number of generated mutants that can be detected by at least one test configuration within that sample. Following Algorithm 1, we create an abstract test suite for each mutant, comprising test cases designed to detect it. These test cases include presence conditions linked to features, indicating the product configurations where the test case can identify the mutant. Upon completion, our algorithm ensures that for any product configuration where a mutant is detectable, a corresponding test case is generated. This detailed information is then utilized to accurately calculate a sample's mutation-detection score.

Section 3.3 introduces a family-based mutant-detection methodology designed to assess the efficacy of diverse Product Line (PL) analysis strategies, with a particular focus on sample-based PL testing. Our approach involves first creating a collection of mutants from a PL implementation (referencing Section 3.2) through the application of code-mutation and mapping-mutation operators. To quantify effectiveness for a given sample, we ascertain how many of these generated mutants are discoverable by at least one test configuration within that sample. As per Algorithm 1, we construct an abstract test suite for each mutant, populated with test cases capable of detecting it. These test cases are augmented with presence conditions over features, specifying the product configurations where a test case can successfully identify the mutant. The algorithm guarantees that, upon successful execution, for every product configuration capable of detecting a mutant, at least one relevant test case is produced. This supplementary data is crucial for precisely determining the mutation-detection score of a particular sample.

text: This quasi-experiment was designed to be performed in two days by two scoping teams in charge of separately scoping the AAL platform as a PL. Group 1 applied treatment 1, which consisted of first using PuLSE-Eco to conduct the scoping process, already taking into consideration the evolution concern, and then applying PLEvo- Scoping; while Group 2 applied treatment 2, which consisted of interweaving the activi- ties of PuLSE-Eco and PLEvo-Scoping. The purpose of treatment 1 was to allow a clear distinction between the results before and after applying PLEvo-Scoping, while the purpose of treatment 2 was to avoid the confounding factor (present in treatment 1) of providing the scoping team with extra time to think about PL scope evolution after applying PuLSE-Eco. This confounding factor would put in doubt whether the obtained benefits were a result of this extra time or a result of the application of PLEvo-Scoping. In addition, the application of PLEvo-Scoping in the two treatments aimed at strength- ening the validity of the results through corroboration. Two days were allocated to each treatment due to time restrictions.
paraphrases: Two scoping teams conducted this two-day quasi-experiment to independently scope the AAL platform as a Product Line. Group 1 followed Treatment 1, initially using PuLSE-Eco for scoping with evolution in mind, then applying PLEvo-Scoping. Group 2 implemented Treatment 2, which integrated PuLSE-Eco and PLEvo-Scoping activities. Treatment 1 aimed to clearly differentiate pre- and post-PLEvo-Scoping results, while Treatment 2 sought to eliminate the confounding factor (present in Treatment 1) of providing additional time for evolution considerations after PuLSE-Eco, which could obscure the true benefits of PLEvo-Scoping. The application of PLEvo-Scoping across both treatments enhanced result validity through corroboration. Each treatment was allotted two days due to time constraints.

This quasi-experiment involved two scoping teams, over two days, independently scoping the AAL platform as a Product Line. Group 1 employed Treatment 1, which entailed first conducting the scoping process with PuLSE-Eco (considering evolution), followed by PLEvo-Scoping. Group 2, on the other hand, used Treatment 2, which involved integrating PuLSE-Eco and PLEvo-Scoping activities concurrently. Treatment 1 was designed to highlight the impact of PLEvo-Scoping by comparing results before and after its application, whereas Treatment 2 aimed to prevent the confounding effect (observed in Treatment 1) of allowing the scoping team extra time to ponder PL scope evolution after using PuLSE-Eco, thereby ensuring that any observed benefits were clearly attributable to PLEvo-Scoping itself. Furthermore, applying PLEvo-Scoping in both treatments helped reinforce the validity of the findings through cross-validation. Time limitations restricted each treatment to two days.

text: we performed initial experiments on two of the feature models (E-shop and WebPortal) and in these initial experiments we discovered that the algorithms (when the (n + 1) approach and direct encoding are used) returned relatively few valid products. This was followed by experiments with two case studies that had realistic values of attributes rather than randomly generated attributes (as used in previous work) and then experiments with the larger randomly generated feature model.

Initial experiments on the E-shop and WebPortal feature models indicated that algorithms, when employing the (n + 1) approach and direct encoding, yielded a relatively small number of valid products. This observation spurred the development of two improvements: a new representation and the 1 + n approach. Following this, we conducted experiments with all six published models. text: First, we evaluate their performance on the Linux kernel bench- mark described earlier in this paper, both in terms of quality and diversity of solutions while varying the evolution targets. We show the average results of 30 runs for each evolution target and each algorithm. We perform first this thorough and detailed study of the Linux kernel in order to give the reader a good sense of what is happening with the two algorithms. We also evaluate the signif- icance of the results obtained by eSATIBEA over those of SATIBEA at four key optimisation snapshots (i.e., the initial, first, middle and last generations of the genetic algorithms). Then, we extend the comparison to the 4 other data sets and study the gain that eSATIBEA brings over SATIBEA according to the evolution targets on every single metric. This broader evaluation will give us a sense of how stable are the algorithms (as they will be used against data sets of different varieties) and how robust our conclusions are.
paraphrases: We first assess their performance on the previously described Linux kernel benchmark, focusing on both solution quality and diversity while altering evolution targets. We present average results from 30 runs for each evolution target and algorithm. This in-depth Linux kernel analysis provides insight into the algorithms' behavior. We also determine the statistical significance of eSATIBEA's results compared to SATIBEA at four critical optimization points (initial, first, middle, and final genetic algorithm generations). Subsequently, we broaden this comparison to include four additional datasets, examining eSATIBEA's advantage over SATIBEA across all metrics for various evolution targets. This comprehensive evaluation helps us gauge the algorithms' stability across diverse datasets and the robustness of our findings.

Initially, we evaluate their performance on the Linux kernel benchmark, as detailed earlier, examining both the quality and diversity of solutions across varying evolution targets. For each evolution target and algorithm, we report the average results from 30 runs. This comprehensive examination of the Linux kernel serves to provide the reader with a clear understanding of how the two algorithms behave. We also analyze the statistical significance of eSATIBEA's results compared to SATIBEA at four key optimization stages: the initial, first, middle, and final generations of the genetic algorithms. Following this, we extend our comparison to four other datasets, investigating the performance improvement eSATIBEA offers over SATIBEA with respect to evolution targets on every metric. This wider assessment will allow us to determine the algorithms' stability when applied to different types of data and the overall robustness of our conclusions.

text: To measure program comprehension, we designed tasks that can only be solved if subjects understand according source code. We used two kinds of tasks: maintenance and static tasks [8]. In maintenance tasks, subjects are instructed to locate/fix a bug, while in static tasks, subjects should examine the structure of the source code. In a previous experiment [10], we found that colors speed up program comprehension only for static tasks, but not in maintenance tasks. Hence, we focused on static tasks, but included few maintenance tasks to control whether our results still hold. All tasks are typical for a maintenance programmer, when she is looking for bugs in certain features and/or files. Altogether, we had 10 tasks: 2 warming up tasks, 6 static tasks, and 2 maintenance tasks. The warming up tasks were designed to let subjects familiarize with the experimental setting and were not analyzed. Regarding static tasks, we had three different types: 1: Identifying all files in which source code of a certain feature was implemented. 2: Locating nested #ifdef statements. 3: Identifying all features that occur in a certain file. For each type, we prepared two tasks. As example, we present the first static task (S1): S1: In which files does feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS occur? For maintenance tasks, we carefully introduced bugs into the source code. Those bugs and according bug descriptions we presented subjects were typical in C programs implementing software in the domain of operating systems, which we made sure by consulting an expert in C and Xenomai. We present the description of the first maintenance task to illustrate them: M1: If the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_ DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) should be un- loaded, a segmentation fault is thrown. The problem occurs, when features CONFIG_XENO_ DRIVERS_CAN and CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_ SJA1000 and CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_ SJA1000_PEAK_DNG are selected.
paraphrases: To assess program comprehension, we devised tasks requiring source code understanding for completion, categorized as maintenance or static tasks [8]. Maintenance tasks involved bug location/fixing, while static tasks focused on source code structure examination. Previous research [10] showed colors improve comprehension only for static tasks, not maintenance. Therefore, we primarily focused on static tasks, including a few maintenance tasks to validate our findings. All tasks simulated typical maintenance programmer activities. We used 10 tasks: 2 warm-up (unanalyzed), 6 static, and 2 maintenance. Static tasks were of three types, each with two instances: identifying files for a feature, locating nested #ifdefs, and identifying features in a file. An example static task (S1) is: "In which files does feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS occur?" For maintenance tasks, we meticulously inserted realistic bugs into C operating system code, validated by a C/Xenomai expert. An example maintenance task (M1) is: "Unloading the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) causes a segmentation fault when CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN, CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000, and CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG features are selected."

Our method for gauging program comprehension involved tasks solvable only through a deep understanding of the relevant source code. We employed two categories of tasks: maintenance and static [8]. Maintenance tasks required participants to identify or rectify a bug, whereas static tasks necessitated an analysis of the source code's structure. A prior experiment [10] indicated that color enhancements only facilitated program comprehension for static tasks, not for maintenance tasks. Consequently, our primary focus was on static tasks, although we incorporated a small number of maintenance tasks to ensure the generalizability of our results. All tasks mimicked scenarios a maintenance programmer might encounter when searching for bugs in specific features or files. In total, we designed 10 tasks: 2 for warming up (excluded from analysis), 6 static tasks, and 2 maintenance tasks. The static tasks comprised three distinct types, each with two instances: 1) pinpointing all files containing the source code for a particular feature; 2) locating nested #ifdef statements; and 3) identifying all features present in a given file. For illustration, static task S1 asked: "In which files does feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS occur?" For the maintenance tasks, we meticulously embedded bugs into the source code, and the corresponding bug descriptions presented to subjects were representative of typical issues in C programs within the operating systems domain, a fact confirmed by consulting an expert in C and Xenomai. As an example, maintenance task M1 stated: "A segmentation fault occurs when attempting to unload the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG), specifically when features CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN, CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000, and CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG are simultaneously selected."

text: In order to evaluate the model difference algorithm, referring to the experiment method of the literature[5], Given two product feature model M1 and M2, we denote expected changes and the detected changes by our approach as Me={<f1, f2, changetype>} and Mr={<f1, f2, changetype>} respectively, where f1 refers to a feature in M1, f2 is the corresponding feature of f1 in M2, and changetype is the type of changes between the two features. The changetype can be unchanged, add, change(rename). ... After the model difference, model merge algorithm can be used to realizing the model merge. We evaluate the model merge from accuracy aspect. The composition is effective if it neither produces too many incorrect compositions nor misses too many correct compositions. Precision and recall is used to capture this intuition. Precision measures quality and is the ratio of correct composition found to the total number of composition found. Recall measures coverage and is the ratio of the correct composition found to the total number of all correct composition. The experiment corpus 5 is extracted from UNIONmode. Seven groups of data are extracted for experiment and the experiment result is the average of the entire seven group.
paraphrases: To assess the model difference algorithm, we followed the experimental procedure outlined in literature [5]. With two product feature models, M1 and M2, we identified expected changes (Me) and changes detected by our method (Mr). Me and Mr are represented as sets of triples, <f1, f2, changetype>, where f1 is a feature in M1, f2 is its counterpart in M2, and changetype indicates if the feature is unchanged, added, or renamed. Following the model difference, a merge algorithm was applied to combine the models. We assessed the accuracy of this merge. An effective composition avoids both an excess of incorrect merges and a deficit of correct ones. This concept was quantified using precision and recall. Precision indicates the quality of the merge by measuring the proportion of correct compositions among all found compositions. Recall reflects the completeness of the merge, calculated as the ratio of correct compositions found to all possible correct compositions. The experimental data set (corpus 5) originated from UNIONmode, with seven distinct data groups used for the experiment. The reported result is the average across these seven groups.

Our model difference algorithm was evaluated using the methodology from [5]. For a given pair of product feature models, M1 and M2, we define Me as the set of anticipated changes and Mr as the set of changes identified by our approach. Both Me and Mr are structured as {<f1, f2, changetype>}, where f1 is a feature from M1, f2 is its corresponding feature in M2, and 'changetype' specifies whether the feature remained the same, was added, or was renamed. Following the differentiation process, a model merge algorithm was employed for integration. The accuracy of this merge was then assessed. A successful composition is characterized by minimizing both false positive (incorrect) and false negative (missed correct) merges. This balance was measured using precision and recall. Precision quantifies the correctness of the found compositions (correct compositions / total found compositions), while recall measures how thoroughly correct compositions were identified (correct compositions found / total correct compositions). The experiment utilized corpus 5 from UNIONmode, with the final results being the average derived from seven distinct data sets.
