text: Exp 1: The experiment is divided into two parts. In each part, CSA is evaluated with a different set of problem samples. The objective is to explore how CSA performance varies when the problem size (number of features per model) and type of constraints vary. In the first part, the 18 algorithm configurations are executed with samples of models of different sizes, ranging from 10 features to 450 features, increasing the number in steps of 10 (i.e., 45 total samples). Each experiment step is performed with a sample of 200 problem instances, and the average value is computed in order to reduce the fluctuations due to randomness (e.g., the random seeds used to generate problem instances). In the second part, the 18 CSA configurations are executed with 5 samples of 200 problems each one. The number of features per model is fixed to 30 to focus on the influence of model constraints on the performance. This number was selected from the average number of features per model reported in Table 6. From one sample to another we vary the type of constraints incorporated to the models. The configurations of these constraints per sample are described below. _Exp 2: The experiment comprises the execution of the 8 algorithms previously mentioned (GAFES, Greedy, and the 6 CSA approximate configurations) with a set of samples of problem instances. Each sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository. Since GAFES and Greedy algorithms only support basic CTCs (i.e., constraints with 2 features at most), in this experiment non-basic CTCs, which are the 17.26% of CTCs, are removed from models. Problem instances include a linear objective to be maximized and a single linear inequality restriction as global constraint, since this is the problem formalization supported by both algorithms. To this end, models are extended with 2 randomly generated attributes per features (a f , b f ), using a uniform distribution over (0, 1). One attribute is used to define the linear objective function, and the other one to define the inequality restriction. The experiment is carried out with 4 different samples of problems, each one with a different value of restriction ratio. In the first sample, the restriction ratio is equal to 1 (100%), so that the restriction cannot be violated by any solution. The other three samples use restriction ratios of 90%, 80% and 70%, respectively. By reducing the value of the restriction ratio, the problem becomes more restrictive and harder to solve, since less combinations of features can satisfy the constraint. Thus, by using different ratios, we can observe how the performance of approximate algorithms degrades as the problem becomes harder. _Exp 3: The experiment comprises the execution of the 8 algorithms previously mentioned (0-1 LP, BoolOpt and 6 CSA exact configurations) with a set of samples of problem instances. Similar to the previous experiment, a sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository. Since 0-1 LP supports linear functions, problems are stated as the optimization of a linear objective function (|O F | = 1) with a variable number of linear inequality restrictions (|GC| = n). The first sample contains instances with 0 inequality restrictions, and the other samples contain instances with 1, 2 and 5 inequality restrictions, with a fixed restriction ratio of 90%. _Exp 4: We run the experiment with 2 samples of problem instances, each one with a different distribution of feature interactions. Similar to previous experiments, each sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository enriched with attributes generated by Thor. In sample #1, models contain 1 interaction per feature, all of degree 2. In sample #2, models contain 2 interactions per feature: 67% of degree 2, 23% of degree 3 and 10% of degree 4. No inequality restrictions are considered, and the objective function is a multi-linear polynomial function including one term for each feature and interaction attribute generated by Thor.
paraphrases: **Experiment 1**: This experiment comprises two segments, each evaluating CSA with distinct problem samples to understand how its performance changes based on problem size (features per model) and constraint types. The first segment involved running 18 algorithm configurations on models varying from 10 to 450 features (45 samples, increasing by 10 features per step). Each step used 200 problem instances, with average values calculated to minimize random fluctuations. The second segment utilized the same 18 CSA configurations on 5 samples, each with 200 problems. Here, the number of features per model was fixed at 30 (based on Table 6's average) to isolate the impact of model constraints, which were varied across samples as detailed below.

**Experiment 2**: This experiment assessed 8 algorithms (GAFES, Greedy, and 6 approximate CSA configurations) using multiple problem instance samples. Each sample contained 882 instances derived from SPLOT repository models. Since GAFES and Greedy only handle basic CTCs (max 2 features), non-basic CTCs (17.26% of all CTCs) were excluded. Problem instances involved maximizing a linear objective and satisfying a single linear inequality global constraint, aligning with the formalization supported by these algorithms. Models were augmented with two uniformly distributed random attributes per feature (a_f, b_f) from (0, 1) – one for the objective function and one for the inequality restriction. Four problem samples were used, each with a different restriction ratio: 100% (no violation possible), 90%, 80%, and 70%. Lower ratios make problems more restrictive and thus harder, allowing observation of algorithm performance degradation.

**Experiment 3**: This experiment involved running 8 algorithms (0-1 LP, BoolOpt, and 6 exact CSA configurations) on problem instance samples. Each sample, like in Experiment 2, consisted of 882 instances from the SPLOT repository. For 0-1 LP, which supports linear functions, problems were formulated as optimizing a single linear objective function (|OF| = 1) subject to a varying number of linear inequality restrictions (|GC| = n). The first sample had no inequality restrictions, while subsequent samples had 1, 2, and 5 restrictions, all with a fixed restriction ratio of 90%.

**Experiment 4**: This experiment used 2 problem instance samples, each with a unique distribution of feature interactions. Similar to previous experiments, each sample contained 882 problem instances from the SPLOT repository, enhanced with Thor-generated attributes. Sample #1 featured models with one degree-2 interaction per feature. Sample #2 models had two interactions per feature: 67% of degree 2, 23% of degree 3, and 10% of degree 4. No inequality restrictions were applied, and the objective function was a multi-linear polynomial, incorporating terms for each feature and interaction attribute generated by Thor.

**Exp 1**: The first experiment was split into two parts, each evaluating the CSA's performance with different problem sets. The goal was to understand how CSA behaves when problem complexity (number of features) and constraint types vary. In the initial part, 18 CSA configurations were run on 45 distinct model samples, with feature counts ranging from 10 to 450, increasing by 10 features per sample. Each step involved 200 problem instances, and average values were calculated to minimize random variability. The second part tested the same 18 CSA configurations on 5 samples, each containing 200 problems. Here, the feature count per model was fixed at 30 (based on Table 6's average) to specifically analyze the impact of different model constraint types, which were varied across the samples as detailed subsequently.

**Exp 2**: This experiment involved executing 8 algorithms (GAFES, Greedy, and six approximate CSA setups) on several sets of problem instances. Each set comprised 882 problems generated from SPLOT repository models. Given that GAFES and Greedy only support basic CTCs (up to 2 features), non-basic CTCs (17.26% of the total) were removed. The problems were structured with a linear objective function to maximize and a single linear inequality as a global constraint, which is compatible with both algorithms. To achieve this, models were augmented with two randomly generated attributes per feature (a_f, b_f) from a uniform (0, 1) distribution, one for the objective and one for the inequality. The experiment utilized four distinct problem samples, each with a different restriction ratio: 100% (making the restriction impossible to violate), 90%, 80%, and 70%. Decreasing the restriction ratio makes the problem more constrained and challenging, allowing observation of how approximate algorithms' performance degrades under increased difficulty.

**Exp 3**: This experiment focused on 8 algorithms (0-1 LP, BoolOpt, and six exact CSA configurations) using multiple problem instance samples. Similar to Exp 2, each sample consisted of 882 instances from the SPLOT repository. Since 0-1 LP can handle linear functions, problems were formulated as optimizing a single linear objective function (|OF| = 1) subject to a variable number of linear inequality restrictions (|GC| = n). The first sample had no inequality restrictions, while subsequent samples contained 1, 2, and 5 restrictions, all maintaining a fixed restriction ratio of 90%.

**Exp 4**: This experiment was conducted with two problem instance samples, each representing a different distribution of feature interactions. Consistent with prior experiments, each sample included 882 problem instances sourced from the SPLOT repository, enhanced with attributes generated by Thor. In Sample #1, models had one interaction per feature, all of degree 2. Sample #2 models included two interactions per feature: 67% of degree 2, 23% of degree 3, and 10% of degree 4. No inequality restrictions were imposed, and the objective function was a multi-linear polynomial, incorporating terms for each feature and Thor-generated interaction attribute.

In this case study, 100 mutants were produced for each of the 12 FMs. We then constructed three categories of test suites: one exclusively with dissimilar products, one with an even split of similar and dissimilar products, and one solely with similar products. This test suite generation and mutation score assessment cycle was repeated 100 times. Additionally, for each FM, we created test suites comprising 100 products that included both similar and dissimilar items. To ensure randomness, a product prioritization was applied 100 times. Finally, for every subset of k products, ranging from 0 to 100, we determined the corresponding mutation score.

text: Participants were required to identify and represent variabilities in class diagrams of the E-Commerce (Gomaa, 2004) and AGMSPLs by means of the application of stereotypes and definition of properties. Therefore, we evaluated the variabilities whether they were correctly or incorrectly modeled in a given SPL. Note that for the study carried out in this paper, no UML modeling tools were used. See Section 3.2.8 for more details. Correct and incorrect variability modeling was based on the following criteria: no points when there is no such a way for deriving a product according to the semantic rules for each approach; and one point when partial or full products can be derived according to the semantic rules for each approach.
paraphrases: Participants were tasked with identifying and illustrating variabilities within class diagrams of E-Commerce (Gomaa, 2004) and AGMSPLs, using stereotypes and property definitions. We then assessed whether these variabilities were modeled accurately or inaccurately within a specific SPL. It's important to note that no UML modeling tools were employed in this study (refer to Section 3.2.8 for further details). The criteria for correct and incorrect variability modeling were: zero points if no product could be derived based on the semantic rules of a given approach, and one point if partial or complete products could be derived following those same semantic rules.

The study required participants to pinpoint and depict variabilities in the class diagrams of E-Commerce (Gomaa, 2004) and AGMSPLs, primarily through the use of stereotypes and property definitions. Our evaluation focused on the accuracy of these variability models within a designated SPL. It should be highlighted that this research did not utilize any UML modeling tools; more information can be found in Section 3.2.8. The assessment of modeling correctness was based on a simple scoring system: a variability received no points if its semantic rules prevented product derivation, whereas it earned one point if its semantic rules allowed for the derivation of at least partial or full products.

text: For assessing program comprehension, we designed two static tasks (S1, S2) and four maintenance tasks (M1–M4). In static tasks, subjects should locate feature code. In the first static task (S1), subjects should, for each feature, locate all files containing feature code and mark the results on a sheet of paper (referred to as grid template). It showed the relationship of code to features in a matrix, such that the columns contained the file names, and the rows the feature names. For the color version, the feature names of the grid template had the same background color as in the source code, whereas for the ifdef version, the grid template had no background colors. In the second static task (S2), subjects should locate shared code (i.e. code that concerned more than one feature, e.g., SMSFeature & CopyPhoto). Locating feature code is a typical task for a developer, when she is familiarizing herself with an SPL. Furthermore, a developer is often looking for feature code when solving a bug, because bugs can often be narrowed down to certain features or feature combinations. Especially, combinations of features are of interest in the implementation of SPLs, since they can represent feature interactions that are especially difficult to get right (Kästner 2010). For all maintenance tasks, we carefully introduced different bugs into the source code, which were all located in annotated code fragments. In a pre-test with 7 students, we selected bugs that were neither too easy nor too difficult to find. Four bugs matched our criteria, which we ordered by increasing difficulty according to the results of our pre-test. For each bug, subjects received a bug description similar to the ones users would enter in a bug-tracking system. The description also named the feature in which the bug occurs. This assured that we evaluate the influence of background colors, because subjects focus on feature code and, thus, background colors, instead of spending their time in non-annotated code fragments. For each task, subjects should locate the bug (name class and method), explain why it occurs, and suggest a solution. Using this information, we judged whether the cause of a bug was located correctly. As an example, we present the bug description of the first maintenance task: M1: If pictures in an album should be sorted by views, they are displayed unsorted anyway. Feature, in which the bug occurs: CountViews. The bug was located in the class PhotoListController and caused by an empty method body of bubbleSort. In addition to the six tasks, we designed a warming-up task to let subjects familiarize with the experimental setting (subjects should count the number of features of MobileMedia). The result of this task was not analyzed. ... We used the same tasks as for our first experiment, including the warming-up task (W0). However, we changed the order of the tasks to M1, M3, S1, M4, M2, S2. To evaluate participants' understanding of programs, we devised a set of tasks comprising two static tasks (S1, S2) and four maintenance tasks (M1–M4). The static tasks required subjects to identify feature code. Specifically, in S1, they had to pinpoint all files containing code for a given feature and record their findings on a "grid template," which visually mapped code to features. For the color-coded version, feature names on the grid matched the source code's background color, while the ifdef version used a grid without background colors. S2 instructed participants to locate shared code, meaning code used by multiple features (e.g., SMSFeature & CopyPhoto). Locating feature code is a routine activity for developers learning an SPL or debugging, as bugs frequently trace back to particular features or their combinations, especially complex interactions in SPLs (Kästner 2010). For the maintenance tasks, we intentionally embedded various bugs within annotated code fragments. Through a pre-test with 7 students, we identified four bugs that were neither too easy nor too difficult, and then arranged them by increasing complexity. Each bug was presented with a description akin to what a user would submit in a bug-tracking system, also specifying the affected feature. This setup ensured we could assess the impact of background colors, as subjects would concentrate on the feature code and its associated colors, rather than unexplored code sections. For each task, participants needed to find the bug (identifying the class and method), explain its occurrence, and propose a fix. This information allowed us to determine if the bug's root cause was correctly identified. As an illustration, the first maintenance task (M1) involved a bug where pictures sorted by views in an album were still displayed unsorted, a problem found in the 'CountViews' feature within the PhotoListController class due to an empty bubbleSort method. Additionally, a warm-up task was included for subjects to become accustomed to the experimental setup (counting MobileMedia features), but its results were not considered for analysis. ... We utilized the same tasks from our initial experiment, including the warm-up task (W0), but altered the task sequence to M1, M3, S1, M4, M2, S2. This alternating pattern of static and maintenance tasks aimed to determine if participants would shift between different code representations as per our hypothesis. ... For measuring program comprehension, we developed several tasks, primarily static tasks, because our initial experiment showed that background colors helped with static tasks, but not maintenance tasks. However, we included a few maintenance tasks to confirm these earlier findings. In total, we had 10 tasks: two warm-up tasks (W1, W2) that were excluded from analysis, six static tasks (S1–S6), and two maintenance tasks (M1, M2). The static tasks were categorized into three types, with two tasks for each type: 1. Identifying all files where a specific feature was implemented (S1, S4). 2. Locating nested ifdef directives, which are important for understanding feature interactions (S2, S5). 3. Identifying all features present in a particular file (S3, S6). An example for a static task is S1: "Which files contain the feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS?" For maintenance tasks, we followed the same methodology as the first experiment, introducing bugs into the source code and providing participants with typical bug descriptions that included the feature selections where the bug occurred. We consulted an expert in C and Xenomai to ensure the bugs were characteristic of C programs. For instance, the first maintenance task (M1) was: "Unloading the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) leads to a segmentation fault. This issue arises when features CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN, CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000, and CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG are all selected. The bug was caused by an omitted null check in the code, specifically changing `if (ckfn && (err = ckfn(block)) != 0)` to `if ((err = ckfn(block)) != 0)`. If the `ckfn` variable is accessed when null, a segmentation fault occurs."

text: To measure program comprehension, we designed tasks that can only be solved if the subjects understand the related source code. We used two kinds of tasks: maintenance and static tasks [28]. In maintenance tasks, the subjects are instructed to locate/fix a bug, whereas in static tasks, the subjects should examine the structure of the source code. In a previous experiment [20], we found that colours speed up program comprehension only for static tasks, but not in maintenance tasks. Hence, we focused on static tasks, but included a few maintenance tasks to confirm our results. All tasks are typical for a maintenance programmer, when she is looking for bugs in certain features and/or files. We had ten tasks: two warming up tasks (W1, W2), six static tasks (S1–S6) and two maintenance tasks (M1, M2). The warming up tasks were designed to let the subjects familiarise themselves with the experimental setting and were not analysed. - For each type, we prepared two tasks. If yes, in which files? At which lines does the inner feature start and end? -- S3: Which features occur in file xenomai/ksrc/nucleus/sched.h? -- M1: If the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) should be unloaded, a segmentation fault is thrown.

These tasks fell into two categories: maintenance and static tasks [28]. Maintenance tasks involved instructing participants to find or fix a bug, while static tasks required them to analyze the source code's structure. Our prior experiment [20] indicated that visual cues like colors only enhanced program comprehension for static tasks, not for maintenance tasks. Consequently, we primarily focused on static tasks but incorporated a few maintenance tasks to revalidate our findings. All tasks mirrored common activities for a maintenance programmer, such as searching for bugs within specific features or files. We designed a total of ten tasks: two warm-up tasks (W1, W2) to acclimate subjects to the experiment, which were excluded from analysis, six static tasks (S1–S6), and two maintenance tasks (M1, M2). S2: "Are features CONFIG_XENO_OPT_PRIOCPL and CONFIG_XENO_OPT_SCHED_SPORADIC found together (nested) anywhere? If so, in which files, and at what lines do the inner features begin and end?" S3: "What features are present in the file xenomai/ksrc/nucleus/sched.h?" M1: "Unloading the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) leads to a segmentation fault."

Our evaluation of program comprehension relied on tasks that could only be solved by subjects who genuinely understood the associated source code. We utilized two distinct task types: maintenance and static tasks [28]. Maintenance tasks directed subjects to locate and/or rectify a bug, whereas static tasks required them to investigate the inherent structure of the source code. A previous experiment [20] revealed that colors accelerated program comprehension exclusively for static tasks, not for maintenance tasks. Therefore, our primary focus was on static tasks, though we included a limited number of maintenance tasks to corroborate our earlier results. All tasks simulated scenarios typical for a maintenance programmer, such as when they are searching for bugs within particular features and/or files. We devised ten tasks in total: two warm-up tasks (W1, W2) designed for participant familiarization with the experimental setup, which were not analyzed, six static tasks (S1–S6), and two maintenance tasks (M1, M2). For each task category, we prepared two specific tasks. As an illustration, we present one task from each type: S1: "Identify the files where feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS is present." S2: "Do the features CONFIG_XENO_OPT_PRIOCPL and CONFIG_XENO_OPT_SCHED_SPORADIC appear together (i.e., nested)? If yes, list the files and the start/end lines of the inner feature." S3: "List the features found in the file xenomai/ksrc/nucleus/sched.h." M1: "A segmentation fault occurs when attempting to unload the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG)."

text: 3.2.1 First hypotheses: effect of stability on inconsistency rate In the first hypothesis, we speculate that a high variation of the design characteristics of the design models may lead to a higher incidence of inconsistencies; since, it increases the chance for an incorrect manipulation of the design charac- teristic by the composition heuristics. In fact, modifications fromsevereevolutionsmayleadthecompositionheuristicsto be ineffective or even prohibitive. In addition, these inconsis- tencies may also propagate. As a higher incidence of changes is found in unstable models, we hypothesize that unstable models tend to have a higher (or equal to) inconsistency rate than stable models. The first hypothesis evaluates whether the inconsistency rate in unstable models is significantly higher (or equal to) than in stable models. Thus, our hypotheses are summarized as follows: Null Hypothesis 1, H1−0: Stable design models have similar or higher inconsis- tency rate than unstable design models. H1−0:Rate(stabledesignmodels)≥Rate(unstabledesign models). Alternative Hypothesis 1, H1−1: Stabledesignmodels havealower inconsistencyratethan unstable design models. H1−1:Rate(stabledesignmodels)<Rate(unstabledesign models). By testing this first hypothesis, we evaluate if stability is a good indicator to identify the most critical MCM in term of inconsistency rate from a sequence of MCM produced from multiple software development teams. Hence, developers can then review the design models having a higher density of composition inconsistencies. We believe that this strategy is a more effective one than going through all MCM produced or assuming an overoptimistic position where all MCM pro- duced is a MAB. ... 3.2.2 Second hypothesis: effect of stability on developer effort As previously mentioned, developers tend to invest different quantity of effort to derive MAB from MCM. Today, model managers are unable to grasp how much effort this trans- formation can demand. This variation is because developers need to resolve different types of problems in a composed model, from a simple renaming of elements to complex mod- ifications in the structure of the composed model. In fact, the structure of the composed models may be affected in different ways during the composition, e.g., creating unex- pected interdependences between the model elements. Even worse, these modifications in the structure of the model may cause ripple effects, i.e., inconsistency propagation between the model elements. The introduction of one inconsistency can often lead to multiple other inconsistencies because of a “knock-on” effect. An example would be the inconsistency whereby a client component is missing an important opera- tion in the interface of a server component (see example in Sect. 2.4). This semantic inconsistency leads to a “knock- on” syntactic inconsistency if another component requires the operation. In the worst case, there may be long chains of inconsistencies all derived from a single inconsistency. Given a composed model at hand, developers need to know if they will invest little or too much effort to transform MCM into MAB, given the problem at hand. Based on this knowl- edge, they will be able to prioritize the review of the output composed models and to better comprehend the effort to be invested, e.g., reviewing the models that require higher effort first and those requiring less effort after. With this in mind, we are interested in understanding the possible difference of effort to resolve inconsistencies in stable and unstable design models. The expectation is that stable models require a lower developers’ effort to produce the output intended model. This expectation is based on the speculation that unstable mod- els may demand more restructuring modifications than stable models; hence, requiring more effort. This leads to the second null and alternative hypotheses as follows: Null Hypothesis 2, H2−0: Stable models require similar or higher effort to resolve inconsistencies than unstable models. H2−0: Effort(stable models) ≥Effort(unstable models). Alternative Hypothesis 2, H2−1: Stable models tend to require a lower inconsistency res- olution effort than unstable ones. H2−1: Effort(stable models) < Effort(unstable models). By testing this first hypothesis, we evaluate if stability is a useful indicator to identify the most critical effort-consuming cases in which severe semantic inconsistencies in archi- tectural components are more often. This knowledge helps model managers to allocate qualified developers to overcome the composition inconsistencies in MCM.
paraphrases: 3.2.1 First hypotheses: the impact of stability on inconsistency rates. We hypothesize that significant changes in design characteristics within design models increase inconsistencies due to potential errors in manipulating these characteristics via composition heuristics. Such inconsistencies can also spread, and given the higher frequency of changes in unstable models, we predict that unstable models will have an equal or higher inconsistency rate compared to stable ones. This first hypothesis examines whether the inconsistency rate in unstable models is significantly higher than, or equal to, that in stable models.
Null Hypothesis 1 (H1-0): Stable design models exhibit an inconsistency rate similar to or greater than unstable design models. (H1-0: Rate(stable design models) ≥ Rate(unstable design models)).
Alternative Hypothesis 1 (H1-1): Stable design models have a lower inconsistency rate than unstable design models. (H1-1: Rate(stable design models) < Rate(unstable design models)).

Testing this hypothesis helps us determine if stability can identify critical MCMs based on inconsistency rates from various software development teams, enabling developers to prioritize reviewing models with more composition inconsistencies, a strategy we believe is more effective than reviewing all MCMs or assuming they are all MABs.

3.2.2 Second hypothesis: the impact of stability on developer effort. Developers vary in the effort they put into transforming MCMs into MABs, and model managers currently lack a way to gauge this effort. This variation stems from the diverse problems developers must solve in composed models, ranging from simple renaming to complex structural changes. Composition can alter model structure in unexpected ways, leading to interdependencies and ripple effects where one inconsistency triggers many others (e.g., a missing operation causing a syntactic inconsistency). In the worst case, a single inconsistency can propagate into long chains. Developers need to estimate the effort required to convert an MCM to an MAB to prioritize reviews and allocate resources effectively. We therefore investigate the difference in effort needed to resolve inconsistencies in stable versus unstable models. We anticipate stable models requiring less developer effort because unstable models likely necessitate more restructuring.
Null Hypothesis 2 (H2-0): Stable models demand similar or greater effort to resolve inconsistencies than unstable models. (H2-0: Effort(stable models) ≥ Effort(unstable models)).
Alternative Hypothesis 2 (H2-1): Stable models require less effort to resolve inconsistencies than unstable models. (H2-1: Effort(stable models) < Effort(unstable models)).

This second hypothesis helps us assess if stability indicates cases requiring significant effort due to severe semantic inconsistencies in architectural components, guiding model managers in assigning skilled developers to address composition inconsistencies in MCMs.

3.2.1 First hypotheses: The effect of stability on inconsistency rate. We propose that significant variations in design characteristics within design models elevate the likelihood of inconsistencies. This is because such variations increase the potential for incorrect manipulation of design features by composition heuristics. Furthermore, substantial modifications resulting from extensive evolutions can render these heuristics ineffective or even unfeasible, and the resulting inconsistencies may spread. Since unstable models exhibit a higher frequency of changes, we hypothesize that their inconsistency rate will be higher than (or equal to) that of stable models. This initial hypothesis evaluates whether unstable models show a significantly higher (or equivalent) inconsistency rate compared to stable models.

Null Hypothesis 1 (H1-0): Stable design models have an inconsistency rate that is similar to or greater than that of unstable design models. (H1-0: Rate(stable design models) ≥ Rate(unstable design models)).
Alternative Hypothesis 1 (H1-1): Stable design models exhibit a lower inconsistency rate than unstable design models. (H1-1: Rate(stable design models) < Rate(unstable design models)).

By testing this hypothesis, we aim to determine if stability serves as a reliable indicator for identifying the most critical MCMs, in terms of inconsistency rate, among those produced by multiple software development teams. This insight would enable developers to focus their review efforts on design models with a higher concentration of composition inconsistencies, a strategy we believe is more efficient than reviewing all MCMs or assuming they are all correct (MABs).

3.2.2 Second hypothesis: The effect of stability on developer effort. As noted, the effort developers invest in transforming MCMs into MABs varies, and current model managers struggle to estimate this demand. This variability arises because developers must address a range of issues in composed models, from minor element renamings to complex structural changes. The composition process can introduce unforeseen interdependencies between model elements, and structural modifications can create ripple effects, propagating inconsistencies. Even a single inconsistency can trigger a cascade of others, such as a missing operation in a server component's interface leading to a semantic inconsistency, which then causes a syntactic inconsistency if another component relies on that operation. In the worst-case scenario, one inconsistency can spawn extensive chains of subsequent inconsistencies. Given a composed model, developers need to gauge the effort required to convert the MCM to an MAB to prioritize model reviews and better understand resource allocation (e.g., reviewing high-effort models first). Consequently, we seek to understand the potential differences in effort required to resolve inconsistencies in stable versus unstable design models. We expect stable models to demand less developer effort to achieve the intended output, based on the premise that unstable models likely require more extensive restructuring, thus increasing effort.
Null Hypothesis 2 (H2-0): Stable models demand similar or greater effort to resolve inconsistencies compared to unstable models. (H2-0: Effort(stable models) ≥ Effort(unstable models)).
Alternative Hypothesis 2 (H2-1): Stable models tend to require less effort to resolve inconsistencies than unstable ones. (H2-1: Effort(stable models) < Effort(unstable models)).

Testing this second hypothesis helps us determine if stability is a useful indicator for identifying critical, effort-intensive scenarios where severe semantic inconsistencies frequently occur in architectural components. This knowledge would assist model managers in assigning skilled developers to address composition inconsistencies in MCMs.

text: We exploit the quantitative data to facilitate a hypothesis confirmation , where we use the defined research questions as hypothesis. To investigate whether a hypothesis can be confirmed, we apply the following data analysis. ... RQ1 We assess the number of unchanged, modified, and new variants determined by the higher-order delta application reasoning when stepping to the next SPL version under test. ... RQ2 We examine the number of retest goals derived by our change impact analysis (incremental model slicing). Retest goals indicate that applied model changes have an impact on already tested behavior between subsequently variants and versions of variants under test. ... RQ3 We compare the number of selected and generated test cases by our framework to the number of test cases executed by retest-all ( Yoo and Harman, 2007 ) to check for a reduction in test cases to be executed. In addition, we assess the time required for both types of change impact analyses to reason about the efficiency of our selection technique according to the cost model defined by Leung and White ( Leung and White, 1991 ). ... RQ4 We evaluate the fault detection rate of our framework compared to retest-all ( Yoo and Harman, 2007 ). Unfortunately, the two subject SPLs do not provide a real fault history. Hence, we use simulated ones derived by taking the changes applied to a test model when stepping to a subsequent variant or version of a variant into account. For the derivation of faults, we combine the changes captured in the respective model regression deltas, i.e., added transitions as well as source and target states of removed transitions, with randomly chosen transitions from the test model. Those faults denote erroneous artifact interactions caused by changes and their impact on common behavior. We generate for each variant and version of a variant a corresponding set of those simulated faults. Depending on the size of the fault set, we create a maximum of different data sets, where each time a random selection of 10% of the faults is made to obtain random fault data sets. The set of test cases to be retested determined by our framework and the set of test cases for retest-all ( Yoo and Harman, 2007 ) are then executed to assess the fault detection rate. ... RQ5 We examine the number of retest goals derived by our change impact analysis similar to RQ1 as they indicate the retest potential to reason about, but we apply different testing orders to our approach. The testing orders are computed for the initial SPL versions based on existing product prioritization techniques ( Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017; Lity et al., 2017; Al-Hajjaji et al., 2014; Henard et al., 2014 ) as well as random generation. For the random generation, we generate 100 product orders for each of the two subject SPLs. In addition, we select (1) four prioritization techniques ( Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017; Al-Hajjaji et al., 2014; Henard et al., 2014 ) focusing on the dissimilarity between products, e.g., in terms of feature selection, to increase the coverage of elements or features, and (2) we use a testing order obtained in previous work ( Lity et al., 2017 ), where the overall differences between subsequent variants in terms of applied change operations captured in model regression deltas are minimized. The selected techniques are applicable due to the available artifacts in this experiment required as input, i.e., delta sets and feature configurations. To this end, we apply the feature similarity Al-Hajjaji et al. (2014) and delta similarity technique ( Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017 ) of Al-Hajjaji et al., the global maximum distance (GMD) and local maximum distance (LMD) approach from Henard et al. (2014) , and from our previous work ( Lity et al., 2017 ) the NEARIN algorithm.
paraphrases: We utilize quantitative data to validate our hypotheses, which are derived from the research questions. To determine if a hypothesis holds true, we employ the following data analysis procedures: RQ1 involves quantifying the unchanging, altered, and newly introduced variants identified by higher-order delta application reasoning during the transition to the subsequent SPL version under examination. RQ2 focuses on the number of retest goals produced by our change impact analysis (using incremental model slicing), where these goals signify that changes in the model affect previously tested behaviors across successive variants and their versions. RQ3 entails comparing the quantity of test cases selected and generated by our framework against those executed by the 'retest-all' method (Yoo and Harman, 2007) to ascertain any reduction in test cases. Furthermore, we evaluate the time expenditure for both types of change impact analyses to assess the efficiency of our selection approach, guided by the cost model by Leung and White (1991). RQ4 assesses our framework's fault detection rate relative to 'retest-all' (Yoo and Harman, 2007). As actual fault histories are unavailable for the two SPLs, we simulate faults by considering changes applied to a test model during transitions to subsequent variants or variant versions. Faults are generated by combining changes from model regression deltas (e.g., added transitions, source/target states of removed transitions) with randomly chosen transitions from the test model. These simulated faults represent incorrect artifact interactions caused by changes and their effect on shared behavior. For each variant and version, a corresponding set of simulated faults is created. Based on the fault set size, we generate various data sets, each involving a random selection of 10% of faults to create diverse random fault data sets. The test cases slated for retesting by our framework and those for 'retest-all' are then executed to determine the fault detection rate. RQ5, similar to RQ1, investigates the number of retest goals from our change impact analysis, which serve as an indicator of retesting potential. However, this RQ employs different testing orders. These orders are computed for initial SPL versions using established product prioritization techniques (e.g., Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017; Lity et al., 2017; Al-Hajjaji et al., 2014; Henard et al., 2014) and random generation. For random generation, 100 product orders are created for each SPL. Additionally, we choose (1) four prioritization techniques (Al-Hajjaji ets al., 2017, 2014; Henard et al., 2014) that prioritize product dissimilarity (e.g., in feature selection) to enhance coverage, and (2) a testing order from prior work (Lity et al., 2017) that minimizes overall differences in change operations between successive variants. These techniques are applicable due to the experiment's input requirements: delta sets and feature configurations. Specifically, we apply Al-Hajjaji et al.'s feature similarity (2014) and delta similarity (2017) techniques, Henard et al.'s (2014) global maximum distance (GMD) and local maximum distance (LMD) approaches, and the NEARIN algorithm from our previous work (Lity et al., 2017).

We use quantitative data to confirm our hypotheses, which are directly formulated from our research questions. To assess hypothesis validity, we conduct the following data analyses: RQ1 aims to quantify the variants that remain unchanged, are modified, or are newly introduced when advancing to the next SPL version, as determined by higher-order delta application reasoning. RQ2 explores the quantity of retest goals generated by our change impact analysis, which utilizes incremental model slicing. These retest goals signify that changes implemented in the model affect behavior that was previously tested across sequential variants and their versions. RQ3 involves a comparison between the number of test cases selected and produced by our framework and the number of test cases executed by the 'retest-all' approach (Yoo and Harman, 2007), with the goal of identifying any reduction in necessary test cases. Moreover, we evaluate the time consumed by both change impact analysis methods to gauge the efficiency of our selection technique, based on the cost model by Leung and White (1991). RQ4 evaluates the fault detection capability of our framework against that of 'retest-all' (Yoo and Harman, 2007). Since the two SPLs under study lack authentic fault histories, we create simulated faults by incorporating the changes made to a test model when transitioning to a subsequent variant or variant version. Fault derivation involves combining changes from model regression deltas (e.g., added transitions, source/target states of removed transitions) with randomly chosen transitions from the test model. These faults represent erroneous interactions between artifacts caused by modifications and their effect on common behavior. For each variant and its version, a corresponding set of these simulated faults is generated. Depending on the size of the fault set, we create a maximum number of distinct data sets, with each iteration involving a random selection of 10% of the faults to produce varied random fault data sets. The test cases designated for retesting by our framework, along with those for 'retest-all' (Yoo and Harman, 2007), are then executed to ascertain the fault detection rate. RQ5, mirroring RQ1, investigates the number of retest goals produced by our change impact analysis as an indicator of retest potential, but with the application of various testing orders to our approach. The testing orders for the initial SPL versions are calculated using established product prioritization techniques (Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017; Lity et al., 2017; Al-Hajjaji et al., 2014; Henard et al., 2014) as well as through random generation. For the random generation method, 100 product orders are created for each of the two SPLs. Additionally, we select (1) four prioritization techniques (Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017; Al-Hajjaji et al., 2014; Henard et al., 2014) that emphasize dissimilarity between products, such as in feature selection, to enhance coverage of elements or features, and (2) a testing order from previous work (Lity et al., 2017) that minimizes the overall differences in applied change operations captured in model regression deltas between successive variants. The chosen techniques are applicable because the necessary input artifacts, including delta sets and feature configurations, are available in this experiment. To achieve this, we employ the feature similarity (2014) and delta similarity (2017) techniques by Al-Hajjaji et al., the global maximum distance (GMD) and local maximum distance (LMD) methods from Henard et al. (2014), and the NEARIN algorithm from our earlier research (Lity et al., 2017).

The proper way to make such a choice is an open issue in the literature. Too many term-topics leads to the association of irrelevant terms and too few term-topics leads to loosely relevant terms. We are unable to use a fixed number of term-topics (#term-topics) because we have different sizes of code-topic documents. text: We evaluated the performance of the studied algorithms in terms of three aspects: (1) the quality of the approximate Pareto front produced, (2) the convergence to the exact Pareto front, and (3) the diversity of the solutions produced. As suggested by Zitzler et al. [60], we measured the quality of an approximate (Pareto) front using the following three metrics: – Hypervolume (HV) [6]. This metric calculates the volume of the subspace covered by an approximate front A. It evaluates how well the approximate front A fulfills the optimization objectives. A higher HV indicates a better Pareto front. – Epsilon (ε) [60]. This metric calculates the shortest dis- tance that is required to transform every solution in an approximate front A to dominate the reference front R. It evaluates how close an approximate front A is to the reference front R. A lower ε indicates a better Pareto front. – Inverted Generational Distance (IGD) [29]. This metric calculates theaveragedistancefromthesolutions belong- ing to the reference front R to the closest solution in an approximate front A. It complements the ε metric to eval- uate how close an approximate front A is to the reference front R. A lower IGD indicates a better Pareto front. We measured the convergence to the exact Pareto front using the following metric: – Error Ratio (ER) [32]. This metric calculates the percent- age of solutions in an approximate front A that are not solutions in the reference front R. It evaluates the pro- portion of non-true solution in an approximate front A. A lower ER indicates a better Pareto front. We measured the diversity using the following metric: – Generalized Spread (GS) [12]. This metric calculates the extent of spread in the solutions of an approximate front A. It evaluates the distribution of all solutions among all the optimization objectives. A higher GS indicates a better Pareto front.
paraphrases: We assessed the algorithms' performance across three dimensions: the quality of the generated approximate Pareto front, its convergence to the true Pareto front, and the diversity of the resulting solutions. Following Zitzler et al. [60], we used Hypervolume (HV) [6], Epsilon (ε) [60], and Inverted Generational Distance (IGD) [29] to quantify approximate Pareto front quality. HV measures the covered subspace volume, with higher values indicating a better front. Epsilon quantifies the shortest distance for an approximate front A to dominate a reference front R, where a lower ε signifies closer proximity. IGD, complementing ε, calculates the average distance from reference front solutions to the closest solution in an approximate front A; a lower IGD also denotes closer proximity. For convergence to the exact Pareto front, we employed the Error Ratio (ER) [32], which determines the percentage of approximate front solutions that are not true solutions in the reference front R; a lower ER implies better convergence. Finally, we gauged diversity using Generalized Spread (GS) [12], which assesses the distribution of solutions within an approximate front A across all optimization objectives, with a higher GS indicating greater diversity.

text: One factor with two treatments The experiment was designed as a control group study (see Figure 1). The method group (MG) used the integrated ARE instructions according to the template described in [2]. In contrast, the control group (CG) used traditional ARE instructions according to a VM-based ARE approach combined with a TORE [13] guideline. The SPL specification in which the main SPL features and the SPL architecture were described was given to all participants. Thus, the control group was equipped with state of the art material, while the method group was equipped with our novel approach. During the experiment, both groups performed fictitious but controlled elicitation interviews in order to gather requirements. The participants’ performance was measured using the aforementioned variables in order to enable statistical comparison. Each participant was randomly assigned to exactly one group. As far as possible, we tried to assign the participants to the groups alternately. This was the preferred strategy, as we did not know the participants before and considered the order of their commitment as random. However, in order to assure equal distribution of REexperienced and less experienced participants in both groups, their RE background was taken into consideration. Thus, the information about interview experience provided in the pre-questionnaires was used for balancing the groups. A statistical test showed that a significant difference regarding RE experience between the two groups could not be confirmed. However, additional balancing of the participants according to their awareness of basic SPL concepts was not possible, as only six participants had experience in RE and SPL engineering. We discuss in section 3.4. its influence on the results.
paraphrases: The experiment employed a control group design with one factor and two treatments, as illustrated in Figure 1. The method group (MG) followed integrated ARE instructions based on the template in [2], while the control group (CG) utilized traditional ARE instructions derived from a VM-based ARE approach and a TORE [13] guideline. All participants received the SPL specification detailing key features and architecture, meaning the control group worked with standard materials and the method group with our new method. Both groups conducted simulated, controlled elicitation interviews to gather requirements, and their performance was assessed using specific variables for statistical comparison. Participants were randomly assigned to a single group, with alternating assignment preferred due to the unknown nature of participants and assumed randomness of commitment order. Nevertheless, to ensure balanced distribution of RE experience across groups, participants' RE backgrounds were considered, using pre-questionnaire data on interview experience for this purpose. A statistical test confirmed no significant difference in RE experience between groups. Balancing based on SPL conceptual awareness was not feasible due to a limited number (six) of participants with experience in both RE and SPL engineering, an aspect discussed further in section 3.4 regarding its impact on results.

text: We designed one external configuration for a Dr.Chat Mobile application shown in Fig. 14. We also built a scenario suite with a set of expected quality scenarios for a product under construction. The experiment is based on two transactions to be performed with a Dr.Chat Mobile application. The transactions represent a user’s stimulus from an application functional perspective (e.g. execute a consultation transaction). The first transaction (TR1) requires the application user to create and submit a medical consultation. The following steps comprise the transaction. Once the user is logged into the system, the application must locate the user (using either the device’s sensors or manual selection from the index-based lists). The user must then describe his medical condition using text and attachments, including voice or video recording and pictures. Finally, the application sends the consultation to the medical server. The second transaction (TR2) requires the application user to retrieve a previously submitted medical consultation and check its attachments. In this transaction, the user first selects a medical consultation from the medical record stored in cellphone’s memory, then retrieves from the server its attachments including voice or video recordings and pictures. Our experimental design contains two main parts. The first part (XP1) focuses on testing the human analyst’s behavior, while the second (XP2) tests SPAF assistance capabilities. In the first part (XP1), the human analyst must manually select a set of concrete components from the components in the core assets base to instantiate product architecture. Given a scenario suite, the analyst must then find possible sets of components that can fulfil the responses according to the stimulus in the quality scenarios in the context of (TR1) and (TR2). To test the selected components, the human analyst produce a product production plan for each set of components, and use the SPL to derive the product. For each product the suite tests are executed and using the monitoring tools she collects the top-rated ones according to its functional and quality characteristics. In the second part (XP2), the human analyst must model the Dr.Chat Mobile SPL software architecture, variability, component catalog, and scenario suite using the proposed languages for each domain provided by SPAF. The tester must also model one sensitivity point for each scenario in the provided suite case. The human analyst must then run the SPAF tool and collect the top-rated components according to its functional and quality characteristics. The analyst uses the components proposed by SPAF to define the product production plan and then use the SPL to derive the products. A detailed description of the test procedure, subjects, objects, and recording mechanisms is presented below.
paraphrases: Our experiment involved evaluating the Dr.Chat Mobile application through two key transactions and was structured in two main phases. The first phase, XP1, investigated human analyst performance in manually selecting components and creating product architectures based on predefined quality scenarios. The second phase, XP2, assessed the SPAF tool's ability to assist in modeling software architecture and identifying optimal components for product derivation.

The experimental setup for the Dr.Chat Mobile application involved evaluating two distinct user transactions (TR1 and TR2), designed to simulate real-world usage of the application. The study was divided into two phases: XP1, which focused on the human analyst's manual component selection and architectural instantiation for product generation, and XP2, which examined how SPAF capabilities aid analysts in modeling the application's software architecture and selecting suitable components.

text: Before the first trial, the researchers carried out a comparative analysis of the four models to establish the complexity of each feature model applying the following criteria: number of features, the maximum depth of features, and the amount of variability. Based on these three criteria, we categorize the feature models in two different complexity levels: normal complexity and more complex models. Thus, two domains were considered with normal complexity level (mobile devices and library, S01 and S02, respectively) and the other two models considered more complex (context-aware mobile applications and hospitality, C01 and C02, respectively) [de Mello et al., 2014]. Then, researchers evenly distributed all four domains to be inspected in both trials by each subject [de Mello et al., 2014]. However, after analyzing the results from the first trial, we observed that the complexity of the domains did not influence the performance of effectiveness/ efficiency in both trials. On the other hand, we noted that only the inspections performed over complex domains had their effectiveness significantly benefited through using FMCheck. Thus, in this trial, we arbitrary set C01 and C02 to be inspected only in the first trial (ad-hoc), while S01 and S02 were configured to be inspected only in the second trial (FMCheck).
paraphrases: Prior to the initial trial, the four feature models were analyzed for complexity, using criteria like feature count, depth, and variability, and then categorized into "normal" (S01, S02) and "more complex" (C01, C02) levels. While all domains were initially balanced across both trials for each participant, post-first trial analysis revealed that overall complexity didn't impact effectiveness/efficiency. However, FMCheck specifically enhanced effectiveness for complex domains. Consequently, C01 and C02 were assigned only to the first trial (ad-hoc), and S01 and S02 to the second trial (FMCheck).

Before starting the first trial, we assessed the complexity of four feature models based on their feature count, maximum depth, and variability, classifying them as either 'normal' (S01, S02 for mobile devices and library) or 'more complex' (C01, C02 for context-aware mobile apps and hospitality) [de Mello et al., 2014]. Initially, each subject was meant to inspect all four domains across both trials [de Mello et al., 2014]. However, findings from the first trial showed that domain complexity didn't affect overall performance. Instead, FMCheck only significantly improved inspection effectiveness for the more complex domains. Therefore, we decided that C01 and C02 would be inspected ad-hoc in the first trial, and S01 and S02 would be inspected using FMCheck in the second trial.

text: The experiment was performed in two runs, as shown in Figure 1. The experiment requires a comparison of the different quality assurance techniques and a comparison of the different variants. Consequently, we performed a 2*2 factorial design (see Figure 1) where the two factors are 1) the quality assurance technique (functional testing, code-inspection, and 2) the variant of the component (Variant 1 and Variant 2) . Each subject performed a test case creation step and an inspection step on different variants of the component. The students were separated into two groups (G1 and G2) of 6 and 7 people, respectively. Each group was assigned to a component variant which differs in the two runs. Also, the applied quality assurance technique differs between the two runs. This design allows us to compare the defect finding potential of the different techniques on different variants in an unbiased way (note that functional testing gave the students no insight into the code which is inspected in the second run and thus, learning effects are omitted, see Section 3.7).

We employed a 2x2 factorial design with two factors: quality assurance technique (functional testing vs. code inspection) and component variant (Variant 1 vs. Variant 2). Each participant completed both test case creation and inspection tasks on different component variants. Students were divided into two groups (G1 with 6, G2 with 7), with each group receiving a different component variant and applying a different quality assurance technique across the two runs. This setup ensured an unbiased comparison of defect detection capabilities, mitigating learning effects by separating functional testing (no code insight) from code inspection (see Section 3.7).

Our experiment, illustrated in Figure 1, comprised two runs to compare distinct quality assurance techniques and component variants using a 2x2 factorial design. The factors were quality assurance technique (functional testing, code inspection) and component variant (Variant 1, Variant 2). Subjects engaged in test case creation and inspection for different component variants. The 13 students were split into two groups (G1: 6, G2: 7), with each group assigned a unique component variant and quality assurance technique for each run. This design facilitated an unbiased comparison of defect-finding potential, as functional testing did not provide code insight for subsequent inspection, thus preventing learning effects (Section 3.7).

text: The study was executed in April/ May 2012, starting with the completion of the consent form and the characterization form by 14 participants. Then, participants were trained in feature modelling and in the Odyssey-FEX notation. Also, an introductory training (one hour) in software inspection was done, including the guidelines for the execution of the first round. Each participant received an email containing an inspection package, and 12 participants answered until the given deadline, reporting the defects detected in each inspection. Then, the participants were trained (one hour) in FMCheck, by presenting and explaining each evaluation item and examples of defects that could be detected with these items. In the second round, as mentioned earlier, only nine participants maintained their participation in the study, answering to the forwarded packages. Table 11 summarizes the results obtained in the first round, and Table 12 summarizes the results obtained in the second round. To calculate the efficiency (ratio between defects detected and the total of defects), the total of defects corresponds to the sum of distinct defects detected in a FM in both rounds. The sum of defects for each FM is shown in Table 13.
paraphrases: The study, conducted in April and May 2012, began with 14 participants completing consent and characterization forms. These participants then received training in feature modeling and the Odyssey-FEX notation, followed by a one-hour introductory session on software inspection, including guidelines for the first round. An inspection package was emailed to each participant, and 12 responded by the deadline, reporting defects found. Subsequently, participants underwent a one-hour FMCheck training, covering evaluation items and defect examples. In the second round, only nine participants continued, responding to the forwarded packages. Tables 11 and 12 present the results from the first and second rounds, respectively. Efficiency, defined as the ratio of detected defects to total defects, was calculated by summing all unique defects identified in a Feature Model (FM) across both rounds. text: To analyze the obtained result, the Vargha and Delaney statistics and Mann-Whitney U test are used based on the guidelines for reporting statistical tests for randomized algorithms [16]. The Vargha and Delaney statistics is used to calculate !!", which is a non-parametric effect size measure. In our context, !!" is used to compare the probability of yielding higher values for the values of fitness function for two algorithms A and B with different weight strategies. If !!" is 0.5, the two algorithms have equal performance. If !!" is greater than 0.5, A has higher chance to obtain better solutions than B. The Mann-Whitney U test is used to calculate p-value for deciding whether there is a significant difference between A and B. We choose the significance level of 0.05, i.e., there is a significant difference if p-value is less than 0.05. Based on the above description, we define that algorithm A has better performance than algorithm B, if the !!" value is greater than 0.5 and such better performance is significant if p-value is less than 0.05. To address RQ3, we choose the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (!) to measure the relations between the MFV_F and MFV_TR of the algorithms and different number of features and test cases [17]. The value of ! ranges from -1 to 1 and can be interpreted as follows: 1) There is a positive correlation if ρ is greater than 0 and a strong positive correlation if ρ is close to 1; 2) A negative correlation when ρ is less than 0 and a value close to -1 shows a strong negative correlation; 3) A ! close to 0 shows that there is no correlation between the two sets of data. Moreover, we also report significance of correlation using Prob>|!!|, a value lower than 0.05 means that the correlation is statistically significant.
paraphrases: Following the guidelines for statistical reporting in randomized algorithms [16], we employed Vargha and Delaney statistics and the Mann-Whitney U test to analyze our results. The Vargha and Delaney statistic, denoted as !!", serves as a non-parametric effect size measure. Here, it assesses the likelihood that algorithm A, using a particular weight strategy, will achieve superior fitness function values compared to algorithm B. A !!'' value of 0.5 indicates equivalent performance, while a value exceeding 0.5 suggests algorithm A is more likely to produce better solutions than B. To determine if this difference is statistically significant, we used the Mann-Whitney U test to calculate the p-value, setting a significance level of 0.05. Therefore, algorithm A is considered to outperform algorithm B if !!'' > 0.5 and p < 0.05. For RQ3, we utilized Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (!) [17] to quantify the relationship between MFV_F and MFV_TR of the algorithms, considering varying numbers of features and test cases. The correlation coefficient ! ranges from -1 to 1: values greater than 0 signify a positive correlation (stronger as it approaches 1), values less than 0 indicate a negative correlation (stronger as it approaches -1), and values near 0 suggest no correlation. We also report the significance of the correlation using Prob>|!!|, with a value below 0.05 denoting statistical significance.

Our analysis of the results relied on Vargha and Delaney statistics and the Mann-Whitney U test, consistent with established guidelines for reporting statistical tests in randomized algorithms [16]. Specifically, the non-parametric effect size measure !!", derived from Vargha and Delaney statistics, was used to compare the probability of algorithm A achieving higher fitness function values than algorithm B, considering different weighting strategies. A !!'' of 0.5 implies equal performance, whereas a value above 0.5 suggests A is more likely to yield better solutions than B. The Mann-Whitney U test provided the p-value to ascertain the statistical significance of any observed differences between A and B, with a significance level of 0.05 (i.e., a p-value less than 0.05 indicates a significant difference). Consequently, algorithm A is deemed to perform better than algorithm B if !!'' > 0.5, and this superiority is statistically significant if p < 0.05. To address Research Question 3, we computed Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (!) [17] to evaluate the relationship between MFV_F and MFV_TR of the algorithms and the number of features and test cases. The ! value ranges from -1 to 1: a positive ! (> 0, approaching 1 for strong) indicates a positive correlation, a negative ! (< 0, approaching -1 for strong) indicates a negative correlation, and a ! near 0 indicates no correlation. Furthermore, correlation significance was determined by Prob>|!!|, with values below 0.05 signifying statistical significance.

text: To make fair comparisons, we adopted the same techniques suggested by the state-of-the-art [5, 32] for stat- istical testing. Based on the experimental results of 30 executions per algorithm, we conducted a statistical test at the significance level of 5%. We performed the Mann-Whitney U test, which is a non-parametric test and makes fewer assumptions regarding the un- derlying populations. We calculated the estimated probability, i.e., p-value, that an algorithm produces different results than the other. Furthermore, we reported the non-parametric effect size measure ˆA12 [70]. It indicates the performance superiority, and it measures the extent to which an algorithm outperforms the other. The su- periority between algorithms are considered as small, medium and large when ˆA12 value is over 0.56, 0.64 and 0.71, respectively.
paraphrases: To ensure equitable comparisons, we followed the statistical testing methodologies recommended by leading research [5, 32]. After conducting 30 executions for each algorithm, we performed statistical analyses at a 5% significance level. Specifically, we used the Mann-Whitney U test, a non-parametric test that requires fewer assumptions about the underlying data distributions. We then calculated the p-value, representing the probability that an algorithm yields results different from another. Additionally, we reported the non-parametric effect size measure ˆA12 [70], which quantifies an algorithm's performance superiority and the degree to which it outperforms others. An ˆA12 value exceeding 0.56, 0.64, or 0.71 signifies small, medium, or large superiority, respectively.

For a fair comparative analysis, we applied statistical testing techniques consistent with current state-of-the-art practices [5, 32]. Based on 30 experimental runs per algorithm, we conducted a statistical test with a 5% significance level. We chose the Mann-Whitney U test, a non-parametric method requiring fewer assumptions about population distributions. We computed the p-value, which estimates the probability of an algorithm producing different results compared to another. Moreover, we included the non-parametric effect size measure ˆA12 [70], which gauges an algorithm's performance advantage and the extent of its outperformance. Superiority between algorithms is categorized as small (ˆA12 > 0.56), medium (ˆA12 > 0.64), or large (ˆA12 > 0.71).

text: WCEC Accuracy: The first step of the evaluation process con-sisted of determining the actual worst-case energy consumptionvalue for each product. In order to do this, we used the brute-forcealgorithm: we generated all the 7 products, instrumented the sourcecode with energy measurement calls, and then executed each prod-uct 200 times. This was performed by our dynamic energy mea-suring framework, which is responsible for executing the productswith the same input and measure the energy consumption. Sinceour goal is to determine the energy consumed in the worst case,we retrieved the highest value for every product in the 200 mea-surements obtained 7. Just like for the energy model creation, weused RAPL to get the actual measurements, which minimizes theinstrumentation overhead by simply measuring the energy beforeand after the program execution. By combining the created energy model, as described in subsec-tion 5.1, with our technique (implemented in a tool, as described insection 4), we were able to compute accurate estimates for the worstcase energy consumption of every product. The results obtained arepresented in Table 1. ... WCEC Performance: Our static analysis technique works atthe source code level. Thus, it can be seen as an interpreter which,at execution time, parses the code, builds data structures (ASTs andCFGs), and performs complex computations. The WCEC analysisof a specific product will always take more time than executing itscompiled (and optimized) code, as the results of Table 1 confirm(see results displayed in the last two columns). However, it shouldbe noticed that, to measure the energy consumption a of product ina SPL, developers have to generate the product, instrument it withenergy monitoring code, and finally run the product. This overheadis not reflected in the execution times shown in Table 1.
paraphrases: WCEC Accuracy: To begin our evaluation, we established the true worst-case energy consumption for each product using a brute-force approach. This involved generating all 7 products, embedding energy measurement calls into their source code, and running each product 200 times. Our dynamic energy measuring framework handled this process, ensuring consistent input and accurate energy consumption readings. To find the worst-case scenario, we selected the maximum energy value from the 200 measurements for each product. Similar to energy model creation, RAPL was used for measurements to minimize overhead by recording energy before and after execution. By integrating our developed energy model (Section 5.1) with our technique (Section 4 tool), we accurately estimated the worst-case energy consumption for every product, as detailed in Table 1.

WCEC Performance: Our static analysis operates directly on the source code, acting like an interpreter that parses code, constructs data structures (ASTs and CFGs), and executes intricate calculations at runtime. As Table 1 illustrates (refer to the last two columns), WCEC analysis for a product inherently takes longer than running its compiled and optimized version. It's important to note that measuring a product's energy consumption within an SPL requires developers to generate, instrument with monitoring code, and then execute the product; this inherent overhead is not represented in the execution times displayed in Table 1.

WCEC Accuracy: The initial stage of our evaluation involved determining the actual worst-case energy consumption for each product. We achieved this by employing a brute-force algorithm: all seven products were generated, their source code was instrumented with energy measurement calls, and each product was executed 200 times. Our dynamic energy measurement framework managed this process, ensuring products ran with identical inputs and their energy consumption was recorded. To pinpoint the worst-case, we identified the highest energy consumption value from the 200 measurements for each product. As with the energy model development, we utilized RAPL for these measurements to minimize instrumentation overhead by simply recording energy before and after program execution. By combining the established energy model (Subsection 5.1) with our technique (implemented as a tool in Section 4), we could precisely estimate the worst-case energy consumption for all products. These results are presented in Table 1.

WCEC Performance: Our static analysis technique functions at the source code level, essentially acting as an interpreter that, during execution, parses code, builds data structures (ASTs and CFGs), and performs complex calculations. Consequently, analyzing a specific product's WCEC will always be more time-consuming than executing its compiled and optimized code, a fact corroborated by the results in Table 1 (see the last two columns). However, it is crucial to recognize that to measure the energy consumption of a product in an SPL, developers must generate, instrument it with energy monitoring code, and then run it. This inherent overhead is not reflected in the execution times provided in Table 1.

text: The replication of the quasi-experiment adopted the following mechanisms for analyzing the collected data: • Comparison between results of ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections to test the hypotheses. • Calculation of the time spent on the inspections to check efficiency. • Calculation of variance of the defects and standard deviation in a view to comparing effectiveness/ effectiveness between ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections. • Elimination of outliers and verification of data normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (Levene). • Application of a nonparametric test (Wilcoxon) or a parametric test (Student’s t), according to each case.
paraphrases: To analyze the data from the quasi-experiment replication, the following methods were employed: comparing ad-hoc and FMCheck inspection results to test hypotheses; calculating inspection time to assess efficiency; determining the variance and standard deviation of defects to compare the effectiveness of ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections; removing outliers and checking for data normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (Levene); and applying either a nonparametric (Wilcoxon) or parametric (Student's t) test as appropriate for each case.

The collected data from the replicated quasi-experiment were analyzed using these approaches: hypotheses were tested by comparing outcomes from ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections; efficiency was gauged by computing the time spent on inspections; defect variance and standard deviation were calculated to contrast the effectiveness of ad-hoc versus FMCheck inspections; outliers were removed, and data normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (Levene) were verified; and depending on the specific situation, either a nonparametric (Wilcoxon) or parametric (Student’s t) test was applied.
