text: Quality criterion 1 (from Section I-C) is fulfilled by the distribution of the tree width measures in our experiments, as shown in Tables II–IV. The tables show the number of models with a tree width value in a given interval. For example, Table II shows in row 1 that for twG(PP )+ – short for the upper bound of the Gaifman tree-width of the parallel binary counter encoding PP – there are 40 models for which the computed value is within [0, 1] (column 1), 28 models with a tree width in [2, 4], etc. Because the lower and upper bound approximations delivered by the tree width approximation algorithm differ slightly, we computed all correlations for the set of lower and the set of upper bounds separately. We use x−to refer to the lower bound, x+ to refer to the upper bound. Because of the complexity of computing the incidence graph for the models with 1000 features, we were restricted to conduct the analysis on the Gaifman graph for these models. ... To analyze quality criterion 2, we used the solver-specific execution times in addition to the tree width measures to conduct a Spearman’s rank correlation analysis (see [37] for details). We applied a post-hoc significance test to the resulting correlation coefficient. Spearman’s rank correlation is non-parametric and thus we do not need to make assumptions on the distribution of the base data (e.g. normality). A general observation on the solver execution times of the BDD-based solvers is that these solvers were incapable of processing models with cardinality constraints as they ran out of memory. This might be due to our decision to connect BDD solvers directly to the LT n,k P AR encoder without using BDD-specific heuristics, as described in the previous section. Tables V–XIII describe significant correlations between graph width measures and solver execution time revealed by the post-hoc significance test at the 5% significance level. In the four columns, correlations are shown for the lower (-) and upper (+) bound heuristics of the tree width applied to the Gaifman (twG) and the incidence graph (twI). The results of each experiment are grouped according to the analyzed encoding. We describe the correlation between the tree width of the analyzed encoding and the execution time of the solvers that are run on this particular type of encoding. These are highlighted grey in the following tables. In addition, for each encoding, we describe correlations between the tree width of the encoding and the execution time of the solvers on the according models that are not being run on the encoding (but that were run on the other encodings). This allows us to evaluate the suitability of measures to approximate the structural complexity of more than one type of encoding.

Given the slight discrepancies between the lower and upper bound approximations from the tree width algorithm, we calculated all correlations separately for each set of bounds. To assess quality criterion 2, we performed a Spearman’s rank correlation analysis (refer to [37] for specifics), incorporating solver-specific execution times alongside tree width measurements. A post-hoc significance test was applied to the resulting correlation coefficient. As Spearman’s rank correlation is a non-parametric test, it eliminates the need for assumptions about the underlying data distribution (e.g., normality). text: For this purpose, we employ intra-class correlation (ICC). ICC is used to measure the degree of resemblance between the quantitative traits of a group of individ- uals, i.e., the subjective opinions of the participants with regard to the subcharacteristics of maintainability in our case. Table 7 reports the results of this statistical test based on a two- way random effects model with a confidence interval of 95%. ... As the first step of our analysis, we hypothesize that a meaningful correlation between the defined metrics and maintainability can be found (H1). In order to test this hypothesis, we first applied the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test that revealed that our collected data did not have a normal distribution. Therefore, a non-parametric test statistic, the Spearman’s Rho correlation coefficient (significance level of 0.05) was used to investigate any significance relationships. In this step, three types of correlations were studied: Inter-metric Correlation: The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether the defined metrics each represent a different aspect of a feature model and are hence unique or in fact some kind of relationship can be found between these metrics; Metrics Indicativeness: This is the major correlation study of interest, since it investigates whether the defined metrics are useful indicators of maintainability and its subcharacteristics or not; Inter-quality Correlation: Due to the fact that the external quality attribute under study is comprised of three subcharacteristics, correlation studies are performed between each of these subelements to see whether they themselves are correlated in any way. As one instance, the correlation between understandability and analyzability, as being constituting elements of maintainability, will be investigated. Each of these correlation studies reveals some important characteristics of the dependent and independent variables. ... The next hypothesis is that the proposed structural metrics are able to serve as discrimi- natory references for indicating maintainability (H2). The above correlation studies are able to show which of the metrics have a significant relationship with the subelements of maintainability. We further employ the concept of entropy (Fenton and Neil 1999) to see how these proposed metrics are able to reduce the uncertainty associated with the correct level of maintainability of a feature model. Simply stated, entropy is the measure of uncertainty associated with a phenomenon. So in our case, the lack of knowledge about the degree of maintainability of a feature model can be captured in terms of entropy. Now, if the value of one of the proposed metrics is calculated and used for deciding about the maintainability of the model, some useful information about the possible degree of maintainability of that feature model may be gained as a result. For this reason, if a metric has been able to help us reach a better judgement about the maintainability of a feature model, it has been indeed able to reduce our uncertainty and hence reduce the entropy. The amount of reduced entropy as a result of revealing the correct value for a given metric is known as information gain (Kent 1983). It is clear that the higher the information gain for a metric is, the more it is able to reduce the uncertainty about the subcharacter- istics of maintainability and can therefore be used as a useful indicator of this external quality attribute. We use the Kullback–Leibler divergence formulation (Hershey and Olsen 2007) for calculating the information gain of each of the proposed metrics. The higher the information gain for a metric is, the more it is able to reveal useful information about the maintainability of a feature model. ... The last two hypotheses (H3 and H4) are related to the predictive power of the defined metrics for maintainability and also the issue that a small set of metrics would be sufficient to accurately evaluate the maintainability of a feature model. To evaluate these hypotheses, we build four learning machines for predicting the three subcharacteristics of maintain- ability using the proposed metrics. In order to be able to build the learning machines, we create three datasets, one for each of the subcharacteristics of maintainability. Each dataset consists of various rows each of which represents the value of the ten metrics for each of the fourteen feature models, where the elements of each row are the metric values for that feature model and the label to be predicted for that row is the value of one of the sub- characteristics of maintainability. Given these three datasets, the goal is to build a learning machine that is able to accurately predict the label of a feature model (value of the relevant subcharacteristic of maintainability) based on the values of the structural metrics. In our experiments, we have developed four learning machines to predict the maintainability of a feature model from the decision tree and logistic regression family of learning machines. These learning machines are commonly used in the domain of software engineering for tasks such as software quality analysis and effort prediction (Khoshgoftaar et al. 2009; Kocaguneli et al. 2009; Liu et al. 2010): Decision Trees are predictive machine learning techniques that identify the value of a dependent variable based on the value of a set of independent variables. Three variations of decision trees, namely J48, ID3, and CART, have been used in our experiments. It is important to mention that the set of metrics used by the decision tree algorithm to build an accurate prediction model will be considered to be the sufficient subset of the metrics that are required for predicting the subcharacteristics of maintainability. Logistic Regression is a method that is employed for predicting the probability of an event by fitting the reference data points into a logistic curve. We have used a multinomial logistic regression model in our analysis. The Waikato Environment for Knowledge Analysis (WEKA) (Garner 1995), which is a widely used suite of machine learning techniques, was employed to learn and test the built learning machines based on our collected independent and dependent variables.
paraphrases: To assess the similarity of subjective opinions regarding maintainability subcharacteristics, we used Intra-class Correlation (ICC), with results from a two-way random effects model and 95% confidence interval presented in Table 7. Our initial hypothesis (H1) posited a significant correlation between defined metrics and maintainability, which we tested using Spearman's Rho correlation coefficient (significance level 0.05) after a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test showed non-normal data distribution. We investigated three correlation types: Inter-metric Correlation (to check if metrics represent distinct aspects or are related), Metrics Indicativeness (to determine if metrics effectively indicate maintainability and its subcharacteristics), and Inter-quality Correlation (to examine relationships between maintainability's subelements, like understandability and analyzability). These studies helped characterize dependent and independent variables. Subsequently, hypothesis H2 proposed that our structural metrics could serve as discriminators for maintainability. We also utilized entropy (Fenton and Neil 1999) to quantify how these metrics reduce uncertainty about a feature model's maintainability. Entropy represents uncertainty; thus, gaining information from a metric's value about maintainability reduces this uncertainty, a concept known as information gain (Kent 1983). Higher information gain, calculated via Kullback–Leibler divergence (Hershey and Olsen 2007), signifies a metric's greater ability to reveal useful maintainability information and reduce uncertainty. Finally, hypotheses H3 and H4 focused on the predictive power of these metrics and the sufficiency of a small subset for accurate maintainability evaluation. To address these, we developed four learning machines (from decision tree and logistic regression families, commonly used in software engineering for quality and effort prediction) to predict maintainability's three subcharacteristics. We created three datasets, each containing metric values for fourteen feature models and the corresponding maintainability subcharacteristic as the label. Decision trees (J48, ID3, CART) identified a sufficient subset of metrics for prediction, while a multinomial logistic regression model predicted event probabilities. WEKA (Garner 1995) was used to train and test these learning machines.

Our investigation began by employing Intra-class Correlation (ICC) to quantify the agreement among participant opinions on maintainability's subcharacteristics, with detailed statistical results (95% CI, two-way random effects model) in Table 7. We first hypothesized (H1) a substantial link between our metrics and maintainability. Since a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test indicated non-normal data, we used Spearman's Rho (p < 0.05) for correlation analysis. This involved three correlation types: Inter-metric, to assess metric distinctiveness or relationships; Metrics Indicativeness, to evaluate their utility as maintainability indicators; and Inter-quality, to explore correlations among maintainability's subcharacteristics, such as understandability and analyzability. These analyses illuminated the characteristics of our variables. Next, we posited (H2) that the structural metrics could differentiate maintainability levels. We then introduced the concept of entropy (Fenton and Neil 1999) to quantify how these metrics diminish uncertainty concerning a feature model's maintainability. Essentially, entropy measures uncertainty, and gaining information from a metric reduces this uncertainty, yielding "information gain" (Kent 1983). We computed this using Kullback–Leibler divergence (Hershey and Olsen 2007), where higher information gain implies a metric's greater effectiveness in reducing uncertainty about maintainability. For our final hypotheses (H3 and H4), concerning metric predictive power and the efficacy of a minimal metric set for maintainability assessment, we constructed four learning machines (from the decision tree and logistic regression families, chosen for their prevalence in software engineering for tasks like quality analysis and effort prediction). We created three datasets, each representing a maintainability subcharacteristic, comprising metric values for fourteen feature models. Decision tree variations (J48, ID3, CART) helped identify a sufficient metric subset, and a multinomial logistic regression model was employed. The WEKA platform (Garner 1995) facilitated the training and testing of these models using our collected data.

text: We evaluate the performance of our techniques based on two types of metrics, following Wang et al. [61] practi- cal guide for selecting quality indicators: (i) quality metrics: how good is the obtained Pareto front? and (ii) diversity metrics: how large/representative are its solutions? ... In order to validate the significance of our comparison, we per- form a statistical test using a non-parametric test: the two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (MWU). On every target, MWU takes in the different performance values obtained by both eSATiBEA and SAT- IBEA on a given metric from each run (in our case 30). MWU re- turns the p -value that one of the algorithms obtains different val- ues than the other. We consider tests significant when they are be- low a significance level of 0.05. Moreover, given the small number of runs in our experiment, and in order to lower the risk of having incorrect rejection of true null hypothesis, we use a conservative but safe adjustment (i.e., the standard Bonferroni adjustment [4] ) which reduces the chances of their erroneous rejection. Further- more, following the advice in the practical guide proposed by Ar- curi and Briand [4] , we also use the non-parametric Â12 [59] effect size measure which evaluates the ratio of runs from the first al- gorithm that outperform the second one. It is considered in the literature that when Â12 is above 0.71, differences between the al- gorithms are large.
paraphrases: Following Wang et al.'s guidelines [61], we assessed our techniques' performance using two metric categories: quality metrics, which evaluate the Pareto front's effectiveness, and diversity metrics, which measure solution breadth and representativeness. To ensure the statistical validity of our comparisons, we employed the two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (MWU), a non-parametric test. For each target, MWU analyzed the performance values of eSATiBEA and SAT-IBEA across 30 runs for a given metric, yielding a p-value indicating if one algorithm performed significantly differently. We set the significance level at p < 0.05. Due to our limited number of runs, we applied the conservative Bonferroni adjustment [4] to mitigate false positive risks. Additionally, as advised by Arcuri and Briand [4], we used the non-parametric Â12 [59] effect size measure, which quantifies the proportion of runs where the first algorithm outperformed the second; an Â12 value exceeding 0.71 suggests substantial algorithmic differences.

Our techniques' performance was evaluated using two types of metrics, guided by Wang et al.'s practical recommendations [61]: quality metrics, which gauge the Pareto front's efficacy, and diversity metrics, which assess the scope and typicality of solutions. To statistically validate our comparisons, we conducted a two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (MWU), a non-parametric method. For each target, MWU processed the performance data from 30 runs of both eSATiBEA and SAT-IBEA for each metric, generating a p-value that indicated whether one algorithm's results significantly differed from the other's. We considered tests statistically significant when p < 0.05. Given the small number of experimental runs, we incorporated the Bonferroni adjustment [4] as a conservative measure to reduce the likelihood of incorrectly rejecting a true null hypothesis. Furthermore, in line with Arcuri and Briand's practical guide [4], we also utilized the non-parametric Â12 effect size measure [59] to determine the proportion of runs where the first algorithm outperformed the second. A commonly accepted threshold in the literature is that an Â12 value greater than 0.71 signifies considerable differences between algorithms.

text: Composition and measurement stage In total, 180 composi- tions were performed, being 60 in the Mobile Media, 60 in the Shogi Game and 60 in the Checkers Game. The composi- tions were performed manually using the IBM RSA [19,35]. The result of this phase was a document of composition descriptions, including the gathered data from the applica- tion of our metrics suite and all design models created. We used a well-validated suite of inconsistency metrics applied in previous work [14] focused on quantifying syntactic and semantic inconsistencies. The syntactic inconsistencies were quantified using the IBM RSA’s model validation mecha- nism. The semantic inconsistencies were quantified using the SDMetrics tool [46]. In addition, we also check both syntactic and semantic inconsistencies manually because some metrics, e.g., “the number of non-meaningful model elements” depends on the meaning of the model elements and the current modeling tools are unable to compute this metric. The identification of the inconsistencies was performed in three review cycles in order to avoid false positives and false negatives. We also consulted the developers as needed, such as checking and confirming specific cases of semantic incon- sistencies. On the other hand, the well-formedness (syntac- tic and semantic) rules defined in the UML metamodel were automatically checked by the IBM RAS’s model validation mechanism. _Effort assessment stage: The goal of the third phase was to assess the effort to resolve the inconsistencies using the quan- tification method described in Sect. 3.4. The composition heuristics were used to generate the evolved models, so that we could evaluate the effect of stability on the model com- position effort. In order to support a detailed data analy- sis, the assessment phase was further decomposed in two main stages. The first stage is concerned with pinpointing the inconsistency rates produced by the compositions (H1). The second stage aims at assessing the effort to resolve a set of previously identified inconsistencies (H2).
paraphrases: During the composition and measurement stage, 180 compositions were manually created using IBM RSA [19,35], equally divided among Mobile Media, Shogi Game, and Checkers Game (60 each). This phase yielded documentation detailing compositions, metric data, and design models. We employed a validated suite of inconsistency metrics [14] to quantify both syntactic (using IBM RSA's validation) and semantic inconsistencies (using SDMetrics [46]). Manual checks for both types were also performed, especially for metrics like "number of non-meaningful model elements" which current tools cannot assess. Inconsistencies were identified through three review cycles to minimize errors, with developer consultations for specific semantic cases. IBM RSA's mechanism also automatically verified UML metamodel well-formedness rules. The subsequent effort assessment stage focused on quantifying inconsistency resolution effort as per Section 3.4. Composition heuristics generated evolved models to evaluate stability's impact on composition effort. This stage had two sub-stages: H1, identifying inconsistency rates from compositions, and H2, assessing the effort to resolve previously found inconsistencies.

In the composition and measurement phase, a total of 180 compositions were created manually using IBM RSA [19,35], with an even distribution of 60 compositions for Mobile Media, Shogi Game, and Checkers Game. This phase's output included composition descriptions, data from our metric suite, and all generated design models. We leveraged a well-established set of inconsistency metrics from prior research [14] to quantify both syntactic and semantic inconsistencies. IBM RSA's model validation mechanism was used for syntactic inconsistencies, while the SDMetrics tool [46] handled semantic inconsistencies. Additionally, we manually checked both types, particularly for metrics dependent on element meaning (e.g., "number of non-meaningful model elements") that current tools cannot compute. Inconsistencies were identified through three review cycles to prevent false positives and negatives, with developers consulted for specific semantic issues. IBM RSA also automatically verified UML metamodel well-formedness rules. The effort assessment stage, the third phase, aimed to quantify the effort required for inconsistency resolution using the method outlined in Section 3.4. Composition heuristics were utilized to create evolved models, allowing us to evaluate how stability influenced model composition effort. For detailed data analysis, this assessment phase was divided into two main stages: H1, which focused on determining the inconsistency rates produced by the compositions, and H2, which sought to measure the effort to resolve a set of previously identified inconsistencies.

text: All measurements were performed on the same Windows 7 Machine with Intel Core i5 CPU 3.5 GHz and 16 GB RAM. The algorithms are compute-bound and not memory inten- sive. Since Henard et at. reported that SATIBEA stabilizes on its ultimate solutions in 15min [26], we performed each studied algorithm 15min to compute the approximate Pareto front for each subject. To reduce measurement fluctuations caused by random- ness (e.g., the randomness of performing crossover and mutation), we independently executed each algorithm 30 times for each subject to support inferential statistical test- ing for significance and assessment of effect size. We took both the median and mean values of the measurements for analysis.
paraphrases: All tests were conducted on an identical Windows 7 system, equipped with an Intel Core i5 CPU running at 3.5 GHz and 16 GB of RAM. Given that the algorithms are CPU-intensive rather than memory-intensive, and referencing Henard et al.'s finding that SATIBEA reaches stable solutions within 15 minutes, each algorithm under study was run for 15 minutes to generate an approximate Pareto front for every subject. To mitigate variability stemming from random factors like crossover and mutation operations, each algorithm was run 30 times per subject. This approach was adopted to enable robust inferential statistical testing for significance and to evaluate effect size. For our analysis, we considered both the median and mean values derived from these measurements.

Measurements were consistently performed on a Windows 7 machine featuring an Intel Core i5 CPU (3.5 GHz) and 16 GB RAM. The algorithms in question are computationally intensive but not memory-intensive. Drawing from Henard et al.'s work [26], which indicates SATIBEA stabilizes on its final solutions within 15 minutes, we ran each algorithm for 15 minutes to calculate an approximate Pareto front for each subject. To minimize measurement variations due to randomness (e.g., in crossover and mutation), each algorithm was executed 30 times independently per subject, facilitating inferential statistical analysis for significance and effect size. Both the median and mean values from these measurements were utilized for our analysis.

Our research collected two distinct types of data: quantitative and qualitative. The quantitative analysis focused on the fitness values of experimental solutions. We began by plotting the resulting fronts, then evaluated their quality using hypervolume [47] and Euclidean distance to the ideal solution (ED) [23] metrics. Subsequently, we report on each algorithm's execution time. For the qualitative analysis, only one generated architecture was scrutinized due to the infeasibility of manually reviewing all solutions. The aim was to determine: (i) its intrinsic quality; (ii) its practical usefulness for the architect; (iii) whether design patterns were appropriately implemented; and (iv) if any anomalies were present in the PLA design after optimization.

text: Number of Features. First, we measured how calculation time scales as feature models increase in size. Therefore, we varied the size of the generated feature model between 10 and 10 000 features (which is significantly larger than all reported feature models in practice we came across). For each feature model, we performed 10 random edits (not restricted to refactorings or generalizations). As described above, we performed 200 repetitions for each model size, as there is a fluctuation of calculation times depending on the randomly generated models (with the same size) and the randomly performed edits. ... Kind of Edits. Next, we performed the same measurement varying the feature model size from 10 to 10 000, but now we distinguished between different possible edits. This should determine whether changes that make arbitrary edits are more difficult to detect than those selected from Alves’ set of sound operations. We distinguish between three possible kinds of edits: refactorings from the catalog of sound opera- tions, generalizations from the same catalog, and arbitrary edits as described above. Specializations are not considered as they are the inverse of generalizations. Again we applied 10 random edits of this classification (i.e., 10 refactorings, or 10 generalizations, or 10 arbitrary edits) to each feature model. ... Number of Edits. Finally, we measured the calculation time while varying the number of edits for a fixed feature model size of 1000 features. In this way, we can deter- mine whether more edits require longer calculation times. We again distinguish between the three classifications refac- toring, generalization (which includes specialization), and arbitrary edits. ... As special cases, we also measured identical feature mod- els (0 edits) and compared completely independently gen- erated feature models with the same feature names (which is roughly similar to an infinite number of edits and can be regarded as upper bound).
paraphrases: To study the impact of feature model size, we first investigated how calculation time changes with an increasing number of features, ranging from 10 to 10,000 (a range exceeding typically encountered models). For each model size, we introduced 10 random modifications (not limited to refactorings or generalizations), repeating each test 200 times to account for variations arising from randomly generated models and edits. Next, we repeated this experiment, varying feature model sizes from 10 to 10,000, but this time categorizing the edits. Our goal was to ascertain if arbitrary changes are harder to detect than those derived from Alves’ sound operations. We differentiated among three types of edits: refactorings, generalizations (both from the sound operations catalog), and arbitrary edits. Specializations were excluded as they are inverse generalizations. Again, 10 random edits of a specific type (e.g., 10 refactorings) were applied to each feature model. Finally, we examined how calculation time varies with the number of edits, holding the feature model size constant at 1000 features, to see if more edits led to longer calculation times. This also distinguished between refactoring, generalization (including specialization), and arbitrary edits. Additionally, we analyzed special cases: identical feature models (zero edits) and entirely independent models with identical feature names, which approximates an infinite number of edits and serves as an upper bound.

We began by analyzing how calculation time scales with the number of features, testing models ranging from 10 to 10,000 features, a size significantly larger than most practical models. Each feature model was subjected to 10 random modifications (encompassing more than just refactorings or generalizations), with 200 repetitions per model size to mitigate fluctuations from random model generation and edits. Subsequently, we conducted the same size variation (10 to 10,000 features) but focused on the *kind* of edits. This aimed to determine if arbitrary changes are more challenging to detect than those from Alves' catalog of sound operations. We categorized edits into refactorings, generalizations (both from the sound operations catalog), and arbitrary edits (as described previously), excluding specializations as they are inverse generalizations. Again, 10 random edits of a single classification were applied to each feature model. Our final experiment investigated the *number* of edits, fixing the feature model size at 1000 features. This allowed us to see if more edits necessitate longer calculation times, again distinguishing between refactoring, generalization (which includes specialization), and arbitrary edits. We also included edge cases: identical feature models (0 edits) and independently generated feature models with the same feature names, which provides a conceptual upper bound resembling an infinite number of edits.

text: While data from the pre-questionnaire (e.g., age, interview experience, etc.) were directly entered into the statistical tool SPSS, the data gathered during observation (e.g., number of asked relevant questions, etc.) were recounted first in order to reduce the risk of measurement errors. The subjective ratings based on the Likert-scale in the post-questionnaire were collected in MS Excel. Additional qualitative comments were listed in MS Word. All data was processed anonymously and confidentially. For the quantitative observation data, descriptive statistics were then calculated. Further, the data distributions were analyzed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. This was done to determine a suitable hypothesis test based on the different tests’ assumptions regarding data distribution in an independent sample setting. For most hypotheses, we used the t-test for equality of means accordingly, except for those for which the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test had not confirmed equal distribution between the groups. As this was the case for H12, H13, H22, we used the suitable independent samples median test instead. However, as the T-Test is valid even under violation of its assumptions [15], we also used this test for non-parametric (but same) distributions. A cross-check with Mann-Whitney U confirmed that the application of the T-Test led to the same results. As all hypotheses were directional, we used one-tailed results with α=0.05.

text: The analysis on the collected data was carried out employ- ing SPSS PASW Statistics software, release 18.0.0. At first, a Shapiro-Wilks W test [27] was run on the dataset to test if they are normally distributed. This test is used when the number of data points is between 3 and 2 000 [27] and is per- formed because the prerequisite for a lot of statistical tests is knowing whether the data points are normally distributed or not. The test, with a confidence level of 95%, failed to reject the null hypothesis that the data was normally distributed. In other words, we are not assured about the normal distribution of the data points, and therefore, non-parametric statistical tests were appropriate to test our hypotheses. The statistical test that we used for both hypotheses was the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test (also known as Wilcoxon Rank Sum test and Mann-Whitney U test) [27]. This test is a non-parametric equivalent of the well-known T-Test, used for comparing two independent variables to test the null hypoth- esis that the two variables are from the same population and have the same mean values [27]. Therefore, it is most suitable when the research hypothesis is that the two variables are dif- ferent (the mean of data points of one variable is less than, greater than or just different from that of the other). Moreover, a significance level (α) must be set. α is the probability of a statistical error known as “Type I Error”, which happens when a null hypothesis is rejected while it is actually true. When the test is run, values called “p-values” are obtained that represent the significance probability. The p-values are compared against α to test the null hypotheses. When p-value is less than α, the null hypothesis is rejected [27]. In this research, we set α to 0.05, which is a commonly- used level in scientific works [27].
paraphrases: Data analysis was performed using SPSS PASW Statistics software, version 18.0.0. Initially, a Shapiro-Wilks W test [27] was conducted on the dataset to check for normal distribution, a crucial prerequisite for many statistical tests, particularly when data points range from 3 to 2,000 [27]. With a 95% confidence level, this test did not reject the null hypothesis of normal distribution, meaning we couldn't confirm the data's normality. Consequently, non-parametric statistical tests were deemed appropriate for our hypotheses. We employed the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test (also known as Wilcoxon Rank Sum or Mann-Whitney U test) [27], a non-parametric alternative to the T-Test. This test compares two independent variables to see if they originate from the same population and share identical mean values [27], making it ideal for hypotheses suggesting differences between variables (e.g., one mean is less than, greater than, or simply different from the other). We set the significance level (α), representing the probability of a Type I Error (falsely rejecting a true null hypothesis), at 0.05, a standard in scientific studies [27]. P-values, indicating significance probability, were compared against α; if a p-value was below α, the null hypothesis was rejected [27].

The collected data underwent analysis using SPSS PASW Statistics software, release 18.0.0. To ascertain normal distribution—a common requirement for many statistical procedures, especially with 3 to 2,000 data points [27]—a Shapiro-Wilks W test [27] was initially applied. At a 95% confidence level, this test did not allow us to reject the null hypothesis of normality. This outcome suggested that the normal distribution of our data points was not assured, thus necessitating the use of non-parametric statistical tests for our hypotheses. Both hypotheses were tested using the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test [27], also known as the Wilcoxon Rank Sum test or Mann-Whitney U test. This non-parametric counterpart to the T-Test is employed to compare two independent variables, specifically to assess the null hypothesis that they derive from the same population and possess identical mean values [27]. Therefore, it is particularly suitable when the research posits a difference between the two variables (e.g., one variable's mean is smaller, larger, or simply different from the other's). A significance level (α) must also be established; α denotes the likelihood of a "Type I Error," which occurs when a true null hypothesis is mistakenly rejected. During testing, "p-values" are generated, representing the probability of significance. These p-values are then compared to α; if a p-value is less than α, the null hypothesis is rejected [27]. For this research, we adopted an α of 0.05, a widely accepted standard in scientific literature [27].

text: In order to answer RQ1 a quantitative analysis was conducted. In this analysis, we assessed the number of solutions and per- formed an analysis of the Pareto fronts, in order to evaluate the capability of the algorithms in finding a great number and diver- sified solutions (PLAs). In this sense, we calculated the Error Ratio ( Van Veldhuizen, 1999 ) quality indicator for measuring the ratio between the solutions that are present in the approximated true Pareto front ( PF true Approx ) and the ones that are not. The lower the error ratio value, the better it is and a greater number of solutions are in PF true Approx . We used the hypervolume ( Zitzler et al., 2003 ) as the main quality indicator and the Kruskal Wallis (significance level of 95%) ( Derrac et al., 2011 ) as non-parametric statistic test. Hypervolume measures the coverage area of a known Pareto front ( PF known ) on the objective space regarding a nadir (reference) point. The higher the hypervolume, the better the Pareto front. In this work, we normalize the objective values between 0 and 1 and de- fine the nadir point as the worst possible point (1, 1) with a small offset, thus being (1.1, 1.1). Hypervolume was used because it has the capability to evaluate a set of solutions generated by multi-objective algorithms regard- ing convergence and diversity, besides being one of the most used indicators in the literature ( Bringmann et al., 2014 ). In addition, hypervolume is -completeness compliant ( Zitzler et al., 2003 ), which means that, hypervolume can measure if a Pareto front is better than another in terms of dominance relation ( Zitzler et al., 2003 ). It is a useful indicator for what we are trying to assess, since we want to find which resulting Pareto Front is the best one by comparing fronts generated by different sets of operators. Fur- thermore, for calculating the hypervolume, only the objective val- ues of the solutions and the nadir point is needed as entry. Other quality indicators also commonly used in the literature need infor- mation that are not available in this kind of problem. For exam- ple, IGD and GD ( Veldhuizen and Lamont, 1998 ) require the true Pareto Front, which we do not know. Other widely used quality indicator is R2 ( Hansen et al., 1998 ), which needs a weight vec- tor distributed uniformly in the objective space. In such work, we do not accurately know the objective space landscape. The objec- tive functions have maximum and minimum values, but it is not possible to know if these maximum and minimum will be reached during the optimization process. In order to answer RQ2 and RQ3 a qualitative analysis was conducted. In order to validate the effectiveness of the proposed search operators in preserving the architectural styles, we per- formed an analysis of the solutions organization and also analyzed the number of PLAs violated. An analysis of the feature modular- ization (related to FM) was also performed in order to verify the modularity of the PLAs. Taking into account that the architect will choose only one solution from the set of non-dominated solutions, we analyzed, for each experiment, the solutions with the lowest euclidean distance (ED) from the ideal solution. The lower the ED value, the better the trade-off between the objectives. In this work, the ideal solution has the fitness values of the objectives CM and FM equal to zero. ... The statistical test Kruskal Wallis was used in order to deter- mine if the configurations showed statistical differences. The con- figuration with the best significant hypervolume value was cho- sen for each combination of experiment and PLA. When there was not statistical difference (Kruskal Wallis) among hypervolume val- ues we selected the configuration with the lower number of eval- uations (population size ∗number of generations) in order to de- crease the execution time. The final experiment configurations are presented in Table 10 .
paraphrases: To address RQ1, we performed a quantitative analysis, evaluating the number and diversity of solutions (PLAs) found by the algorithms through an examination of Pareto fronts. We utilized the Error Ratio (Van Veldhuizen, 1999) to quantify the proportion of solutions present versus absent in the approximated true Pareto front (PFtrueApprox); a lower error ratio signifies a greater number of solutions within PFtrueApprox. The primary quality indicator was hypervolume (Zitzler et al., 2003), and Kruskal-Wallis (95% significance) (Derrac et al., 2011) served as the non-parametric statistical test. Hypervolume measures the coverage of a known Pareto front (PFknown) relative to a nadir point in the objective space; a higher hypervolume indicates a superior Pareto front. For this study, objective values were normalized to between 0 and 1, with the nadir point defined as (1.1, 1.1) (slightly offset from the worst possible point (1,1)). Hypervolume was chosen for its ability to assess the convergence and diversity of solutions from multi-objective algorithms and its widespread use in literature (Bringmann et al., 2014). Additionally, its ϵ-completeness compliance (Zitzler et al., 2003) allows for direct comparison of Pareto fronts based on dominance. This makes it ideal for determining the best Pareto front among those generated by different operators, requiring only solution objective values and the nadir point as input. Unlike other common indicators like IGD and GD (Veldhuizen and Lamont, 1998), which require an unknown true Pareto front, or R2 (Hansen et al., 1998), which needs a uniformly distributed weight vector (and our objective space landscape isn't precisely known, despite maximum and minimum values), hypervolume circumvents these data limitations.

For RQ2 and RQ3, a qualitative analysis was conducted. To validate the proposed search operators' effectiveness in maintaining architectural styles, we analyzed solution organization and the number of violated PLAs. Feature modularization (FM) was also examined to verify PLA modularity. Assuming an architect selects a single non-dominated solution, we identified, for each experiment, the solution with the minimum Euclidean distance (ED) from the ideal solution (CM and FM fitness values of zero); a smaller ED indicates a better objective trade-off. The Kruskal-Wallis statistical test was applied to detect significant differences between configurations. For each experiment-PLA combination, the configuration with the best significant hypervolume was selected. If no statistical difference in hypervolume existed (Kruskal-Wallis), we chose the configuration with fewer evaluations (population size * number of generations) to reduce execution time. Table 10 presents the final experimental configurations.

A quantitative analysis was performed to address RQ1. This involved evaluating the number and diversity of solutions (PLAs) produced by the algorithms through an analysis of Pareto fronts. We used the Error Ratio (Van Veldhuizen, 1999) as a quality indicator, which quantifies the proportion of solutions on the approximated true Pareto front (PFtrueApprox) compared to those not on it; a lower error ratio indicates a better outcome with more solutions on PFtrueApprox. The primary quality metric was hypervolume (Zitzler et al., 2003), and the Kruskal-Wallis test (with a 95% significance level) (Derrac et al., 2011) served as our non-parametric statistical test. Hypervolume measures the area covered by a known Pareto front (PFknown) in the objective space relative to a nadir (reference) point. A larger hypervolume signifies a superior Pareto front. In this study, we normalized objective values between 0 and 1 and set the nadir point to (1.1, 1.1), a slight offset from the worst possible point (1,1). Hypervolume was chosen for its capability to assess both the convergence and diversity of solutions generated by multi-objective algorithms, and it is a frequently used indicator in the literature (Bringmann et al., 2014). Furthermore, hypervolume is ϵ-completeness compliant (Zitzler ets al., 2003), enabling it to determine if one Pareto front dominates another. This makes it a valuable indicator for our goal of identifying the best resulting Pareto Front by comparing fronts from different operator sets. Crucially, hypervolume calculation only requires the objective values of solutions and the nadir point, unlike other common indicators such as IGD and GD (Veldhuizen and Lamont, 1998), which need an unknown true Pareto Front, or R2 (Hansen et al., 1998), which demands a uniformly distributed weight vector in an objective space whose landscape is not precisely known in this work, despite having maximum and minimum values for objective functions.

For RQ2 and RQ3, a qualitative analysis was conducted. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed search operators in preserving architectural styles, we analyzed the organization of solutions and the count of violated PLAs. We also examined feature modularization (FM) to assess the modularity of the PLAs. Recognizing that an architect would select a single solution from the non-dominated set, we identified the solutions with the smallest Euclidean distance (ED) from the ideal solution (where CM and FM fitness values are zero) for each experiment. A lower ED indicates a more favorable trade-off between objectives. The Kruskal-Wallis statistical test was employed to ascertain statistical differences among configurations. The configuration with the most significant hypervolume value was chosen for each experiment-PLA pairing. If the hypervolume values showed no statistical difference (via Kruskal-Wallis), the configuration with fewer evaluations (population size multiplied by the number of generations) was selected to minimize execution time. Table 10 outlines the final experimental configurations.

text: As analysis clients we used three different generic IFDS-based inter-procedural client analyses. Possible Types computes the possi- ble types for a value reference in the program. Such information can, for instance, be used for virtual-method-call resolution [4]. We track typing information through method boundaries. Field and array as- signments are treated with weak updates in a field-sensitive manner, abstracting from receiver objects through their context-insensitive points-to sets. Reaching Definitions is a reaching-definitions anal- ysis that computes variable definitions for their uses. To obtain inter-procedural flows, we implement a variant that tracks defini- tions through parameter and return-value assignments. Uninitialized Variables finds potentially uninitialized variables. Assume a call foo(x), where x is potentially uninitialized. Our analysis will deter- mine that all uses of the formal parameter of foo may also access an uninitialized value. We provide the source code for all three clients (only approx. 550LOC) in our download package. We include the Java 1.7 runtime libraries in our analysis. To evaluate the efficiency of SPLLIFT against the actual tradi- tional approach, we would ideally want to use a pre-processor to generate all possible products, and then apply the traditional anal- ysis approach to each resulting product, an approach which in our earlier work [25] we called A1. However, we quickly found that this approach is so intractable that it would even preclude us from finishing our experiments in due time. This is because the traditional approach would need to generate, parse and analyze every single product. A prerequisite for each analysis is a call graph, whose com- putation can easily take minutes on its own. Given the large number of possible configurations, it would have taken us years to complete the experiments. (Brabrand et al. [25] did not have this problem because their intra-procedural analyses need no call graph and must only consider up to 2k combinations where k is the maximal number of features within a single method. For our four benchmark subjects k is always ≤9.) We hence decided to compare SPLLIFT not to A1 but instead to our implementation of A2, which only requires a single parsing step and call-graph computation. A2 is thus naturally faster than A1, and therefore any performance gain we can show with respect to A2 would be even higher with respect to A1. We found that even with using A2, some experiments would still take years to complete, though, which is why we nevertheless use a cutoff-time of ten hours.
paraphrases: We utilized three distinct IFDS-based inter-procedural client analyses. These included "Possible Types" to determine potential types for program value references (useful for virtual-method-call resolution), "Reaching Definitions" to track variable definitions across method boundaries and assignments, and "Uninitialized Variables" to identify variables that might be used before initialization. The source code for these clients (around 550 lines) and Java 1.7 runtime libraries are provided. We initially planned to compare SPLLIFT with a traditional approach (A1) that generates all possible products and analyzes each, but this proved too time-consuming due to the need for a separate call graph computation for every product, extending completion to years. Therefore, we opted to compare SPLLIFT with our A2 implementation, which is faster as it only requires one parsing and call-graph step. Any performance improvements observed with A2 would be even more significant compared to A1, although even with A2, some experiments necessitated a ten-hour cutoff time.

Our analysis leveraged three generic IFDS-based inter-procedural clients. "Possible Types" determines the possible types for value references in a program, information that aids virtual-method-call resolution. "Reaching Definitions" tracks variable definitions, including those passed as parameters or returned, to understand inter-procedural data flow. "Uninitialized Variables" identifies variables that might be accessed without prior initialization, such as in a call like `foo(x)` where `x` is potentially uninitialized. All three client's source code (approximately 550 lines) is included in our download, alongside Java 1.7 runtime libraries. Our initial plan to evaluate SPLLIFT's efficiency against a traditional method (A1), which involved pre-processing to generate all products and then individually analyzing them, was deemed unfeasible. The generation, parsing, and analysis of each product, particularly the minutes-long call graph computation for each, would have extended the experiments over many years given the vast number of configurations. This issue was not faced by Brabrand et al. [25] due to their intra-procedural analyses. Consequently, we compared SPLLIFT against our A2 implementation, which is inherently faster due to its single parsing and call-graph computation step. We anticipate that any performance gains shown against A2 would be even more pronounced against A1. Despite using A2, some experiments remained prohibitively long, leading us to implement a ten-hour cutoff.

text: The non-parametric chi-square for independence test was applied to assess whether there are significant differences among the various groups (experienced and inexperienced participants using the same object of study) or the differences are by chance (Downing and Clarke, 1997). The application of this test was important to know, for example, if the degree of difficulty or simplicity of PL4BPM is dependent or independent of the participants’ experience level. Completing the data analysis, a hypothesis test (a population proportion test) was conducted for the decision of acceptance or denial of the null hypothesis, by using a significance level of 10%.

Following this, a population proportion test was performed with a 10% significance level to decide on the null hypothesis.

text: In this section we show and analyze the results obtained in the ex-periment. Firstly, we compare the fronts obtained by each algorithm using two standard quality indicators, Hypervolume and Generational Distance, with the purpose of identifying which MOEA performs best for our purpose. Secondly, we analyze the execution time for each MOEA and for each FM, in order to know which MOEAs are more efficient and whether their efficiency depends on the size of the FM. Thirdly, we compare the objectives’ values obtained in the initial pop-ulation with the values obtained in the final front. This allows us to quantify easily how the fitness of the population evolves along the execution of the algorithm. Fourthly, we apply the Mann–Whitney8 U test (Mann and Whitney, 1947) and the ˆA12 statistic (Vargha and Delaney, 2000) to the values of these metrics to assure that the dif-ferences identified are statistically meaningful. Lastly, we execute the MOEAs on a mobile device, evaluating whether they are efficient enough for the dynamic reconfiguration of mobile applications. ... We apply two statistical tests, Mann–Whitney U test and ˆA12 statistic, which are commonly applied in randomized algorithms, to assure that the differences among MOEAs identified in the previous section are statistically meaningful (Arcuri and Briand, 2014).
paraphrases: This section presents and analyzes the experimental findings. Our initial step involved comparing the performance of each algorithm's generated fronts using Hypervolume and Generational Distance, two established quality metrics, to pinpoint the most effective MOEA for our goals. Next, we examined the execution time of each MOEA for every FM to determine their efficiency and if it correlates with FM size. Thirdly, we tracked the evolution of population fitness by comparing objective values from the initial population with those from the final front. Subsequently, we applied the Mann–Whitney U test and the ˆA12 statistic to the metric values, ensuring the statistical significance of observed differences. Finally, we assessed the MOEAs' suitability for dynamic mobile application reconfiguration by running them on a mobile device.

We present and analyze the experimental results in this section. First, we evaluated the quality of fronts generated by each algorithm using Hypervolume and Generational Distance to identify the optimal MOEA for our objectives. Second, we assessed the execution time of each MOEA for different FMs to determine their efficiency and whether it is influenced by FM size. Third, we compared initial population objective values with final front values to quantify the evolution of population fitness throughout algorithm execution. Fourth, we employed the Mann–Whitney U test and the ˆA12 statistic to confirm the statistical significance of the observed differences in these metrics. Lastly, we ran the MOEAs on a mobile device to gauge their efficiency for dynamic mobile application reconfiguration.

text: The results for each dependent variable constitute a sample, therefore, the first analysis step consists of identifying the statistical distribution for each sample through the Shapiro and Wilk (1965) method. Its null hypothesis claims the population as normally distributed. The Shapiro-Wilk test determines which set of methods must be applied in the steps: hypothesis testing, strength of association between variables, two-sample analysis, and effect size estimation (meta-analysis). The set of parametric methods is applied in samples following the normal distribution, and non-parametric methods for the other ones. The hypothesis testing focuses on investigating differences between quality in the IR methods related to precision, recall, F-measure or execution time. This step is divided into analysis of variance, which analyzes the existence of any difference between methods, and the pairwise comparison, analyzing and indicating the eventual pairs of methods that lead to such result discrepancies. The parametric analysis of variance is addressed by ANOVA (Gelman 2005), complemented with results provided by the pairwise Student’s t test with Hochberg correction (Hochberg 1988) and Tukey’s honest significance difference (HSD) test (Tukey 1949). The non-parametric set comprises the Kruskal and Wallis (1952) method to analyze variances, and the Wilcoxon non-parametric test (Wilcoxon 1945) for pairwise comparison. The analysis of variance reveals differences between IR methods for any dependent variable. Aiming to characterize such differences, an additional hypothesis testing is applied to investigate which methods present greater (or lower) results when compared to others. The Welch’s t-test (Welch 1947) and Wilcoxon test realize it for parametric and non-parametric sets, respectively. Strength of association between experiment variables is the third step of the quantitative analysis. For numerical variables, the association is analyzed through the calculation of the Pearson’s or Spearman’s correlation coefficients (DeGroot and Schervish 2002). The Pearson’s coefficient holds for normally distributed samples, and Spearman’s coefficient is applied in samples following other distributions. On the other hand, the linear regression model (Montgomery et al. 2007) investigates the association between categorical variables, independent from sample distribution. The fourth step is the two-sample analysis, which aims to compare results from different experiment samples. Suitable statistical tests in this scenario are Welch’s t-test, used in the normally distributed samples, and Mann-Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney 1947), which does not require assumption of normal distributions. The first method proposes an adaptation of the Student’s t-test by analyzing two samples which have unequal variances and unequal sample size. The second one indicates whether a randomly selected value from one sample will be greater (or lower) than a randomly selected value from the another sample, both of them with any sample distribution. This experiment design not only seeks the eventual differences between experiment methods, but also intends to characterize eventual behavior differences of a method when applied into different experiment contexts. To achieve it, the last data analysis step is the effect size estimation (or meta-analysis). This is a statistical procedure that allows to integrate the results of a set of studies related to the matter of interest, as an attempt to reach a conclusion about the parameters of interest used in the studies. Meta-analysis is frequently realized by the effective size estimation, quantifying the effects of an experimental method (Kampenes et al. 2007). We adopted the Hedges’ g (Hedges et al. 1985) as a measure of effect size.
paraphrases: Our initial step in analyzing each dependent variable's sample was to determine its statistical distribution using the Shapiro and Wilk (1965) method, whose null hypothesis posits a normally distributed population. This test guided the choice of either parametric (for normally distributed data) or non-parametric methods for subsequent steps: hypothesis testing, assessing variable association, two-sample analysis, and effect size estimation. Hypothesis testing focused on identifying quality differences among IR methods (e.g., precision, recall), involving both variance analysis (ANOVA for parametric, Kruskal and Wallis for non-parametric) and pairwise comparisons (Student’s t-test with Hochberg correction/Tukey’s HSD for parametric, Wilcoxon for non-parametric). Further hypothesis testing, using Welch’s t-test and Wilcoxon, characterized which methods yielded superior or inferior results. The third step involved quantifying variable associations using Pearson’s (normal distributions) or Spearman’s (other distributions) correlation coefficients for numerical data, and linear regression for categorical variables. The fourth step, two-sample analysis, compared different experiment samples using Welch’s t-test (normal distributions) or Mann-Whitney U test (any distribution), with the latter assessing the probability of one sample’s random value exceeding another’s. Finally, to understand method behavior across contexts, effect size estimation (meta-analysis) was performed, using Hedges’ g as the effect size measure to synthesize study results.

The initial phase of our analysis involved characterizing the statistical distribution of each dependent variable's sample using the Shapiro and Wilk (1965) test, which assumes a normal distribution under its null hypothesis. The outcome of this test guided the selection of appropriate statistical methods—parametric for normally distributed samples and non-parametric for others—for subsequent stages: hypothesis testing, assessing inter-variable association, two-sample comparisons, and effect size estimation. Hypothesis testing aimed to uncover quality differences among IR methods in terms of metrics like precision and execution time. This stage encompassed variance analysis (ANOVA for parametric, Kruskal and Wallis for non-parametric) and pairwise comparisons (Student’s t-test with Hochberg correction and Tukey’s HSD for parametric; Wilcoxon for non-parametric) to identify discrepancies between method pairs. Further hypothesis testing, employing Welch’s t-test and Wilcoxon, was conducted to pinpoint methods with superior or inferior results. The third analytical step focused on determining the strength of association between experimental variables; Pearson’s or Spearman’s correlation coefficients were calculated for numerical variables based on their distribution, while linear regression was applied to categorical variables irrespective of distribution. The fourth step, two-sample analysis, compared results from distinct experimental samples using Welch’s t-test for normally distributed data and the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normal distributions, with the latter assessing the likelihood of a random value from one sample being greater or lesser than a random value from another. Beyond identifying method differences, this experimental design also sought to characterize behavioral variations of methods across different experimental contexts. To this end, the final data analysis step involved effect size estimation (meta-analysis), a statistical technique for integrating study results to draw conclusions about key parameters; we specifically used Hedges’ g (Hedges et al. 1985) as our effect size measure.

text: The quantitative data related to response times and errors com- mitted were considered as discrete data. Errors committed were con- sidered as discrete data since there is no evidence that will allow us to safely assign unequal unit weightings to the different types of errors. We used the Shapiro–Wilk test to examine if the data sets complied with the normality assumptions [55]. For this experiment, we used the Shapiro–Wilk test as it does not require that the mean or variance of the hypothesized normal distribution to be specified in advance. Another reason for using the Shapiro–Wilk test is that there was no causal explanation as to the nature of the distribution that the data points are sampled from. Data sets were then compared to detect sta- tistically significant results using the Mann–Whitney U statistic [56]. The Hodges–Lehman method was used to calculate the confidence in- tervals around the difference between medians given at the standard p<0.05 level [32]. Tool support was used to record response time and to perform the scoring of the answers. Time and scoring were performed automati- cally using tool support. Qualitative data was stored in a spreadsheet.
paraphrases: Response times and errors were treated as discrete quantitative data, with errors specifically classified as discrete due to the lack of justification for assigning different weights to error types. We employed the Shapiro–Wilk test [55] to verify the normality of our datasets, choosing this test because it doesn't require pre-specified mean or variance for the hypothesized normal distribution and because the underlying data distribution was unknown. Subsequently, the Mann–Whitney U statistic [56] was used to identify statistically significant differences between datasets. Confidence intervals for median differences were calculated using the Hodges–Lehman method at a p<0.05 significance level [32]. Response times and answer scoring were automatically recorded and performed with tool support, while qualitative data was managed in a spreadsheet.

To ascertain if our datasets adhered to normality assumptions, we applied the Shapiro–Wilk test [55]. This particular test was selected for our experiment because it does not necessitate prior specification of the mean or variance for the assumed normal distribution, and we lacked a causal understanding of the data points' underlying distribution. Following this, we compared datasets using the Mann–Whitney U statistic [56] to uncover any statistically significant findings. Confidence intervals for the difference between medians were computed at the standard p<0.05 level using the Hodges–Lehman method [32]. Tools were utilized to automatically record response times and score answers. Qualitative data was compiled and stored in a spreadsheet.

text: The subjects’ questionnaires were checked by a grader who was not involved in this research and who was given a predefined solution in order to grade the subjects’ answers. The comprehension level, which as noted is a dependent variable in this empirical study, was measured as the number of correct answers (true/false) plus the number of fully or partially correct explanations (arguments): each correct true/false answer was 1 point, while an explanation could be 0, 0.5, or 1 point for representing an incorrect, partial or full argumentation, respectively. Examining the Pearson correlations between the answers, the explanations, and the overall comprehension levels (Witte and Witte 2009; pp. 133–137), we found that the students’ answers and explanations are highly correlated (correlations ranging from 0.637 to 0.992 with a significant level of 0.01). Thus, in the rest of the paper we present and refer only to the comprehension levels which sum the answer and explanation scores.
