Our analysis of Pearson correlations (Witte and Witte 2009) revealed a strong correlation between student answers, explanations, and overall comprehension levels (0.637 to 0.992 at a 0.01 significance level). Therefore, we will solely focus on the combined comprehension levels (answer and explanation scores) throughout the remainder of the paper.

An external grader, unbiased by the research, scored the participants' questionnaires using a pre-defined answer key. In this empirical study, comprehension level, a dependent variable, was quantified by summing the points from correct true/false responses (1 point each) and the points from complete or partial explanations (ranging from 0 for incorrect to 1 for full argumentation). A Pearson correlation analysis (Witte and Witte 2009) indicated a high degree of correlation between student answers, explanations, and their combined comprehension levels (correlations between 0.637 and 0.992, significant at p < 0.01). Consequently, for the rest of the paper, we will exclusively present and discuss the overall comprehension levels, which represent the aggregate of answer and explanation scores.

text: We used three performance metrics to study the results of the experiments. Hypervolume (HV) [Zitzler and Thiele 1999] is a very popular metric in the EMO area due to its good theoretical and practical properties, such as being compliant with Pareto dominance (if one population Pareto dominates another, then it has a higher HV) and not requiring the problem’s Pareto front to be known. HV calculates the volume of the objective space between the obtained solution set and a reference point. A large value is preferable and reflects good performance of the solution set in terms of convergence, extensity, and uniformity. Figure 2 gives an illustration of the HV metric for four solution sets with different performance. As shown, the solution set that has good convergence, extensity, and uniformity (Figure 2(a)) leads to a larger shaded area (HV value) than the other three solution sets that have poor convergence, extensity, or uniformity, respectively (Figure 2(b)–(d)). In the calculation of HV, two crucial issues are the scaling of the search space [Friedrich et al. 2009] and the choice of the reference point [Auger et al. 2009]. Since the objectives in the considered optimization problems take different ranges of values, we normalized the objective value of the obtained solutions according to the problem’s range in the objective space. Also, the reference point was set to the Nadir point of the problem’s range (the point constructed with the worst value on each objective). In addition, note that the exact calculation of the HV metric is often infeasible for a solution set with seven or more objectives, and so for the problems with eight objectives, we estimated the HV result of a solution set by the Monte Carlo sampling method used by Bader and Zitzler [2011]. Here, 10,000,000 sampling points were used to ensure accuracy [Bader and Zitzler 2011]. Since the software engineer is only interested in valid products, we also introduced two metrics to evaluate the ability of each algorithm to return valid products. These metrics are (1) the number of executions where there was at least one valid individual in the final population, denoted VN, and (2) the rate of valid individuals in the final population, denoted VR. Finally, it is necessary to mention that in computing HV, we only used the valid solutions in the population (as invalid solutions could be meaningless for the decision maker). As a result, we computed HV using only the valid individuals in the final population and so used all objectives except the first one (the number of constraints violated). In addition, the results of HV and VR given in the tables were averaged over the executions where at least one valid individual was returned. In cases where valid solutions were not produced in any of the 30 executions (VN = 0), we reported 0 for HV and VR. Since invalid products have no value, the most important metric is the value of VN. A high value for VR means that the software engineer has many valid products from which to choose, and a high value for HV means that these have good performance in terms of convergence and diversity. ... We used rigorous nonparametric statistical tests to compare the HV values returned by the algorithms when using the novel encoding and 1 + n approach.We first tested the hypothesis that all EMO algorithms perform equally using the Kruskal-Wallis test, finding that the hypothesis was rejected at the 95% confidence level. Note that this was the case in all of the experiments reported in this article and so this step is not mentioned again. We then used the post hoc Kruskal-Wallis test (implemented in SPSS) for pairwise comparisons of the six algorithms. In all of the experiments, the final p-value between two algorithms was obtained after the Bonferroni adjustment was made (this step will not be described again). We also used the Mann-Whitney U test to calculate the effect size (ES) of pairwise algorithms. First, the standardized test statistic Z was obtained by the Mann-Whitney U test (implemented by SPSS). Then the ES was calculated using ES = √Z N, where N is the total number of samples.
paraphrases: To analyze our experimental results, we employed three key performance metrics. Hypervolume (HV) [Zitzler and Thiele 1999] was a primary choice in EMO due to its desirable properties, including compliance with Pareto dominance and not requiring prior knowledge of the Pareto front. HV quantifies the objective space volume between the solution set and a reference point; a larger value signifies superior convergence, extensity, and uniformity. For its calculation, we normalized objective values due to varying ranges and set the reference point to the Nadir point. For problems with eight objectives where exact HV computation is infeasible, we used Monte Carlo sampling with 10,000,000 points for accuracy [Bader and Zitzler 2011]. Since only valid products are relevant to software engineers, we also introduced two metrics: VN (number of executions with at least one valid individual) and VR (rate of valid individuals in the final population). Crucially, HV calculations considered only valid solutions. HV and VR results were averaged over successful executions, with zero reported if no valid solutions were produced. VN is the most critical metric, while high VR indicates many valid choices and high HV signifies good performance in valid products. We used rigorous non-parametric statistical tests to compare HV values for different algorithmic approaches. Initially, the Kruskal-Wallis test rejected the hypothesis of equal performance across EMO algorithms at a 95% confidence level in all experiments. Pairwise comparisons were then conducted using a post-hoc Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni adjustment. The Mann-Whitney U test was used to calculate effect size (ES) for pairwise algorithms, deriving ES from the standardized test statistic Z and the total sample size N.

Our experiments were assessed using three performance metrics. Hypervolume (HV) [Zitzler and Thiele 1999] is a widely recognized EMO metric valued for its theoretical and practical advantages, such as adherence to Pareto dominance and independence from a known Pareto front. HV measures the volume within the objective space bounded by the solution set and a reference point; a higher HV indicates better convergence, coverage, and distribution of solutions. We addressed the challenges of HV calculation, specifically search space scaling [Friedrich et al. 2009] and reference point selection [Auger et al. 2009], by normalizing objective values and setting the reference point to the Nadir point. For problems with eight objectives where exact HV is complex, we estimated HV using the Monte Carlo sampling method [Bader and Zitzler 2011] with 10,000,000 samples for precision. To cater to software engineers' interest in valid products, we added two metrics: VN, the count of executions yielding at least one valid individual, and VR, the proportion of valid individuals in the final population. Significantly, HV was computed solely on valid solutions, excluding meaningless invalid ones. Reported HV and VR values were averaged over executions that produced at least one valid individual, and were set to zero if no valid solutions were generated. VN is paramount, as invalid products hold no value. A high VR ensures numerous valid product options, while a high HV signifies superior performance in terms of convergence and diversity among these valid products. For comparing algorithm HV values, particularly with novel encoding and the 1+n approach, we employed robust non-parametric statistical tests. The Kruskal-Wallis test initially confirmed significant performance differences among EMO algorithms at a 95% confidence level across all experiments. Subsequent pairwise comparisons between the six algorithms utilized a post-hoc Kruskal-Wallis test (SPSS), with p-values adjusted via Bonferroni correction. We also quantified effect size (ES) for pairwise algorithmic comparisons using the Mann-Whitney U test, calculating ES as √Z/N from the standardized test statistic Z and total sample size N.

text: 5. Analysis of modularity: In order to investigate their predictive power, we first use the measures described in Section 4.2 to assess the modularity of the three product lines used as our target cases. We focus on quantifying the crosscutting properties of the different features of these systems. In that sense, we compute the Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting metrics for the features and the Degree of tangling for the use cases. As a result of the analysis: (i) the features with poor modularity, i.e. those with higher degree of scattering and crosscut- ting, are obtained; and (ii) use cases addressing more features, i.e. with more tangled concerns, are identified. Moreover, the analysis is used to extract important conclusions, such as the need for a spe- cific metric for crosscutting aiming to help developers to identify some crosscutting situations that scattering and tangling metrics do not capture. Second, once modularity has been assessed, it is compared with different maintainability attributes in Section 6. Then, this section computes all the values needed for the empirical comparison between modularity and maintainability. ... 6.1. Changeability analysis: This section addresses RQ1 testing whether the features with higher impact of changes (no matter whether they are variable or mandatory) are those with higher Degree of crosscutting (Hypothesis 1). In order to have a way to assess the change impact of a feature, we use the idea presented in Ref. [23]. This work is also based on the crosscutting pattern introduced in Section 2 and it de- fines change impact in terms of the elements involved in the change of a source element. Assuming there are two related domains (source and target), the change impact of a source ele- ment is defined as the addition of the number of trace links that must be changed and the number of trace links that must be pre- served. In Fig. 9 an example of several source and target elements related is shown. A change in the source element s2 implies to change target elements t1, t2 and t3. There are three trace links from s2 to these target elements. However, since s1 and s3 are also addressed by two of the target elements changed, the trace links from s1 to t1 and from s3 to t3 must be also preserved, so that s1 and s3 are also affected by the change of s2: impact (s2) = change ((s2, t1), (s2, t2), (s2, t3)) + preserve ((s1, t1), (s3, t3)). Using this assumption, the change impact of a source element can be quantified using our dependency matrix (dm). In particular, the number of trace links affected by a change of a source element sk is calculated counting the number of 1 values of row k and the number of 1 values in the columns where there are 1’s in row k. Applying formula (11), the impact set of a change in each fea- ture in the different releases of MobileMedia has been calculated. Table 17 shows these results. The table shows, for each feature, the number of trace links affected by a change in the feature. These trace links include both the links to be changed and the links to be preserved. Since we are focusing on changes in features, in this analysis we consider modifications to accomplish changes in func- tional specifications or, in general, requirements of the system. An M, V, or O has been added to the feature’s name indicating whether the feature is mandatory, variable or optional, respectively. Note also that the Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting for each feature are also shown in the table in order to be compared with the Impact Set metric. Finally, taking the results obtained by the change impact analysis, the Impact Set metric has been correlated with both Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting metrics. The results are shown in Figs. 10 and 11 where we can see the cor- relations for the eight different releases. We have used the least squares criterion to estimate the linear regression between the variables assessed. Finally, in order to study how tangling affects changeability, the Impact set has been also compared with the Degree of tangling. Note that, the former is a metric defined in terms of source elements whilst the latter is defined based on target elements. Then, in order to compare both measurements, the Concern degree of tangling metric for each concern has been defined. This new metric is calcu- lated by the addition of the Degree of tangling of each use case that addresses the corresponding concern. Then, this metric was com- puted by using the dependency matrix for each release. This matrix was modified to show the Degree of tangling of the different use cases instead of just representing the mappings existing between source and target elements. For the sake of simplicity, the depen- dency matrix for release 7 is the only one shown. This matrix is de- picted in Table 18. As an example, observe that the cells of the first column have been changed by values of 0.28 which is the Degree of tangling of the Add Album use case. The Concern degree of tangling for each concern is shown in the last column of the table. Then, once the Concern degree of tangling have been calculated for each release, these values are compared with the impact set metric previously calculated. Table 19 shows the values obtained for both metrics and for each release. Based on these values, both metrics have been also correlated. The correlation between Impact set and Concern degree of tangling for each release is presented in Fig. 12, from a to h. Regarding to our second analyzed system, the HealthWatcher, Fig. 13 shows the correlation of the Impact Set metric with Degree of Crosscutting in the five releases of the system. Similarly, Fig. 14 shows the correlations between the metrics Impact Set and Concern Degree of Tangling for the same system. The same correlations are also shown for the SmartHome system in Figs. 15 and 16, respectively. ... 6.3. Stability analysis: To date, there is no empirical study that investigates whether scattering and crosscutting negatively affect software stability at requirements level. This section addresses RQ2 by analysing whether the concerns with a higher degree of scattering and cross- cutting are addressed by more unstable use cases than concerns with lower degree of scattering and crosscutting (Hypothesis 2). It also compares the degree of tangling of the use cases in order to study whether those with higher values are more unstable. Sta- bility is highly related to change management so that the more unstable a system is, the more complicated the change management becomes [23]. Unstable models gradually lead to the degeneration of the design maintainability and its quality in gen- eral [23]. Then, we can infer that early crosscutting is likely to have a negative effect on software quality. In this analysis we mainly fo- cus on changes in the functionality of the system, i.e. modifications to accomplish changes in requirements or functional specifications [10]. It is important to highlight that our focus is not on corrective changes performed to remove bugs or on perfective modifications. However, we do not rule out this kind of changes in future analyses and they should be the target of further studies. In order to perform our empirical study, Table 20 shows the use cases (rows) which are modified in the different releases (columns) of the MobileMedia. A modification in a use case is mainly due to: either (i) the concerns, which it addresses, have evolved or (ii) it has been affected by the addition, modification or removal of a concern to the system. In this table, a ‘1’ in a cell represents that the corresponding use case has been modified in that release. As an example, in release 1 (r1) all the cells in the column present the value 1. This is due to the fact that Error Handling is added in this release, and this concern affects all use cases. An ‘‘a’’ in a cell represents that the use case is added in that release. There are also some use cases whose names are modified in a release. These use cases are marked in the ‘‘Renaming’’ column, where the release which introduces the modification in the name is shown (e.g. Add Photo use case modifies its name to Add Media in release 6). Finally, use cases with a number of modifications higher than a threshold value (higher than 1 in our analysis) are marked as unstable. To study how crosscutting properties affect to stability, once the changes affecting each use case are known, these values are used to compare with our metrics. First, we observe the Degree of tangling for each use case in order to analyse if those use cases with a higher number of changes (unstable) are also more tangled (whole data in Ref. [48]). Then, in Table 21 the Degree of tangling for each use case is compared with the number of changes. In order to relate stabil- ity with metrics for source elements, the dependency matrix for re- lease 7 of the MobileMedia was observed to calculate the number of unstable use cases which realise each concern. The results ob- tained are presented in Table 22. In this table, the columns show the unstable use cases, in particular, those with two modifications or more. The concerns are shown in the rows. A cell with 1 repre- sents that the use case addresses the corresponding concern. The last column of the table shows the total number of unstable use cases contributing to each concern. Then, the number of unstable use cases for each concern is re- lated with the degree of scattering and crosscutting for such con- cerns. In particular, Fig. 17 shows the linear regression between the number of unstable use cases and the Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting metrics, respectively. Again, the least squares criteria to estimate the linear regression between the variables as- sessed was used. At a first glance, we may anticipate that use cases addressing scattered or crosscutting concerns are more prone to be unstable. This first intuition is later confirmed by the computation of Pearson’s coefficient, as it is explained in next section. The selec- tion of scattering and tangling metrics is influenced by our purpose of comparing modularity with stability. Then, this is why we select the metrics quantifying crosscutting properties (closely related to modularity). The process to compare modularity and stability was replicated for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems. We do not show here all the data calculated in the process but just show the corre- lations between instability and both Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting metrics. These correlations may be observed in Figs. 18 and 19 for both systems, respectively. ... 6.5. Dependency analysis: It has been already observed that feature dependencies are harmful for maintainability of software assets [17,20,35,39]. How- ever, to date there is no empirical study analysing whether the presence of crosscutting features at requirements level increments dependencies between features, making thus, their maintainability difficult. This section addresses RQ3 investigating whether the presence of crosscutting introduces dependencies between fea- tures (Hypothesis 3.1). This hypothesis is tested by using our con- cern metrics to infer information about the feature dependencies existing in the product line. Moreover, since crosscutting has been compared with change impact and stability in previous sections, we also compare these two maintainability attributes with feature dependencies showing their relation (Hypothesis 3.2). In Ref. [17], the authors introduce the concepts of feature inter- lacing in order to assess feature dependencies in a product line. Interlacing denotes the situation where the implementations of two features, F1 and F2, have one or more components (or operations) in common [17]. The authors introduce the metric Component-level Interlacing Between Concerns (CIBC) which counts the number of components shared by two different features. This metric, among others defined in Refs. [17,18,27,37], have been previously used to assess dependencies at the programming, detailed design or archi- tectural levels. However, to date, they have not been applied to measure dependencies at an earlier stage, i.e. in requirements docu- ments. In this section, the metrics have been applied to the require- ments of the three product lines used in our analyses. In particular we have defined and calculated a new Use Case-level Interlacing Between Concerns (UCIBC) metric, which measures the number of use cases shared by the implementation of two features. Moreover, we have defined a new metric, called Concern Interlacing (CI), as the total number of feature dependencies of a particular feature. The Concern Interlacing metric is calculated by the addition of the UCIBC values for a feature with respect to the rest of features. As an example, in a system where three features (A, B and C) are consid- ered, if feature A shares 2 use cases with feature B and 4 uses cases with feature C, then the Concern Interlacing metric for A is 6. Note that a use case may be computed twice if feature A shares this use case with two different features. Both metrics, UCIBC and CI are calculated using our dependency matrix. In particular, the cal- culation of UCIBC metric is obtained by counting the number of col- umns of the dependency matrix where two particular features have a 1. In other words, this metric can be calculated for all the features by performing the product of the dependency matrix and its trans- pose. The matrix resulting of this product is called the Concern interlacing matrix. CI metric is calculated by counting the values obtained for each row of this matrix (discarding the values obtained in the diagonal). where DM and cimki represent the Dependency matrix and the cell [k, i] of the Concern interlacing matrix, respectively. In order to illustrate the calculation of the UCIBC metric, Table 23 shows the dependency matrix obtained for release 3 of the MobileMedia system. By applying the product of this matrix and its transpose, the Concern Interlacing Matrix shown in Table 24 is obtained. In this matrix, a cell denotes the value of the UCIBC metric for the feature represented in the row with respect to the feature of the corresponding column. The values of the CI metric for each feature are also shown in the last column of this matrix. As an example, observe that the UCIBC metric for Photo and Label features is 2 since these features share the implementation of the AddPhoto and ViewAlbum use cases. However, Photo shares the implementation of DeleteAlbum, AddPhoto and ViewAlbum use cases with the Album concern, thus the metric is 3 for these two features. Finally, the resulting CI metric for photo is 18 since the feature has 18 occurrences of use cases shared with other features or NFCs. Using the dependency matrix for each release, we have calcu- lated the CI metric for the 8 releases of the MobileMedia. The gathered data are shown in Table 25. For each release the degree of crosscutting for each feature has been also shown in order to have a way of comparing both metrics. The last column of the table shows the average of both metrics taking into account the eight re- leases. In this case, we do not show the Degree of scattering metric since, like with the previous analyses, the results obtained are very similar to those obtained for the Degree of crosscutting metric. Anal- ogously, Concern degree of tangling metric is not shown since the results are also consistent and similar to the shown for the Degree of crosscutting metric. Based on the data presented in Table 25, Concern Interlacing and Degree of crosscutting metrics have been compared in order to ob- serve the correlation that exists between both metrics. The corre- lations for each release are shown in Fig. 20, from a to h. Since the Degree of crosscutting metric has been compared with the Concern Interlacing and Change Impact Set metrics, we compare now these two metrics. Intuitively, since Degree of crosscutting is cor- related with Concern Interlacing and Change Impact, these two last metrics should be also correlated. However, in order to check this conclusion, we have empirically compared the two metrics. The re- sults are used to check whether the features with higher concern interlacing (more dependencies) are those with a bigger change impact set. The graphics that show the correlation between Change Impact and Concern Interlacing for each release are shown in Fig. 21. Finally, once Concern Interlacing has been compared with Degree of crosscutting and Change Impact Set metrics, we may also compare it with the stability of the different features. The results allow us to check whether the features with more dependencies are those implemented by more unstable use cases. Fig. 22 shows the corre- lation existing between these two measurements. The data to ob- tain this graphic are extracted from Table 22 (unstable use cases) and Table 25 (concern interlacing average). As we did with the previous studies, we replicated the process for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems in order to check whether the results obtained for the product lines are consistent. The results obtained are shown in the next figures: Figs. 23 and 24 show the correlations between Concern Interlacing and Degree of crosscutting for HealthWatcher and SmartHome, respectively; Fig. 25 does the same for Concern interlacing and Instability. The correlations between Concern Interlacing and Impact Set for these systems are not shown as the results are similar to those presented for Concern Interlacing and Degree of Crosscutting.
paraphrases: **5. Modularity Analysis:** We evaluated the modularity of three product lines by quantifying their features' crosscutting properties using "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" for features, and "Degree of tangling" for use cases. This analysis identified poorly modular features (high scattering and crosscutting) and use cases with tangled concerns, highlighting the need for specialized crosscutting metrics. Subsequently, we compared modularity with various maintainability attributes (Section 6), calculating all necessary values for this empirical comparison.

**6.1. Changeability Analysis:** This section addresses RQ1, investigating if features with higher change impact correlate with a higher "Degree of crosscutting" (Hypothesis 1). We quantify change impact using a method from Ref. [23], which defines it based on the number of trace links needing change or preservation due to a source element modification. Our dependency matrix quantifies this impact, as exemplified by MobileMedia release features (Table 17). We also compare "Impact Set" with "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" (Figs. 10, 11), using linear regression. To understand tangling's effect on changeability, "Impact Set" was compared with "Concern degree of tangling," a new metric calculated from the sum of "Degree of tangling" for related use cases (Table 18, 19, Fig. 12). Similar analyses were performed for HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems (Figs. 13-16).

**6.3. Stability Analysis:** Addressing RQ2, this section explores whether high scattering and crosscutting negatively impact software stability at the requirements level (Hypothesis 2). We also examine if use cases with higher tangling are less stable. Focusing on functional changes, we identified unstable use cases in MobileMedia releases (Table 20) and correlated their "Degree of tangling" with the number of changes (Table 21). We further related concerns' scattering and crosscutting to the number of unstable use cases they involve (Table 22, Fig. 17). These findings were corroborated by Pearson's coefficient and replicated for HealthWatcher and SmartHome (Figs. 18, 19).

**6.5. Dependency Analysis:** For RQ3, we investigate if crosscutting features increase inter-feature dependencies at the requirements level (Hypothesis 3.1) and compare these dependencies with change impact and stability (Hypothesis 3.2). Adapting "feature interlacing" concepts [17], we introduced "Use Case-level Interlacing Between Concerns" (UCIBC) and "Concern Interlacing" (CI) metrics to measure shared use cases and total feature dependencies, respectively. These were calculated using our dependency matrix (Table 23, 24, 25). We then correlated CI with "Degree of crosscutting" (Fig. 20), "Change Impact Set" (Fig. 21), and feature stability (Fig. 22). The consistency of these results was confirmed by replicating the analysis for HealthWatcher and SmartHome (Figs. 23-25).

**5. Modularity Analysis:** To determine the predictive power of our chosen measures, we first assessed the modularity of three target product lines using metrics from Section 4.2. Our focus was on quantifying the crosscutting attributes of features within these systems. Specifically, we computed the "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" for features, and the "Degree of tangling" for use cases. This analysis revealed: (i) features exhibiting poor modularity, characterized by higher scattering and crosscutting, and (ii) use cases that addressed multiple features, indicating more tangled concerns. This analysis also highlighted the necessity for a dedicated crosscutting metric to help developers identify situations not captured by scattering and tangling. Following this, the assessed modularity was compared against various maintainability attributes detailed in Section 6, with all requisite values for this empirical comparison calculated.

**6.1. Changeability Analysis:** This section addresses RQ1 by examining whether features with a greater impact of changes, regardless of being variable or mandatory, also exhibit a higher "Degree of crosscutting" (Hypothesis 1). To quantify a feature's change impact, we adopted the approach outlined in Ref. [23], which defines it based on the number of trace links that must be altered or preserved when a source element changes. This impact is quantified using our dependency matrix. For instance, calculations for the "Impact Set" of changes in MobileMedia features across different releases are presented in Table 17. The "Impact Set" metric was then correlated with both "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" using linear regression (Figures 10 and 11). To explore tangling's influence on changeability, the "Impact Set" was also compared with the newly defined "Concern degree of tangling" metric, which aggregates the "Degree of tangling" of all use cases associated with a given concern (Tables 18 and 19, Figure 12). Similar correlation analyses were conducted for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems (Figures 13-16).

**6.3. Stability Analysis:** Addressing RQ2, this section investigates the impact of scattering and crosscutting on software stability at the requirements level. Specifically, we examine if concerns with higher scattering and crosscutting are associated with more unstable use cases (Hypothesis 2), and if use cases with higher tangling are less stable. Our analysis focused on changes to system functionality, identifying unstable use cases in MobileMedia releases (Table 20). We then correlated the "Degree of tangling" of each use case with its number of changes (Table 21). To connect stability with source element metrics, we calculated the number of unstable use cases for each concern using the MobileMedia release 7 dependency matrix (Table 22). Linear regression (Figure 17) was used to correlate the number of unstable use cases with "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" for these concerns, confirming the initial intuition that scattered or crosscutting concerns tend to be less stable. This stability analysis was replicated for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems (Figures 18 and 19).

**6.5. Dependency Analysis:** This section addresses RQ3, exploring whether the presence of crosscutting features at the requirements level increases inter-feature dependencies, thereby complicating maintainability (Hypothesis 3.1). Given prior comparisons of crosscutting with change impact and stability, we also examine the relationship between these maintainability attributes and feature dependencies (Hypothesis 3.2). We adapted the concept of "feature interlacing" [17] by defining new metrics: "Use Case-level Interlacing Between Concerns" (UCIBC), quantifying shared use cases between features, and "Concern Interlacing" (CI), representing a feature's total dependencies. These metrics are computed from our dependency matrix (Tables 23-25). We then correlated CI with "Degree of crosscutting" (Figure 20), "Change Impact Set" (Figure 21), and feature stability (Figure 22), providing empirical evidence for the relationships between these metrics. The consistency of these findings was validated by replicating the analysis for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems (Figures 23-25).

text: The consistency is checked automatically within the integrated test case evaluator of CITLAB. CITLAB has an integrated logic evaluator to check for inconsistency and whether a parameter (feature) configuration is a valid test case or not. We rely on the fact that the internal evaluator works correctly. The completeness is checked by simply verify for every case study that the number of distinct valid product of our approach is equal to the number of valid products found by the SPLOT analyzer. Note that the number of products including invalid ones may differ, but the number of valid configurations must be the same in order to preserve semantical equivalence. The semantical equivalence ensures a biunivocal correspon- dence between one test case produced by CITLAB and one possible valid product. A major advantage of our approach is that the tester can relay for test generation on different algorithms and tools developed for CIT. paraphrases: The sampling algorithm produces an initial set of unprioritized test cases. These cases are then assessed for their similarity using an enhanced string distance measure. The similarity scores are stored in a hashtable, which the enhanced prioritization algorithm then uses to order the test cases for a prioritized suite. The effectiveness of this prioritization is measured by the Average Fault Detection (APFD) metric, which quantifies the average number of faults revealed according to their position in the prioritized test suite; a higher APFD signifies quicker fault discovery. The fault detection rate indicates the proportion of faults found within specific portions of a test suite. An effective method can identify all faults with a minimal number of test suites. For instance, Technique A's ability to find 100% of faults using only 10% of the test suite in the Web Portal case study demonstrates its high effectiveness in fault detection. This research presents the fault detection rate as a percentage, calculating the number of detected faults at 10% intervals of the test suite (10%, 20%, ..., 100%) to offer a thorough analysis of the outcomes at each stage.

Initially, test cases generated by the sampling algorithm form an unordered collection. These unprioritized test cases have their similarity values computed using an advanced string distance metric. The resulting similarity data is placed into a hashtable. Subsequently, an enhanced prioritization algorithm processes these stored similarity values from the hashtable to arrange the test cases into a prioritized test suite. The Average Fault Detection (APFD) metric is employed to evaluate the success of this prioritization by determining the average count of faults revealed based on their sequence within the prioritized test suite. A greater APFD value denotes a more rapid fault discovery. The term "rate of faults detected" refers to the quantity of faults identified within a specific segment of a test suite. An optimal technique can uncover all faults while utilizing a small number of test suites. For example, Technique A's capacity to detect 100% of faults using only 10% of the test suite in the Web Portal case study establishes it as a highly efficient technique for fault detection. This study expresses the fault detection rate in percentages, with fault detection amounts calculated at every 10% increment of the test suite (10%, 20%, ..., 100%) to provide a comprehensive view of the results at each level.

text: We (1) identify a set of issues that must be addressed to make software product line testing work in practice and (2) provide a framework that combines a set of techniques to solve these issues. The framework inte- grates feature modelling, combinatorial interaction testing and constraint programming techniques. First, we extract variability in a software product line as a feature model with specified feature interdependencies. We then employ an al- gorithm that generates a minimal set of valid test cases cov- ering all 2-way feature interactions for a given time interval. Furthermore, we evaluate the framework on an industrial SPL and show that using the framework saves time and pro- vides better test coverage.
paraphrases: This paper outlines practical challenges in software product line testing and presents a framework that addresses these issues by integrating feature modeling, combinatorial interaction testing, and constraint programming. The framework begins by defining product line variability using a feature model, then uses an algorithm to create a minimal set of test cases covering all two-way feature interactions. Our evaluation of this framework on an industrial software product line demonstrates its effectiveness in reducing time and improving test coverage.

We address the practical challenges of testing software product lines by introducing a comprehensive framework. This framework incorporates feature modeling, combinatorial interaction testing, and constraint programming. Initially, we define the variability within a software product line through a feature model that details interdependencies. Subsequently, an algorithm is utilized to produce a minimum set of valid test cases, ensuring coverage of all two-way feature interactions within a specified timeframe. Our evaluation on an industrial SPL confirms that this framework leads to time savings and enhanced test coverage.

text: SPL domains are usually modelled by means of feature diagrams following the feature-oriented domain analysis (FODA) notation. Finally, the authors compare the performance of their algorithm with two other approaches built on top of boolean logic satisfiability (SAT)-solver technology such as cachet and relsat.

The authors conclude by comparing their algorithm's performance against two SAT-solver based methods, namely cachet and relsat.

The second dependent variable, for hypothesis 2, is the inconsistency resolution effort, denoted as g(MCM). This is quantified by the number of operations—including creations, removals, and updates—required to transform a composed model into its intended state. We calculate these operations because they mirror the primary actions developers undertake to evolve software in real-world scenarios [28], thereby providing an estimate of the effort involved in resolving inconsistencies. text: According to the type of study (i.e. repeated measures design), hypotheses (causality-comparative questions), and independent and dependent variables; appropriate tests were identified for the hypotheses. Generally, for repeated measure designs where each participant performs the tasks on all the groups (e.g., the basic tool and visually-enhanced tool groups), the suitable paired test is employed. Since the dependent variables (i.e., completion time, number of correct answers, ease-of-use, and ease-of-learning) are numerical and the independent variable (i.e., visualization technique) is categorical with two levels, we can either use one-tailed paired t-test or Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test. One-tailed paired t-test is a well-known statistical test for comparing the means of two groups of data with normal distribution. It is also suitable for the samples with small sizes. The Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test is a none-parametric statistic test which is an alternative to the paired t-test when the sample is not normally distributed. To identify appropriate test for the hypotheses, we investigated normality of the involved variables: 1) time completion variable is continuous variable and based on the Shapiro W test it has a normal distribution. Therefore, the one-tailed paired t-test was used for comparing the mean of this variable in two groups (Hypotheses 1 and 3); 2) the number of correct answers, based on the Shapiro W test, was not distributed normally, so we used the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test for comparing two samples in terms of accuracy (Hypotheses 2 and 4); 3) the collected data regarding ease-of-use and ease-of-learning also did not have normal distribution, so we used the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test to compare two tools in terms of these variables (Hypotheses 4 and 6). As mentioned in Section 5.2.1, complexity of a feature model is considered as a confounding variable and we designed two variants for each task – one with simple feature model and one with complex feature model – to handle this variable. As a result, two variant of hypotheses 1-4 were tested - one for simple task (e.g. simple comprehension task) and one for complex task (e.g. complex comprehension task).

Given that our dependent variables (completion time, correct answers, ease-of-use, ease-of-learning) are numerical and the independent variable (visualization technique) is categorical with two levels, we considered either a one-tailed paired t-test or a Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test. The one-tailed paired t-test is a standard method for comparing means of two normally distributed datasets, even with small sample sizes. The Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test, a non-parametric alternative, is used when data are not normally distributed. To determine the correct test for each hypothesis, we first checked the normality of our variables. For completion time, which is continuous and normally distributed (Shapiro W test), we used the one-tailed paired t-test for Hypotheses 1 and 3. The number of correct answers, however, was not normally distributed (Shapiro W test), so we applied the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test for accuracy comparisons in Hypotheses 2 and 4. Similarly, ease-of-use and ease-of-learning data were not normally distributed, leading us to use the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test for comparing the two tools on these variables (Hypotheses 4 and 6). To address the confounding variable of feature model complexity, as noted in Section 5.2.1, we created two versions of each task – one with a simple and one with a complex feature model. Consequently, Hypotheses 1-4 were tested in both a simple and a complex task context (e.g., simple vs. complex comprehension tasks).

Our selection of appropriate statistical tests for the hypotheses was guided by the study's repeated measures design, the causal-comparative nature of our research questions, and the characteristics of our independent and dependent variables. In repeated measures studies, where participants engage with all experimental conditions (e.g., both the basic and visually-enhanced tools), paired statistical tests are typically used. Since our dependent variables (completion time, correct answers, ease-of-use, and ease-of-learning) are quantitative, and our independent variable (visualization technique) is categorical with two groups, we chose between the one-tailed paired t-test and the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test. The one-tailed paired t-test is a common parametric test for comparing the means of two normally distributed groups, even with small samples. Conversely, the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test is a non-parametric equivalent employed when data do not meet the assumption of normal distribution. To decide which test to apply, we assessed the normality of each relevant variable. For completion time, which was a continuous variable with a normal distribution confirmed by the Shapiro W test, we utilized the one-tailed paired t-test for Hypotheses 1 and 3. However, the number of correct answers did not exhibit a normal distribution according to the Shapiro W test, prompting us to use the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test for accuracy comparisons in Hypotheses 2 and 4. Similarly, the data for ease-of-use and ease-of-learning also lacked normal distribution, leading us to apply the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test for comparing the two tools on these measures (Hypotheses 4 and 6). Furthermore, as outlined in Section 5.2.1, feature model complexity was controlled as a confounding variable by developing simple and complex versions of each task. This approach meant that Hypotheses 1-4 were evaluated across both simple and complex task scenarios (e.g., simple vs. complex comprehension tasks).

text: We compared SPLat with different approaches for test execution. We considered two na ̈ıve approaches that run tests against all valid configurations: NewJVM and Reuse- JVM. The NewJVM approach spawns a new JVM for each distinct test run. Each test run executes only one valid con- figuration of the SPL. It is important to note that the cost of this approach includes the cost of spawning a new JVM. The ReuseJVM approach uses the same JVM across several test runs, thus avoiding the overhead of repeatedly spawn- ing JVMs for each different test and configuration. This ap- proach requires the tester to explicitly provide a reset func- tion (Section 3.4). Because the tester likely has to write a reset function anyway, we conjecture that this approach is a viable alternative to save runtime cost. For example, the tester may already need to restore parts of the state stored outside the JVM such as files or database. We also compared SPLat with a simplified version of a previously proposed static analysis [20] for pruning con- figurations. Whereas [20] performs reachability analysis, control-flow and data-flow analyses, the simplified version, which we call SRA (Static Reachability Analysis), only per- forms the reachability analysis to determine which configu- rations are reachable from a given test and thus can be seen as the static analysis counterpart to SPLat. SRA builds a call graph using inter-procedural, context-insensitive, flow- insensitive, and path-insensitive points-to analysis and col- lects the features syntactically present in the methods of the call graph. Only the valid combinations of these reachable features from a test need to be run for that test. Finally, we compared SPLat with an artificial technique that has zero cost to compute the set of configurations on which each test need to run. More precisely, we use a tech- nique that gives the same results as SPLat but only counts the cost of executing tests for these configurations, not the cost of computing these configurations. We call this tech- nique Ideal. The overhead of SPLat is the difference be- tween the overall cost of SPLat explorations and the cost of executing tests for Ideal.
paraphrases: To evaluate SPLat, we benchmarked it against several testing methods. These included two basic strategies, NewJVM and ReuseJVM, both of which execute tests across all permissible configurations. NewJVM initiates a new Java Virtual Machine for every individual test execution, with each execution targeting a single valid System Under Test configuration. A key aspect of NewJVM's cost is the overhead of launching each new JVM. In contrast, ReuseJVM reuses a single JVM for multiple test runs, thereby eliminating the repeated JVM startup costs associated with diverse tests and configurations. This method necessitates the tester to supply a specific reset function (detailed in Section 3.4). We hypothesize that ReuseJVM is a practical, cost-saving option for runtime, as testers often need to implement such reset functions to restore external states like files or databases. Our evaluation also involved comparing SPLat with a simplified version of an existing static analysis technique [20] used for filtering configurations. While the original [20] employs reachability, control-flow, and data-flow analyses, our simplified version, SRA (Static Reachability Analysis), focuses solely on reachability analysis. SRA identifies configurations accessible from a given test, effectively acting as a static analysis equivalent to SPLat. SRA constructs a call graph using inter-procedural, context-insensitive, flow-insensitive, and path-insensitive points-to analysis, then gathers the syntactically defined features within the call graph's methods. Only valid combinations of these accessible features for a test are then executed. Lastly, we contrasted SPLat with an idealized, cost-free technique, which we termed "Ideal." This technique yields identical configuration sets to SPLat but incurs no computational cost for determining these configurations, only for executing the tests. The performance overhead of SPLat is calculated as the difference between its total exploration cost and the test execution cost of the Ideal technique.

Our study evaluated SPLat's performance by comparing it to several alternative test execution strategies. We examined two straightforward methods that run tests on every valid configuration: NewJVM and ReuseJVM. NewJVM generates a new Java Virtual Machine for each separate test run, with each run designed for a single valid System Product Line configuration. It's important to recognize that the overhead of starting a new JVM is a component of NewJVM's total cost. Conversely, ReuseJVM utilizes the same JVM across multiple test executions, thereby avoiding the repetitive cost of launching JVMs for different tests and configurations. This approach requires the tester to provide a specific reset function (as described in Section 3.4). We propose that ReuseJVM is a feasible and cost-effective alternative for reducing runtime, given that testers are frequently required to implement reset functions to restore external states, such as database or file system changes. Additionally, we compared SPLat to a simplified version of an earlier static analysis technique [20] for pruning configurations. Unlike the full [20] which uses reachability, control-flow, and data-flow analyses, our simplified version, SRA (Static Reachability Analysis), only performs reachability analysis. SRA identifies which configurations are reachable from a particular test, thus serving as a static analysis counterpart to SPLat. SRA constructs a call graph using an inter-procedural, context-insensitive, flow-insensitive, and path-insensitive points-to analysis and then gathers the features found syntactically in the call graph's methods. Only the valid combinations of these reachable features for a specific test are then executed. Finally, we compared SPLat against a theoretical, zero-cost method for determining the configurations needed for each test. This method, which we called Ideal, produces the same results as SPLat but only accounts for the cost of running the tests on these configurations, not the cost of calculating them. SPLat's overhead is defined as the difference between its total exploration cost and the test execution cost of Ideal.

text: To evaluate whether these differences are statistically sig- nificant, we followed the guidelines suggested by Arcuri and Briand in [1] by performing a Mann-Whitney U Test. It is a non-parametric statistical hypothesis test for assess- ing whether one of two samples of independent observations tends to have larger values than the other. We obtain from this test a probability called p-value which represents the probability that the two samples are equal. It is conventional in statistics to consider that the difference is not significant if the p-value is higher than the 5% level. The experiments involving this statistical test used two-tailed tests. ... To evaluate whether the differences are significant, we per- formed a Mann-Whitney U Test, as presented in Section 4.2.1. For each comparison (F, F2 and F3 on F1 comparison basis and F, F1 and F3 on F2 comparison basis), we got one p-value per FM, i.e. 8 in the total. Each p-value results from the comparison between the 30 values obtained on the 30 runs by the proposed approach with those obtained at random.
paraphrases: To determine the statistical significance of these differences, we conducted a Mann-Whitney U Test, adhering to the recommendations of Arcuri and Briand [1]. This non-parametric hypothesis test evaluates if one of two independent sample sets generally possesses greater values than the other. The test yields a p-value, which indicates the likelihood that the two samples are identical. In statistical practice, a difference is typically considered non-significant if the p-value exceeds 5%. Our statistical tests were all two-tailed. ... To ascertain the significance of the differences, a Mann-Whitney U Test was performed, as outlined in Section 4.2.1. For every comparison (F, F2, and F3 against F1, and F, F1, and F3 against F2), we derived one p-value per Feature Model (FM), totaling eight p-values. Each p-value was derived by comparing the 30 values from the 30 runs of our proposed method against those obtained randomly.

Following Arcuri and Briand's guidelines [1], we performed a Mann-Whitney U Test to assess the statistical significance of the observed differences. This non-parametric statistical test is designed to determine if one of two independent sets of observations tends to exhibit larger values than the other. The test produces a p-value, representing the probability that the two samples are indistinguishable. Statistically, if the p-value surpasses the 5% threshold, the difference is generally not considered significant. All experiments utilizing this statistical test employed two-tailed tests. ... To assess the significance of the differences, we applied a Mann-Whitney U Test, as detailed in Section 4.2.1. For each set of comparisons (F, F2, and F3 in relation to F1; and F, F1, and F3 in relation to F2), we generated one p-value per Feature Model, resulting in a total of eight p-values. Each p-value was calculated by comparing the 30 values generated by our approach over 30 runs against values obtained through random sampling.

text: In future work, first, we plan to extend PACOGEN to N-wise fea- ture coverage, allowing the generation of test configurations with higher or lower interaction strength (e.g., N = 3 and N = 1). This involves the development of an algorithm to generate N-tuples in addition to a special additional constraint to enforce the coverage of N-wise interactions. Second, we plan to analyse the correlation be- tween pairwise-coverage and error-detection effectiveness of a test suite. Third, we will analyse the performance of PACOGEN using prob- lems in the transition phase (in between under-constrained and over- constrained problems), as this is the area where the hardest problems lie. Finally, we plan to integrate PACOGEN with the industry-strength variability management technology we are currently developing. We envision to fully integrate PACOGEN in our industrial partner’s test- ing framework that runs in a continuous integration environment. However, this process is challenging, as it requires not only techni- cal adoption, but also organisational and cultural changes at different levels in the company.
paraphrases: Moving forward, our initial step involves expanding PACOGEN to encompass N-wise feature coverage. This will enable the creation of test configurations with varying interaction strengths (e.g., N=3 or N=1). To achieve this, we'll need to develop an algorithm capable of generating N-tuples and incorporate a specific constraint to guarantee comprehensive N-wise interaction coverage.
Secondly, we intend to investigate the relationship between pairwise coverage and how effective a test suite is at detecting errors.

Third, we plan to evaluate PACOGEN's performance when addressing problems in the transition phase, which fall between under-constrained and over-constrained scenarios, as these represent the most complex challenges.

Lastly, our aim is to incorporate PACOGEN into the robust variability management technology we are currently developing, ultimately integrating it into our industrial partner's continuous integration testing framework. This integration, however, presents a significant challenge, demanding not only technical implementation but also organizational and cultural shifts throughout the company.

text: On the basis of these promising results we plan first to continue investigating constraint-based exploration of variability spaces in future work. In particular, we plan to include the values of attributes associated to features in the selection process. For example, if features are associated to execution times, or energy consumption, it is possible to reuse our constraint model to optimize quality of service requirements. Second, we will investigate extensions of our work to consider the relationships between several variability spaces. For example, in component-based systems, the configuration of one component can have an impact on the way another component can be configured. Thus, when sampling the configuration space for the first component it is necessary to consider the dependencies with the configuration space of the second component. This should prevent selecting only configurations that force the second component to be in a narrow area of its configuration space.
paraphrases: Building on these encouraging findings, our immediate future work involves further exploration of constraint-based variability spaces. Specifically, we intend to incorporate attribute values linked to features into the selection process. For instance, if features relate to execution times or energy consumption, our constraint model could be repurposed to optimize quality of service requirements. Secondly, we will explore expanding our research to account for interrelationships between multiple variability spaces. In component-based systems, for example, one component's configuration can affect another's, necessitating consideration of these dependencies when sampling the first component's configuration space. This approach should prevent limiting the second component to a restricted configuration area.

text: As a future work, we plan to conduct the external valida- tion of the study. Another poten- tial area of work can be identifying service variability models for multi-domains, in which, the variability model of multiple business processes are taken at the same time as the material for service identification, in a way that we can have appropri- ate measures for both spatial and temporal reusability of the identified services.

text: As a future work, we will improve the efficiency of our algorithms. For doing so, we plan to study additional data structures for representing states in FTA. In our current implementation, such states are represented by triplets com- posed of an explicit location, a binary decision diagram, and a difference bound matrix. As alternatives, we plan to use ei- ther Multi-Terminal BDD or a data structure that combines zone and binary variables representations. For the latter, Clock Restriction Diagrams [20] and appear as promising candidates. Also, we plan to extend FTA modelling to non-Boolean features. This would allow to directly express real-time con- straints in terms of a feature attributes. As an example, the running speed of a processor may drastically influence the execution time of a software. Considering this extension would definitively impact on our model-checking procedure. Indeed, in this context we would not be able to use binary decision diagrams or SAT solver to reason on sets of prod- ucts. Second, we may not be able to translate the FTA into an infinite FTS anymore.
paraphrases: In the future, we aim to enhance the efficiency of our algorithms by exploring alternative data structures for FTA state representation. Currently, states are defined by a triplet comprising a location, a binary decision diagram, and a difference bound matrix. We intend to investigate Multi-Terminal BDDs or hybrid structures that merge zone and binary variable representations, with Clock Restriction Diagrams [20] showing particular promise. Additionally, we plan to expand FTA modeling to incorporate non-Boolean features, enabling direct expression of real-time constraints based on feature attributes. For instance, a processor's speed significantly affects software execution time. This expansion would necessitate changes to our model-checking process, as we would no longer be able to utilize binary decision diagrams or SAT solvers for reasoning about product sets, and translating the FTA into an infinite FTS might become unfeasible.

text: Several challenges remain for our future work in two main directions, namely: – We intend to extend our suite with new operations and testing techniques. We also plan to evaluate our suite with other tools and in development scenarios using FaMa and report our experiences to the community. – We also plan to explore the benefits obtained when combining our suite with other automated testing methods. In a previous work [30], we presented an automated test data generator for the analysis of feature models with promising results. It generates random follow–up test cases based on the relations between inputs feature models and theirs expected outputs (so-called metamorphic testing). However, it is known that metamorphic testing produce better results when combined with other test case selection strategies that generate the initial set of test cases. We intend to use our suite to guide the generation of test cases in our automated test data generator and study the gains in efficiency and efficacy.
paraphrases: Our future work will address several challenges, focusing on two primary areas: First, we aim to expand our software suite by incorporating new operations and testing techniques. We also plan to benchmark our suite against other tools and within development contexts utilizing FaMa, sharing our findings with the broader community. Second, we intend to investigate the advantages of integrating our suite with other automated testing methodologies. Our prior research [30] introduced an automated test data generator for feature model analysis, which yielded encouraging results by generating random follow-up test cases through metamorphic testing. Given that metamorphic testing's effectiveness is enhanced when combined with other test case selection strategies for initial test case generation, we propose to leverage our suite to direct the creation of test cases within our automated test data generator, thereby analyzing improvements in both efficiency and effectiveness.

text: The optimization of software to be (more) energy ex001ccient is becoming a major concern for the software industry. text: We (1) identify a set of issues that must be addressed to make software product line testing work in practice and (2) provide a framework that combines a set of techniques to solve these issues. The framework integrates feature modelling, combinatorial interaction testing and constraint programming techniques. First, we extract variability in a software product line as a feature model with speci ed feature interdependencies. We then employ an algorithm that generates a minimal set of valid test cases covering all 2-way feature interactions for a given time interval. Furthermore, we evaluate the framework on an industrial SPL and show that using the framework saves time and provides better test coverage.
paraphrases: This paper addresses challenges in practical software product line testing by proposing a framework that integrates feature modeling, combinatorial interaction testing, and constraint programming. We begin by defining software product line variability through a feature model that includes feature interdependencies. Subsequently, an algorithm is used to create a minimal set of valid test cases, ensuring coverage of all 2-way feature interactions within a specified timeframe. Our evaluation of this framework on an industrial SPL demonstrates its ability to reduce time and enhance test coverage.

text: We have performed experiments on several SPLOT feature models, the results of which show that the test suite generation strategies based on the proposed coverage criteria are effective in significantly reducing the number of required tests and at the same time maintaining a high fault coverage ratio.
paraphrases: Our experiments on various SPLOT feature models demonstrate that the proposed coverage-criteria-based test suite generation strategies effectively decrease the number of necessary tests while preserving a high fault coverage.

The experimental findings from our work on multiple SPLOT feature models indicate that test suite generation strategies utilizing the suggested coverage criteria successfully lower the test count without sacrificing high fault coverage.

This paper presents a Feature Selection optimization solution in SPL by using Genetic Algorithm. We used genetic algorithms (GA) to find out most reusable features, which contribute, maximum in software product line. We developed real-world feature model for a multi feature laptop device and examined the constraints, which are mandatory, optional, include and exclude. We optimized a small-set feature model (20 - 250 features) and five largeset feature model (500 - 10000 features) and report that GA can produce fast, efficient and effective results irrespective of increase in feature model size.
paraphrases: Researchers needed an algorithm to identify highly impactful features for optimal product configurations, but finding the best feature selection is an NP-hard problem. This paper introduces a practical and efficient genetic algorithm for automating product configuration in software product lines, specifically for optimizing feature selection.

Our research addresses the challenge of designing optimal product configurations by employing a genetic algorithm to efficiently select highly contributing features within software product lines, a task typically considered NP-hard. We demonstrate that this GA-based approach delivers fast, efficient, and effective results, even with larger feature models, as evidenced by its application to a multi-feature laptop device and its performance on various feature model sizes.

text: This paper provides three contributions to the study of multi-step configuration for SPLs. First, we present a formal model of multi-step SPL configuration and map this model to constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). Second, we show how solutions to these SPL configuration problems can be automatically derived with a constraint solver by mapping them to CSPs. Moreover, we show how feature model changes can be mapped to our approach in a multi-step scenario by using feature model drift. Third, we present empirical results demonstrating that our CSP-based reasoning technique can scale to SPL models with hundreds of features and multiple configuration steps.
paraphrases: This paper makes three key contributions to understanding multi-step configuration for Software Product Lines (SPLs). Firstly, it introduces a formal model for multi-step SPL configuration, translating it into constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). Secondly, it illustrates how a constraint solver can automatically generate solutions for these SPL configuration problems by leveraging CSP mapping, and also demonstrates how feature model changes can be accommodated within a multi-step context through feature model drift. Lastly, the paper provides empirical evidence that this CSP-based reasoning method is scalable, handling SPL models with numerous features and several configuration stages.

Our paper advances the field of multi-step configuration for SPLs through three main contributions. We first establish a formal model for multi-step SPL configuration, converting it into constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). Our second contribution details how these SPL configuration issues can be solved automatically using a constraint solver by framing them as CSPs, and further explains how feature model drift allows for incorporating feature model changes into our multi-step approach. Finally, we present empirical data proving the scalability of our CSP-based reasoning technique, even for SPL models featuring hundreds of features and multiple configuration stages.

This paper investigates model checking within Software Product Lines (SPLs). We present a novel symbolic model-checking algorithm for SPLs, utilizing both induction and a SAT solver. To enhance efficiency, we incorporated a feature cube enlargement technique to lessen the frequency of SAT solver invocations, and an incremental SAT-solving method to reduce repeated calculations across SAT instances. The validity of our algorithms has been rigorously established. Experimental outcomes from numerous cases reveal a substantial advancement of our technique compared to established BDD-based methods.

text: Speciﬁcally, we measured the time needed to compute the or-groups from a matrix with 1000 conﬁgurations, a maximum domain size of 10 and a number of variables ranging from 5 to 70.
