The procedure is composed of 3 steps. First, it selects a set of products whose matrices have at least 75% of feature and attributes in common. Then, it merges the corresponding matrices of the selected product to obtain a conﬁguration matrix. Unfortunately, the resulting conﬁguration matrix may contain empty cells. Such cells have no clear semantics from a vari- ability point of view. The last step of the procedure consists in giving an interpretation to these cells. If a feature or an attribute contain only integers, the empty cells are inter- preted as ”0”. Otherwise, the empty cells are interpreted as ”No” which means that the feature or attribute is absent.
paraphrases: We evaluated the computation time for "or-groups" from a matrix of 1000 configurations, a maximum domain size of 10, and a variable count between 5 and 70, with a 30-minute timeout. We then assessed scalability by varying variables (5-2000), configurations (5-200,000), and maximum domain size (5-10,000) in random matrices. The total time complexity was further analyzed by breaking it down into algorithmic steps. Additionally, an automated method was created to extract configuration matrices from Best Buy's website, involving three steps: selecting products with at least 75% common features/attributes, merging their matrices, and then interpreting empty cells as "0" for integers or "No" for absent features/attributes.

Our study focused on measuring the time required to calculate "or-groups" from a matrix of 1000 configurations, a maximum domain size of 10, and 5 to 70 variables, imposing a 30-minute time limit for efficiency. We also investigated scalability by synthesizing random matrices, varying the number of variables from 5 to 2000 (with 1000 configurations and a max domain size of 10), the number of configurations from 5 to 200,000 (with 100 variables and a max domain size of 10), and the maximum domain size from 5 to 10,000 (with 10 variables and 10,000 configurations). To further comprehend the algorithm's overall time complexity, we examined its distribution across different stages, as depicted in Figure 11. Furthermore, we developed an automated technique to derive configuration matrices from the Best Buy website. This process involves three stages: first, selecting products with at least a 75% overlap in features and attributes; second, merging their respective matrices to form a configuration matrix; and finally, assigning meaning to any empty cells in the resulting matrix. If a feature or attribute is numeric, empty cells are assigned "0"; otherwise, they are marked as "No" to signify absence.

text: Exp 1: For assessing program comprehension, we designed two static tasks (S1, S2) and four maintenance tasks (M1–M4). In static tasks, subjects should locate feature code. In the first static task (S1), subjects should, for each feature, locate all files containing feature code and mark the results on a sheet of paper (referred to as grid template). It showed the relationship of code to features in a matrix, such that the columns contained the file names, and the rows the feature names. For the color version, the feature names of the grid template had the same background color as in the source code, whereas for the ifdef version, the grid template had no background colors. In the second static task (S2), subjects should locate shared code (i.e. code that concerned more than one feature, e.g., SMSFeature & CopyPhoto). Locating feature code is a typical task for a developer, when she is familiarizing herself with an SPL. Furthermore, a developer is often looking for feature code when solving a bug, because bugs can often be narrowed down to certain features or feature combinations. Especially, combinations of features are of interest in the implementation of SPLs, since they can represent feature interactions that are especially difficult to get right (Kästner 2010). For all maintenance tasks, we carefully introduced different bugs into the source code, which were all located in annotated code fragments. In a pre-test with 7 students, we selected bugs that were neither too easy nor too difficult to find. Four bugs matched our criteria, which we ordered by increasing difficulty according to the results of our pre-test. For each bug, subjects received a bug description similar to the ones users would enter in a bug-tracking system. The description also named the feature in which the bug occurs. This assured that we evaluate the influence of background colors, because subjects focus on feature code and, thus, background colors, instead of spending their time in non-annotated code fragments. For each task, subjects should locate the bug (name class and method), explain why it occurs, and suggest a solution. Using this information, we judged whether the cause of a bug was located correctly. As an example, we present the bug description of the first maintenance task: M1: If pictures in an album should be sorted by views, they are displayed unsorted anyway. Feature, in which the bug occurs: CountViews. The bug was located in the class PhotoListController and caused by an empty method body of bubbleSort. In addition to the six tasks, we designed a warming-up task to let subjects familiarize with the experimental setting (subjects should count the number of features of MobileMedia). The result of this task was not analyzed. Exp 2: We used the same tasks as for our first experiment, including the warming-up task (W0). However, we changed the order of the tasks to M1, M3, S1, M4, M2, S2. We alternated static and maintenance tasks, such that we could observe whether subjects actually switch between both representations in line with our hypothesis. Exp 3: To measure program comprehension, we designed a number of tasks. We focused on static tasks, because we found in our first experiment a benefit of background colors for static tasks, but not for maintenance tasks. However, we included a few maintenance tasks to control whether our findings still hold. Altogether, we had 10 tasks: 2 warming-up tasks (W1, W2; not included in the analysis), 6 static tasks (S1–S6), and 2 maintenance tasks (M1, M2). We had three different types of static tasks, two tasks per type: 1: Identifying all files in which a certain feature was implemented (S1, S4). 2: Locating nested ifdef directives, which is important for reasoning about feature interactions, cf. Section 5.1.4 (S2, S5). 3: Identifying all features that occur in a certain file (S3, S6). As example, we present the first static task (S1): S1: In which files does feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS occur? For maintenance tasks, we proceeded as for the first experiment. That is, we introduced bugs into the source code and gave subjects a typical bug description that included the feature selections in which the bug occurred. We consulted an expert in C and Xenomai to make sure that the bugs were typical for C programs. As example, we present the first maintenance task: M1: If the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) should be unloaded, a segmentation fault is thrown. The problem occurs, when features CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN and CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000 and CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG are selected. In the code, we omitted the check whether a variable was null. Instead of if (ckfn && (err = ckfn(block)) != 0), the code said if ((err = ckfn(block)) != 0). If that variable would be accessed when it is null, a segmentation fault would be thrown.
paraphrases: Exp 1 involved two static (S1, S2) and four maintenance tasks (M1-M4) to assess program comprehension. Static tasks required subjects to locate feature code, either within specific files (S1, aided by a color-coded grid template) or shared code (S2). Maintenance tasks involved identifying and solving pre-introduced bugs in annotated code, with difficulty verified through a pre-test. Subjects received bug descriptions, located the bug's class and method, explained its cause, and proposed a solution. A warm-up task (W0) was also included but not analyzed. Exp 2 used the same tasks but in a reordered sequence (M1, M3, S1, M4, M2, S2), alternating static and maintenance tasks to observe switching behavior. Exp 3 focused on static tasks (S1-S6) due to observed benefits of background colors in Exp 1, with a few maintenance tasks (M1, M2) included to validate findings. This experiment featured three types of static tasks (identifying feature files, nested ifdefs, and features in files) and maintenance tasks similar to Exp 1, with expert-verified C program bugs.

For Exp 1, we assessed program comprehension using two static tasks (S1, S2) and four maintenance tasks (M1-M4). The static tasks involved subjects finding feature code; specifically, S1 required them to identify all files containing code for a given feature and record it on a grid template that mapped code to features, distinguishing between color-coded and ifdef versions. S2 involved locating code shared by multiple features. These tasks mimic typical developer activities like familiarization with an SPL or bug fixing, where understanding feature interactions is crucial. For the maintenance tasks, we embedded various bugs into annotated code segments, carefully selected via a 7-student pre-test to ensure appropriate difficulty. Subjects received bug descriptions, located the bug's class and method, explained its cause, and suggested a fix, allowing us to evaluate accurate bug identification. An example bug description (M1) is provided. A non-analyzed warm-up task (W0) familiarized subjects with the experimental setup. Exp 2 mirrored Exp 1's tasks, including W0, but changed the task order to M1, M3, S1, M4, M2, S2, alternating static and maintenance tasks to observe representation switching. Exp 3 aimed to measure program comprehension through a series of tasks, primarily static (S1-S6) due to findings from Exp 1 showing background color benefits there, but also including two maintenance tasks (M1, M2) to confirm prior results. This experiment included two warm-up tasks (W1, W2, not analyzed) and six static tasks across three types: identifying feature implementation files (S1, S4), locating nested ifdef directives (S2, S5), and identifying features in a file (S3, S6), with an example (S1) provided. Maintenance tasks followed Exp 1's procedure, using expert-verified, typical C program bugs, with an example (M1) given.

text: Empirical tuning procedures were conducted with AGM-1 and AGM-3 for NSGA-II and PAES according to [42] aiming at deﬁning the population size, mutation rate and crossover rate. The tuning results were compared using the indicator HV. Firstly, the population size was tested and conﬁgurations with populations formed by 100 individuals covered conﬁgurations using 50 and 70 individuals for both algorithms. So, the population size for the NSGAII versions and the external archive size for PAES were set as 100. Secondly, the mutation rate was tuned using three conﬁgurations: {0.8, 0.9, 1.0}. Solutions achieved with the rate 0.9 outperformed solutions found by the other conﬁgurations for both MOEAs. Finally, the crossover rate was empirically adjusted for NSGA-II. The value 0.1 outperformed the other tested values: {0.2, 0.04}. The values tested in the parameters tuning were extracted from experiments conducted in [12], [14], [18], [19]. The maximum number of generations was set as 300 and it was used as stop criterion for all algorithms. Each experiment was executed 30 times for each PLA in order to know the behavior of each algorithm to solve the problem [43].
paraphrases: We performed empirical tuning for NSGA-II and PAES using AGM-1 and AGM-3, following reference [42], to determine optimal population size, mutation rate, and crossover rate, comparing results with the HV indicator. A population size of 100 individuals was found to be superior for both algorithms, encompassing smaller sizes, and thus adopted for NSGA-II versions and PAES's external archive. A mutation rate of 0.9 proved most effective across all MOEAs tested (0.8, 0.9, 1.0). For NSGA-II, a crossover rate of 0.1 outperformed 0.2 and 0.04. These parameter values were based on prior research [12, 14, 18, 19]. All algorithms ran for a maximum of 300 generations, which served as the stopping criterion, and each experiment was repeated 30 times per PLA to understand algorithmic behavior [43].

Empirical tuning procedures were carried out for NSGA-II and PAES with AGM-1 and AGM-3, as detailed in [42], to optimize population size, mutation rate, and crossover rate, with the HV indicator used for result comparison. Initial testing showed that a population size of 100 individuals was sufficient for both algorithms, outperforming configurations with 50 and 70 individuals; consequently, 100 was set as the population size for NSGA-II and the external archive size for PAES. Subsequent tuning of the mutation rate, comparing 0.8, 0.9, and 1.0, revealed that 0.9 yielded superior solutions for both MOEAs. Lastly, NSGA-II's crossover rate was empirically adjusted, with 0.1 demonstrating better performance than 0.2 and 0.04. The parameter values used for tuning were derived from previous experiments [12, 14, 18, 19]. All algorithms had a maximum generation limit of 300, which served as the termination condition, and each experiment was run 30 times for every PLA to thoroughly assess each algorithm's problem-solving behavior [43].

text: - Next, GS-F1 and GS-F2 were manually adjusted to attend P1 and P2 speciﬁcities, generating the suites SP1-F1, SP2-F1, SP1-F2 and SP2-F2. Each test suite comprises 6 test cases. We learned from earlier experiment executions that this was a reasonable amount of tests to execute in this interval of time.- Using the TestWatcher, we simulate a test environment with some simpliﬁcations. Remembering Section 2, when the tester puts the test case on hold to investigate whether there is a defect on the product or just a test issue, he/she carries out diﬀerent tasks depending on the environment structure. To consider and simulate all those situations we worked on the following approach in both experiments: while executing tests, whenever the tester had to investigate if there was a defect on the product, he/she paused test execution, using the Test-Watcher, and asked the experiment conductor, who knew previously the issues present on the test suites. If there was a test inaccuracy, the conductor instructed the tester to ignore the issue resuming test execution and writing an observation on the TestWatcher, explaining what was wrong with the test, for example, if a step did not apply for the product under test. Otherwise, if there was a product defect, he would tell the tester to create a CR. After that, the conductor would take note of the investigation interruption. We then manually adapted GS-F1 and GS-F2 to meet the specific requirements of P1 and P2, thereby creating test suites SP1-F1, SP2-F1, SP1-F2, and SP2-F2. Each of these suites contained 6 test cases. This particular scope was chosen to allow subjects two hours to complete two test suites (one for each product), totaling 12 test cases—a duration we found reasonable from previous experiments. A simulated test environment, albeit simplified, was established using the TestWatcher. As discussed in Section 2, a tester's actions when pausing to investigate a potential product defect or test-related issue vary based on the environment. To account for this, our approach in both experiments was as follows: when a tester needed to investigate a possible product defect, they would pause test execution via the TestWatcher and consult the experiment conductor, who had prior knowledge of issues within the test suites. If the problem stemmed from a test inaccuracy, the conductor would instruct the tester to disregard it, resume testing, and log an observation in the TestWatcher explaining the flaw (e.g., an irrelevant step). Conversely, if a genuine product defect was present, the tester would be directed to generate a Change Request (CR). The conductor would then record this investigative interruption. At the experiment's conclusion, the conductor would possess a record of all instances where testers halted execution due to test inaccuracies.

text: To measure program comprehension, we designed tasks that can only be solved if the subjects understand the related source code. We used two kinds of tasks: maintenance and static tasks [28]. In maintenance tasks, the subjects are instructed to locate/ﬁx a bug, whereas in static tasks, the subjects should examine the structure of the source code. In a previous experiment [20], we found that colours speed up program comprehension only for static tasks, but not in maintenance tasks. Hence, we focused on static tasks, but included a few maintenance tasks to conﬁrm our results. All tasks are typical for a maintenance programmer, when she is looking for bugs in certain features and/or ﬁles. We had ten tasks: two warming up tasks (W1, W2), six static tasks (S1–S6) and two maintenance tasks (M1, M2). The warming up tasks were designed to let the subjects familiarise themselves with the experimental setting and were not analysed. Regarding static tasks, we had three different types: 1. Identifying all ﬁles in which source code of a certain feature is implemented. 2. Locating nested #ifdef statements. 3. Identifying all features that occur in a certain ﬁle. For each type, we prepared two tasks. For example, we present one task for each type: S1: In which ﬁles does feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_ STATS occur? S2: Do features CONFIG_XENO_OPT_PRIOCPL and CONFIG_XENO_OPT_SCHED_SPORADIC occur together (i.e. nested) somewhere? If yes, in which ﬁles? At which lines does the inner feature start and end? S3: Which features occur in ﬁle xenomai/ksrc/nucleus/ sched.h? For maintenance tasks, we carefully introduced bugs into the source code, which the subjects were instructed to locate (name ﬁle and method, why it occurs and how it could be solved). Those bugs and related bug descriptions were presented to the subjects typically in C programs implementing software in the domain of operating systems, which we made sure by consulting an expert in C and Xenomai. We present the bug description of the ﬁrst maintenance task to illustrate them: M1: If the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) should be unloaded, a segmentation fault is thrown.
paraphrases: To assess program comprehension, we designed tasks specifically requiring subjects to understand the relevant source code for their solution. We employed two categories of tasks: maintenance and static tasks [28]. Maintenance tasks involved instructing subjects to find or fix a bug, while static tasks required them to analyze the structure of the source code. Our previous experiment [20] indicated that using colors enhanced program comprehension exclusively for static tasks, not for maintenance tasks. Consequently, we primarily focused on static tasks, though we included a few maintenance tasks to validate our earlier findings. All tasks were representative of those a maintenance programmer would encounter when searching for bugs within specific features or files. We developed ten tasks in total: two warm-up tasks (W1, W2), six static tasks (S1–S6), and two maintenance tasks (M1, M2). The warm-up tasks served to acclimate subjects to the experimental environment and were not included in the analysis. The static tasks comprised three distinct types: 1. Pinpointing all files containing the source code for a particular feature. 2. Identifying nested #ifdef statements. 3. Determining all features present in a specific file. Each type had two associated tasks. For instance, examples include: S1: Where is feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS implemented? S2: Are CONFIG_XENO_OPT_PRIOCPL and CONFIG_XENO_OPT_SCHED_SPORADIC nested together? If so, in which files and at what lines does the nested feature begin and end? S3: What features are found in xenomai/ksrc/nucleus/sched.h? For maintenance tasks, we intentionally inserted bugs into the source code, which subjects were instructed to identify (specifying the file, method, cause, and solution). These bugs, along with their descriptions, were typically presented within C programs used in operating systems, a detail verified by consulting a C and Xenomai expert. As an illustration, the description for the first maintenance task is: M1: Unloading the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) results in a segmentation fault.

Our method for evaluating program comprehension involved creating tasks that demanded a thorough understanding of the underlying source code to be completed. We categorized these tasks into two types: maintenance and static [28]. Maintenance tasks instructed participants to locate and resolve bugs, while static tasks required them to examine the source code's structure. Previous research [20] showed that visual cues (colors) only improved comprehension in static tasks, not maintenance tasks. Thus, we emphasized static tasks, although we incorporated a small number of maintenance tasks to confirm our prior observations. All tasks mirrored typical scenarios for maintenance programmers investigating bugs within specific features or files. A total of ten tasks were designed: two warm-up tasks (W1, W2), six static tasks (S1–S6), and two maintenance tasks (M1, M2). The warm-up tasks were solely for familiarization and were excluded from analysis. Static tasks were further divided into three categories: 1. Identifying all files where a given feature's source code resides. 2. Locating instances of nested #ifdef statements. 3. Determining which features are present in a particular file. Two tasks were prepared for each category. Examples include: S1: Which files implement the CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS feature? S2: Do the features CONFIG_XENO_OPT_PRIOCPL and CONFIG_XENO_OPT_SCHED_SPORADIC appear together (i.e., nested) anywhere? If yes, specify the files and the start and end lines of the inner feature. S3: What features are found in the file xenomai/ksrc/nucleus/sched.h? For the maintenance tasks, we deliberately introduced bugs into the source code, which subjects were asked to pinpoint (including the file, method, reason for the bug, and a potential fix). These bugs and their descriptions were typically embedded in C programs from the operating systems domain, a context validated by an expert in C and Xenomai. An example of a maintenance bug description is: M1: A segmentation fault occurs when attempting to unload the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG).

text: This quasi-experiment was designed to be performed in two days by two scoping teams in charge of separately scoping the AAL platform as a PL. Group 1 applied treatment 1, which consisted of first using PuLSE-Eco to conduct the scoping process, already taking into consideration the evolution concern, and then applying PLEvo-Scoping; while Group 2 applied treatment 2, which consisted of interweaving the activities of PuLSE-Eco and PLEvo-Scoping. The purpose of treatment 1 was to allow a clear distinction between the results before and after applying PLEvo-Scoping, while the purpose of treatment 2 was to avoid the confounding factor (present in treatment 1) of providing the scoping team with extra time to think about PL scope evolution after applying PuLSE-Eco. This confounding factor would put in doubt whether the obtained benefits were a result of this extra time or a result of the application of PLEvo-Scoping. In addition, the application of PLEvo-Scoping in the two treatments aimed at strengthening the validity of the results through corroboration. Two days were allocated to each treatment due to time restrictions.

text: The understandability and changeability sub-quality attributes from maintainability were chosen and two following tasks were devised to enable measuring the effects of visualization and interaction interventions on these quality attributes: Understanding and interpreting feature model configuration (Comprehension task): During a feature model configuration, software developers should have a good insight into the feature model and integration of its non-functional properties allowing for efficient comprehension of models (time-wise). Also, an effective representation causes to avoid the misunderstanding of relations between features and non-functional properties, and incorrect decisions during the configuration process. Comprehending change to perform (Changing task): Stakeholders’ requirements change during the development of applications. Changes in requirements urge changes in a configured feature model. Therefore, understanding required changes in the configured feature model and making right decisions to select or deselect features based on the changed requirements is common activity in a configuration process. Thus, a representation that facilitates making changes and helps to point out the impacts of change easily, correctly, and quickly is desirable.
paraphrases: To assess how visualization and interaction interventions impact maintainability's sub-attributes of understandability and changeability, two tasks were designed. The "Comprehension task" involved evaluating how well developers could understand and interpret feature model configurations, including their non-functional properties, to ensure efficient and accurate model comprehension, thereby preventing misinterpretations and errors. The "Changing task" focused on evaluating the ease and correctness with which developers could understand and implement necessary modifications to a configured feature model in response to evolving stakeholder requirements, highlighting the need for representations that clearly show the impact of changes.

We selected understandability and changeability, key aspects of maintainability, and created two tasks to gauge the influence of visualization and interaction techniques on them. The first task, "Comprehension," assessed how effectively developers could grasp feature model configurations and their non-functional attributes, aiming for quick and accurate understanding to prevent errors. The second task, "Changing," evaluated how easily developers could identify, decide upon, and implement modifications to a configured feature model when requirements shifted, emphasizing the importance of representations that clearly illustrate the effects of such changes.

text: The developed optimization model consists of 2 parts. The first part is an objective function, which is directly influenced by the number of available features and their utility values. In this study, each feature was assigned with a utility value produced by a random function with normal distribution. The second part is devoted to the linear constraints so that the feature and goal models’ structures are transformed into linear constraints using the developed transformation rules. To consider the mapping links, we connected the generated feature models’ leaf features to the leaf elements in the goal models.
paraphrases: The optimization model developed comprises two main components. The first component is an objective function, whose value is determined by the quantity and utility of available features; each feature's utility was randomly assigned based on a normal distribution. The second component consists of linear constraints, derived by applying specific transformation rules to convert the structures of feature and goal models into linear equations. To account for interconnections, the leaf features of the generated feature models were linked to the corresponding leaf elements in the goal models.

Our optimization model has two primary sections. The initial section is an objective function, directly impacted by the count of features and their assigned utility values, which were randomly generated following a normal distribution. The subsequent section details the linear constraints, where the structural elements of feature and goal models are converted into these constraints using our defined transformation rules. We also established mapping links by connecting the lowest-level features of our generated models to the corresponding terminal elements in the goal models.

text: The experiment is divided into two parts. In each part, CSA is evaluated with a different set of problem samples. The objective is to explore how CSA performance varies when the problem size (number of features per model) and type of constraints vary. In the ﬁrst part, the 18 algorithm conﬁgurations are executed with samples of models of different sizes, ranging from 10 features to 450 features, increasing the number in steps of 10 (i.e., 45 total samples). Each experiment step is performed with a sample of 200 problem instances, and the average value is computed in order to reduce the ﬂuctuations due to randomness (e.g., the random seeds used to generate problem instances). In the second part, the 18 CSA conﬁgurations are executed with 5 samples of 200 problems each one. The number of features per model is ﬁxed to 30 to focus on the inﬂuence of model constraints on the performance. This number was selected from the average number of features per model reported in Table 6. From one sample to another we vary the type of constraints incorporated to the models. The conﬁgurations of these constraints per sample are described below... The experiment comprises the execution of the 8 algorithms previously mentioned (GAFES, Greedy, and the 6 CSA approximate conﬁgurations) with a set of samples of problem instances. Each sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository. Since GAFES and Greedy algorithms only support basic CTCs (i.e., constraints with 2 features at most), in this experiment non-basic CTCs, which are the 17.26% of CTCs, are removed from models. Problem instances include a linear objective to be maximized and a single linear inequality restriction as global constraint, since this is the problem formalization supported by both algorithms. To this end, models are extended with 2 randomly generated attributes per features (a f , b f ), using a uniform distribution over (0, 1). One attribute is used to deﬁne the linear objective function, and the other one to deﬁne the inequality restriction. The experiment is carried out with 4 different samples of problems, each one with a different value of restriction ratio. In the ﬁrst sample, the restriction ratio is equal to 1 (100%), so that the restriction cannot be violated by any solution. The other three samples use restriction ratios of 90%, 80% and 70%, respectively. By reducing the value of the restriction ratio, the problem becomes more restrictive and harder to solve, since less combinations of features can satisfy the constraint. Thus, by using different ratios, we can observe how the performance of approximate algorithms degrades as the problem becomes harder... The experiment comprises the execution of the 8 algorithms previously mentioned (0-1 LP, BoolOpt and 6 CSA exact conﬁgurations) with a set of samples of problem instances. Similar to the previous experiment, a sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository. Since 0-1 LP supports linear functions, problems are stated as the optimization of a linear objective function (|O F| = 1) with a variable number of linear inequality restrictions (|GC| = n). The ﬁrst sample contains instances with 0 inequality restrictions, and the other samples contain instances with 1, 2 and 5 inequality restrictions, with a ﬁxed restriction ratio of 90%... We run the experiment with 2 samples of problem instances, each one with a different distribution of feature interactions. Similar to previous experiments, each sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository enriched with attributes generated by Thor. In sample #1, models contain 1 interaction per feature, all of degree 2. In sample #2, models contain 2 interactions per feature: 67% of degree 2, 23% of degree 3 and 10% of degree 4. No inequality restrictions are considered, and the objective function is a multi-linear polynomial function including one term for each feature and interaction attribute generated by Thor.

text: We structured the work as follows: we performed initial experiments on two of the feature models (E-shop and WebPortal) and in these initial experiments we discovered that the algorithms (when the (n + 1) approach and direct encoding are used) returned relatively few valid products. This led to two enhancements: a new representation and the 1 + n approach. We then carried out experiments using the six published models. This was followed by experiments with two case studies that had realistic values of attributes rather than randomly generated attributes (as used in previous work) and then experiments with the larger randomly generated feature model.
paraphrases: Our research began with initial tests on the E-shop and WebPortal feature models. These early trials revealed that when employing the (n + 1) approach and direct encoding, the algorithms produced a limited number of valid products. Consequently, we implemented two improvements: a revised representation and the 1 + n approach. Subsequent experiments were conducted using the six published models. Following this, we performed experiments with two case studies that incorporated realistic attribute values, as opposed to the randomly generated ones used previously, and concluded with tests on a larger randomly generated feature model.

The study was organized in stages. Initially, we tested two feature models, E-shop and WebPortal, and observed that algorithms using the (n + 1) approach and direct encoding yielded few valid products. This finding prompted us to develop a new representation and the 1 + n approach. We then experimented with the six existing models. Next, we conducted experiments using two case studies with realistic attribute values, a departure from the random attributes used before, and finally, tested a larger randomly generated feature model.

text: In order to evaluate the model difference algorithm, referring to the experiment method of the literature[5], Given two product feature model M1 and M2, we denote expected changes and the detected changes by our approach as Me={<f1, f2, changetype>} and Mr={<f1, f2, changetype>} respectively, where f1 refers to a feature in M1, f2 is the corresponding feature of f1 in M2, and changetype is the type of changes between the two features. The changetype can be unchanged, add, change(rename)....After the model difference, model merge algorithm can be used to realizing the model merge. We evaluate the model merge from accuracy aspect. The composition is effective if it neither produces too many incorrect compositions nor misses too many correct compositions. Precision and recall is used to capture this intuition. Precision measures quality and is the ratio of correct composition found to the total number of composition found. Recall measures coverage and is the ratio of the correct composition found to the total number of all correct composition. The experiment corpus 5 is extracted from UNIONmode. Seven groups of data are extracted for experiment and the experiment result is the average of the entire seven group.
paraphrases: To assess the model difference algorithm, following the experimental methodology from literature [5], we define expected changes as Me={<f1, f2, changetype>} and changes detected by our approach as Mr={<f1, f2, changetype>}, given two product feature models M1 and M2. Here, f1 is a feature in M1, f2 is its corresponding feature in M2, and changetype indicates the type of modification between them (e.g., unchanged, add, change/rename). Once the model differences are identified, a model merge algorithm can be applied to combine them. We evaluate the model merge based on its accuracy. An effective composition avoids both excessive incorrect compositions and insufficient correct compositions. Precision and recall are employed to quantify this. Precision, a measure of quality, is the ratio of correctly identified compositions to the total compositions found. Recall, a measure of coverage, is the ratio of correctly identified compositions to all existing correct compositions. The experimental data, corpus 5, was sourced from UNIONmode. Seven distinct data groups were extracted for the experiment, and the reported result represents the average across all seven groups.

Following the experimental approach outlined in literature [5], we evaluate the model difference algorithm by considering two product feature models, M1 and M2. We represent the anticipated changes as Me={<f1, f2, changetype>} and the changes detected by our method as Mr={<f1, f2, changetype>}. In these notations, f1 refers to a feature in M1, f2 is its counterpart in M2, and changetype describes the specific alteration (e.g., unchanged, added, renamed). After determining the model differences, a model merge algorithm can then be used for integration. Our evaluation of the model merge focuses on its accuracy: a successful composition is one that neither generates too many erroneous combinations nor overlooks too many correct ones. This concept is quantified using precision and recall. Precision indicates the quality by calculating the proportion of correctly identified compositions relative to all compositions found, while recall assesses coverage by determining the proportion of correctly identified compositions relative to all truly correct compositions. The experimental dataset, corpus 5, was derived from UNIONmode. The experiment involved seven separate data groups, and the final reported result is an average taken across all these groups.

text: During the experiment, subjects have to update logistic systems derived from the Egemin’s SPL. The goal of an update is to bring a system from its current (as-is) state to the expected new state (to-be). To update the system a subject has to stop and start relevant services, and remove, replace and add resources (.Net assemblies and executables). During an update, either the architecture-centric approach or the baseline approach is used. The updates are performed on variants of the Kimberly Clark (KC) logistic system. The system is installed in the standard location (Program Files/Egemin) and is operational. The KC logistic system consists of an E’tricc service, an E’wms service, an E’pia service (logistic platform), and the associated clients (see Figure 1). For the purpose of the experiments we have deﬁned three kinds of the update scenarios: S0 Learning scenario kind - these are easy scenarios which require simple changes that affect one of the subsystems. The aim of the learning scenarios is to familiarize subjects with the system under update and the usage of our tool. SA Simple scenario kind - in these scenarios, the E’wms or E’tricc services and corresponding client screens are object of the update. The number of changes is limited. To perform the correct update two processes must be restarted. SB Complex scenario kind - in these scenarios, the whole logistic system is affected by the update. Most of the running processes have to be restarted to perform the update correctly. The concrete scenarios were prepared by Egemin’s senior architect, who did not participate in the experiment as a subject. The proposed scenarios are similar to the updates Egemin integrators perform in practice. We asked the subjects to perform two updates for each scenario kind, one with the architecture-centric approach, the other with the baseline approach. We prepared pairs of similar scenarios to ensure objectivity and avoid interference between treatments.

text: RH1: Background colors improve program comprehension in large SPLs. Large means, that the source code consist of at least 40,000 lines of code (von Mayrhauser & Vans, 1995) and considerably more than 7 ± 2 features, such that humans cannot distinguish colors without direct comparison, if we used a one-to-one mapping of colors to features. text: We exploit the quantitative data to facilitate a hypothesis conﬁrmation, where we use the deﬁned research questions as hypothesis. To investigate whether a hypothesis can be conﬁrmed, we apply the following data analysis. RQ1 We assess the number of unchanged, modiﬁed, and new variants determined by the higher-order delta application reasoning when stepping to the next SPL version under test. RQ2 We examine the number of retest goals derived by our change impact analysis (incremental model slicing). Retest goals indicate that applied model changes have an impact on already tested behavior between subsequently variants and versions of variants under test. RQ3 We compare the number of selected and generated test cases by our framework to the number of test cases executed by retest-all [14] to check for a reduction in test cases to be executed. In addition, we assess the time required for both types of change impact analyses to reason about the eﬃciency of our selection technique according to the cost model deﬁned by Leung and White [61]. RQ4 We evaluate the fault detection rate of our framework compared to retest-all [14]. Unfortunately, the two subject SPLs do not provide a real fault history. Hence, we use simulated ones derived by taking the changes applied to a test model when stepping to a subsequent variant or version of a variant into account. For the derivation of faults, we combine the changes captured in the respective model regression deltas, i.e., added transitions as well as source and target states of removed transitions, with randomly chosen transitions from the test model. Those faults denote erroneous artifact interactions caused by changes and their impact on common behavior. We generate for each variant and version of a variant a corresponding set of those simulated faults. Depending on the size of the fault set, we create a maximum of diﬀerent data sets, where each time a random selection of 10% of the faults is made to obtain random fault data sets. The set of test cases to be retested determined by our framework and the set of test cases for retest-all [14] are then executed to assess the fault detection rate. RQ5 We examine the number of retest goals derived by our change impact analysis similar to RQ1 as they indicate the retest potential to reason about, but we apply diﬀerent testing orders to our approach. The testing orders are computed for the initial SPL versions based on existing product prioritization techniques [54, 56, 62, 63] as well as random generation. For the random generation, we generate 100 product orders for each of the two subject SPLs. In addition, we select (1) four prioritization techniques [54, 62, 63] focusing on the dissimilarity between products, e.g., in terms of feature selection, to increase the coverage of elements or features, and (2) we use a testing order obtained in previous work [56], where the overall diﬀerences between subsequent variants in terms of applied change operations captured in model regression deltas are minimized. The selected techniques are applicable due to the available artifacts in this experiment required as input, i.e., delta sets and feature conﬁgurations. To this end, we apply the feature similarity [63] and delta similarity technique [62] of Al-Hajjaji et al., the global maximum distance (GMD) and local maximum distance (LMD) approach from Henard et al. [54], and from our previous work [56] the NEARIN algorithm.
paraphrases: We utilize quantitative data to validate our hypotheses, which are directly derived from our research questions. To confirm these hypotheses, we conduct the following data analysis: RQ1 evaluates the unchanged, modified, and new variants resulting from higher-order delta application when moving to the next SPL version. RQ2 investigates the number of retest goals identified by our change impact analysis (incremental model slicing), signifying that model changes affect previously tested behavior across variants. RQ3 compares the test cases selected and generated by our framework against those executed by retest-all [14] to determine if our method reduces the number of test cases. It also analyzes the time efficiency of our selection technique using the Leung and White cost model [61]. RQ4 assesses our framework's fault detection rate against retest-all [14]. Since real fault histories are unavailable, we simulate faults based on changes applied to test models between subsequent variants, combining model regression delta changes with random test model transitions to represent erroneous interactions. We generate simulated fault sets for each variant, creating multiple data sets by randomly selecting 10% of faults. Both our framework's retested cases and retest-all's cases are then executed to measure fault detection. RQ5 examines retest goals from our change impact analysis, similar to RQ1, but applies different testing orders to our approach. These orders are generated for initial SPL versions using existing product prioritization techniques [54, 56, 62, 63] and random generation (100 orders per SPL). We also select four prioritization techniques [54, 62, 63] that prioritize product dissimilarity to enhance coverage, and incorporate a testing order from previous work [56] that minimizes differences between successive variants. These techniques are suitable because the experiment provides necessary inputs like delta sets and feature configurations, leading us to apply methods such as feature similarity [63], delta similarity [62], GMD/LMD [54], and NEARIN [56].

We employ quantitative data for hypothesis confirmation, where our research questions serve as the hypotheses. To confirm these, we conduct a detailed data analysis. RQ1 measures the number of unchanged, modified, and new variants determined by higher-order delta application in the progression of SPL versions. RQ2 focuses on the retest goals identified through our incremental model slicing-based change impact analysis, indicating how model changes affect established behavior across variants. For RQ4, we assess our framework's fault detection rate versus "retest-all" [14]. Due to the absence of real fault histories in the subject SPLs, we simulate faults by integrating changes from model regression deltas (e.g., added/removed transitions and states) with random test model transitions, representing erroneous interactions. We generate distinct sets of these simulated faults for each variant, and create multiple random fault data sets by sampling 10% of faults. Fault detection is then measured by executing both our framework's retested cases and "retest-all"'s cases. RQ5 explores retest goals from our change impact analysis (similar to RQ1) but with varied testing orders. These orders are computed for initial SPL versions using established product prioritization techniques [54, 56, 62, 63] and random generation (100 orders per SPL). We specifically choose four dissimilarity-focused prioritization techniques [54, 62, 63] to improve feature coverage, and an order from prior research [56] that minimizes differences between successive variants. The applicability of these techniques is ensured by the experimental availability of delta sets and feature configurations, allowing us to implement methods like feature similarity [63], delta similarity [62], GMD/LMD [54], and the NEARIN algorithm [56].

text: 3.2.1 First hypotheses: effect of stability on inconsistency rate: In the first hypothesis, we speculate that a high variation of the design characteristics of the design models may lead to a higher incidence of inconsistencies; since, it increases the chance for an incorrect manipulation of the design characteristic by the composition heuristics. In fact, modifications from severe evolutions may lead the composition heuristics to be ineffective or even prohibitive. In addition, these inconsistencies may also propagate. As a higher incidence of changes is found in unstable models, we hypothesize that unstable models tend to have a higher (or equal to) inconsistency rate than stablemodels. The first hypothesis evaluates whether the inconsistency rate in unstable models is significantly higher (or equal to) than in stable models. Thus, our hypotheses are summarized as follows: Null Hypothesis 1, H1−0: Stable design models have similar or higher inconsistency rate than unstable design models. H1−0:Rate(stable designmodels)≥Rate(unstable design models). Alternative Hypothesis 1, H1−1: Stable designmodels have a lower inconsistency rate than unstable design models. H1−1:Rate(stable designmodels)<Rate(unstable design models). By testing this first hypothesis, we evaluate if stability is a good indicator to identify the most critical MCM in term of inconsistency rate from a sequence of MCM produced from multiple software development teams. Hence, developers can then review the design models having a higher density of composition inconsistencies. We believe that this strategy is a more effective one than going through all MCM produced or assuming an overoptimistic position where all MCM produced is a MAB. 3.2.2 Second hypothesis: effect of stability on developer effort: As previously mentioned, developers tend to invest different quantity of effort to derive MAB from MCM. Today, model managers are unable to grasp how much effort this transformation can demand. This variation is because developers need to resolve different types of problems in a composed model, from a simple renaming of elements to complex modifications in the structure of the composed model. In fact, the structure of the composed models may be affected in different ways during the composition, e.g., creating unexpected interdependences between the model elements. Even worse, these modifications in the structure of the model may cause ripple effects, i.e., inconsistency propagation between the model elements. The introduction of one inconsistency can often lead to multiple other inconsistencies because of a “knock-on” effect. An example would be the inconsistency whereby a client component is missing an important operation in the interface of a server component (see example in Sect. 2.4). This semantic inconsistency leads to a “knockon” syntactic inconsistency if another component requires the operation. In the worst case, there may be long chains of inconsistencies all derived from a single inconsistency. Given a composed model at hand, developers need to know if they will invest little or too much effort to transform MCM into MAB, given the problem at hand. Based on this knowledge, they will be able to prioritize the review of the output composed models and to better comprehend the effort to be invested, e.g., reviewing themodels that require higher effort first and those requiring less effort after. With this in mind, we are interested in understanding the possible difference of effort to resolve inconsistencies in stable and unstable design models. The expectation is that stablemodels require a lower developers’ effort to produce the output intended model. This expectation is based on the speculation that unstable models may demand more restructuringmodifications than stable models; hence, requiring more effort. This leads to the second null and alternative hypotheses as follows: Null Hypothesis 2, H2−0: Stable models require similar or higher effort to resolve inconsistencies than unstable models. H2−0: Effort(stable models) ≥ Effort(unstable models). Alternative Hypothesis 2, H2−1: Stable models tend to require a lower inconsistency resolution effort than unstable ones. H2−1: Effort(stable models) < Effort(unstable models). By testing this first hypothesis, we evaluate if stability is a useful indicator to identify the most critical effort-consuming cases in which severe semantic inconsistencies in architectural components are more often. This knowledge heSPL model managers to allocate qualified developers to overcome the composition inconsistencies in MCM.
paraphrases: Our first set of hypotheses explores how model stability impacts the rate of inconsistencies. We theorize that significant variability in design model characteristics can increase inconsistencies by making composition heuristics prone to incorrect manipulations, especially with severe evolutionary changes that can render these heuristics ineffective or even detrimental, and allow inconsistencies to spread. Given that unstable models typically undergo more changes, we predict they will exhibit an inconsistency rate equal to or higher than stable models. This leads to Null Hypothesis 1 (H1-0): Stable design models have an inconsistency rate similar to or higher than unstable models, while Alternative Hypothesis 1 (H1-1) proposes stable models have a lower inconsistency rate. By testing this, we aim to determine if stability effectively pinpoints critical multi-component models (MCMs) with high inconsistency rates, allowing developers to prioritize review more efficiently than examining all MCMs.

Our second hypothesis concerns the influence of stability on the effort developers expend. We acknowledge that the effort to convert MCMs into MABs varies widely due to diverse problems, from simple renames to complex structural changes and ripple effects of inconsistencies. Managers currently lack insight into this effort. A single inconsistency can cascade into many others, as exemplified by a missing operation causing semantic and subsequent syntactic inconsistencies. Developers require this insight to prioritize reviews and understand necessary effort. We anticipate that stable models will demand less developer effort for inconsistency resolution because unstable models are likely to require more extensive restructuring. Thus, Null Hypothesis 2 (H2-0) states: Stable models demand similar or greater effort to resolve inconsistencies than unstable models, whereas Alternative Hypothesis 2 (H2-1) posits that stable models require less effort. Evaluating this helps identify effort-intensive scenarios, assisting managers in assigning appropriate developers to address complex composition inconsistencies.

Again, Thum’s survey (Thum et al., 2009) shows that these parameters reﬂect real feature models. In Experiment 3 (Section 7.4), we ﬁxed the following parameters: total number of features n = 1000, maximum number of children = 10, type of child group = (50%, 25%, 25%), optional child = 50%, variables in cross-tree constrains = 2, and generated feature models with different percentage of cross-tree constraints from 0 to 30%. ... In order to create a feature selection optimization problem, values for the resource consumption and value of each feature must be generated. These values are created by generating pseudo-random numbers for the following problem parameters: (1) the resources consumed by each terminal feature r(tﬁ) = random(Rmax); (2) the resources consumed by each non-terminal feature r(nﬁ) = 0; (3) the value per unit resource that can be consumed by each terminal feature unitV = random(UnitVmax); (4) the value for each terminal feature v(tﬁ) = r(tﬁ) × unitV + random(Vmax); and (5) the value for each non-terminal feature v(nﬁ) = 0. Here, Rmax, UnitVmax, and Vmax are the upper bound on resource requirements, unit price of a resource, and the extra value of a feature after its consumed resource price. The value of each feature is not directly proportional to its resource consumption. The function random(i) returns an integer from 0 to (i − 1), following a uniform distribution. The total resources available for feature selections are then constrained to Rc = Rmax × nTF × 0.8 where nTF is the number of all terminal features in a feature model. For larger problems, we needed to generate problems for which we knew the optimal solution value. We used Akbar et al. (2001) test pattern generation technique to overcome this challenge. Akbar’s generation approach sets the problem parameters as follows: (1) a valid selection of terminal features is randomly chosen by the problem generator to serve as the optimal solution; (2) if S is the set of features randomly chosen to be in the optimal solution, then the generator sets R′(S) = R(S) = fi ∈ Sr(ﬁ) so that the available resources exactly equal the resources needed for the optimal feature selection; and (3) the value associated with each of the randomly chosen optimal features is set to v′(ﬁ) = r(ﬁ) × unitV + Vmax. Thus V ′(S) = fi ∈ Sv′(ﬁ) = fi ∈ S(r(ﬁ) × unitV + Vmax), which guarantees that there is no feature selection that ﬁts within the resource constraints and has a higher value than the feature selection that the problem generator selected to serve as the optimal solution.

text: First dependent variable The dependent variable of hypothesis 1 is the inconsistency rate. It quantifies the amount of composition inconsistencies (Sect. 2.4) divided by the total number of elements in the composed model. That is, it allows computing the density of composition inconsistencies in the output composed models. This metric makes it possible to assess the difference between the inconsistency rate of stable models and unstable models (H1). It is important to point out that the inconsistency rate is defined from multiple inconsistency metrics (see Table 2). ... Second dependent variable The dependent variable of the hypothesis2istheinconsistencyresolutioneffort, g(MCM)—that is, the number of operations (creations, removals, and updates) required to transform the composed model into the intended model. We compute these operations because they represent the main operations performed by developers to evolve software in realistic settings [28]. Thus, this computation represents an estimation of the inconsistency resolution effort. The collected measures of inconsistency rate are used to assess if the composed model has inconsistencies after the composition heuristic is applied (diff(MCM, MAB) > 0). Then, a set of removals, updates, and creations are performed to resolve the inconsistencies. As a result, the intended model is produced and the inconsistency resolution effort is com-puted.
paraphrases: The first dependent variable, inconsistency rate, measures the proportion of composition inconsistencies relative to the total elements in the composed model, indicating the density of such inconsistencies. This allows for comparing inconsistency rates between stable and unstable models as per Hypothesis 1, with the rate being derived from various inconsistency metrics (Table 2). The second dependent variable, inconsistency resolution effort, g(MCM), is quantified by the number of operations (creating, removing, updating) needed to transform the composed model into its desired state. These operations are critical as they reflect typical developer actions in software evolution, thus providing an estimate of the effort involved in resolving inconsistencies. Inconsistency rate measurements determine if inconsistencies exist after applying the composition heuristic (diff(MCM, MAB) > 0); if so, operations are executed to resolve them, leading to the intended model and calculation of the resolution effort.

For Hypothesis 1, we use the inconsistency rate as the dependent variable, calculated as the ratio of composition inconsistencies (detailed in Section 2.4) to the total elements in the composed model, which gives us the density of these inconsistencies in the final models. This metric enables us to evaluate the difference in inconsistency rates between stable and unstable models, as specified in H1, and it's important to note that this rate is based on several inconsistency metrics (refer to Table 2). For Hypothesis 2, the dependent variable is the inconsistency resolution effort, g(MCM), which represents the total number of operations (creations, removals, and updates) necessary to convert the composed model into the desired model. We measure these operations because they are fundamental to how developers modify software in real-world scenarios [28], thereby providing an estimated measure of the effort required for inconsistency resolution. The observed inconsistency rates help determine if the composed model contains inconsistencies after the composition heuristic is applied (i.e., diff(MCM, MAB) > 0). If inconsistencies are present, a series of removals, updates, and creations are performed to fix them, resulting in the intended model and a calculated inconsistency resolution effort.

We define several metrics: M1 is the model's size in bytes, expressed as a standard arithmetic expression for parametric methods or as a sum of arithmetic products (corresponding to ADD paths) for ADDs. In both cases, the formula is UTF-8 encoded and free of whitespace. For PBA, M1 is the total size of each evaluated product model. M2 counts the number of parameter occurrences (where a parameter signifies a feature) within the model or formula. M3 quantifies the number of constant occurrences, which corresponds to the number of leaves in ADDs. M4 measures the time in seconds required to compute the average reliability across all products in the Software Product Line (SPL). M5 tracks the model's size in bytes as a function of the number of features, and M6 tracks the time in seconds as a function of the number of features. Notably, metrics M2 and M3 are not applicable to PBA models because PBA does not account for variability.

text: We designed one external conﬁguration for a Dr.Chat Mobile application shown in Fig. 14. We also built a scenario suite with a set of expected quality scenarios for a product under construc-tion. The experiment is based on two transactions to be performed with a Dr.Chat Mobile application. The transactions represent a user’s stimulus from an application functional perspective (e.g. execute a consultation transaction). The ﬁrst transaction (TR1) requires the application user to create and submit a medical consultation. The following steps comprise the transaction. Once the user is logged into the system, the application must locate the user (using either the device’s sen-sors or manual selection from the index-based lists). The user must then describe his medical condition using text and attachments, including voice or video recording and pictures. Finally, the appli-cation sends the consultation to the medical server. The second transaction (TR2) requires the application user to retrieve a previously submitted medical consultation and check its attachments. In this transaction, the user ﬁrst selects a medical consultation from the medical record stored in cellphone’s mem-ory, then retrieves from the server its attachments including voice or video recordings and pictures. Our experimental design contains two main parts. The ﬁrst part (XP1) focuses on testing the human analyst’s behavior, while the second (XP2) tests SPAF assistance capabilities. In the ﬁrst part (XP1), the human analyst must manually select a set of concrete components from the components in the core assets base to instantiate product architecture. Given a scenario suite, the analyst must then ﬁnd possible sets of components that can fulﬁl the responses according to the stimulus in the quality scenarios in the context of (TR1) and (TR2). To test the selected components, the human analyst produce a product production plan for each set of components, and use the SPL to derive the product. For each product the suite tests are executed and using the monitoring tools she collects the top-rated ones according to its functional and quality characteristics. In the second part (XP2), the human analyst must model the Dr.Chat Mobile SPL software architecture, variability, component catalog, and scenario suite using the proposed languages for each domain provided by SPAF. The tester must also model one sensitiv-ity point for each scenario in the provided suite case. The human analyst must then run the SPAF tool and collect the top-rated com-ponents according to its functional and quality characteristics. The analyst uses the components proposed by SPAF to deﬁne the prod-uct production plan and then use the SPL to derive the products. A detailed description of the test procedure, subjects, objects, and recording mechanisms is presented below. What type of experimental design has been chosen? One Factor with two treatments.
paraphrases: The experimental design for the Dr.Chat Mobile application focuses on evaluating two distinct transactions (TR1: submitting a consultation; TR2: retrieving a consultation) as treatments for a single factor. The study is divided into two main parts: XP1 assesses human analyst behavior in manually selecting components for product architecture based on scenario suites for TR1 and TR2, while XP2 evaluates SPAF's assistance in modeling the application's architecture and identifying top-rated components.

text: One Factor with two treatments. The experiment was designed as a control group study (see Figure 1). The method group (MG) used the integrated ARE instructions according to the template described in [2]. In contrast, the control group (CG) used traditional ARE instructions according to a VM-based ARE approach combined with a TORE [13] guideline. The SPL specification in which the main SPL features and the SPL architecture were described was given to all participants. Thus, the control group was equipped with state of the art material, while the method group was equipped with our novel approach. During the experiment, both groups performed fictitious but controlled elicitation interviews in order to gather requirements. The participants’ performance was measured using the aforementioned variables in order to enable statistical comparison. Each participant was randomly assigned to exactly one group. As far as possible, we tried to assign the participants to the groups alternately. This was the preferred strategy, as we did not know the participants before and considered the order of their commitment as random. However, in order to assure equal distribution of RE-experienced and less experienced participants in both groups, their RE background was taken into consideration. Thus, the information about interview experience provided in the pre-questionnaires was used for balancing the groups. A statistical test showed that a significant difference regarding RE experience between the two groups could not be confirmed. However, additional balancing of the participants according to their awareness of basic SPL concepts was not possible, as only six participants had experience in RE and SPL engineering. We discuss in section 3.4. its influence on the results.
paraphrases: The study involved a single factor with two conditions and was structured as a control group experiment. The method group received novel integrated ARE instructions, while the control group used established, traditional ARE instructions. Both groups were given the same SPL specification and performed mock elicitation interviews. Participant performance was assessed with specific variables for statistical analysis. Participants were randomly assigned to one group, with an effort to alternate assignments, assuming random commitment order. To ensure balanced experience levels, participants' RE backgrounds from pre-questionnaires were used to distribute experienced and less experienced individuals evenly. A statistical test confirmed no significant difference in RE experience between the groups. However, balancing for SPL concept awareness was not feasible due to a limited number of experienced participants, a factor discussed in section 3.4 regarding its impact on the results.

text: Exp 1: To evaluate our research hypotheses, we used a between-subjects design, which means we split our sample in two groups and compared the performance between both groups, the ifdef group (21 subjects) and the color group (22 subjects). The ifdef group worked with the ifdef version, the color group worked with the color version of the source code. To assure that both groups are comparable, we matched both groups according to the value of the programming experience questionnaire, age, and gender. One subject was color blind and assigned to the ifdef group. Type: One Factor with two treatments. Exp 3: Since our sample was rather small, we used a within-subjects design with two phases (i.e., we let each subject complete tasks with both tool versions). Group A worked with the color version in the first phase and switched to the ifdef version in the second phase, whereas group B worked with the ifdef version in the first phase and switched to the color version in the second phase. In each phase, both groups worked with the same tasks in the following order: W1, S1, S2, S3, M1 in the first phase, and W2, S4, S5, S6, M2 in the second phase.15 Hence, group A solved tasks W1, S1, S2, S3, and M1 with the color version and W2, S4, S5, S6, and M2 with the ifdef version (vice versa for group B). Corresponding tasks of both phases (i.e., W1/W2, S1/S4, S2/S5, S3/S6, M1/M2) were designed to be comparable (e.g., the same number of features had to be entered as solution). This allows us to compare the results within phases (between groups), and between phases (within groups). Type: One Factor with two treatments.
paraphrases: Experiment 1 utilized a between-subjects design with one factor and two treatments. We divided our participants into two distinct groups, the 'ifdef' group (21 individuals) and the 'color' group (22 individuals), to compare their performance. The 'ifdef' group used the 'ifdef' source code version, while the 'color' group used the 'color' source code version. To ensure comparability, participants were matched based on programming experience, age, and gender, with one color-blind participant assigned to the 'ifdef' group. Experiment 3, due to a small sample size, employed a within-subjects design with one factor and two treatments across two phases, meaning each participant used both tool versions. Group A started with the 'color' version then switched to 'ifdef', while Group B began with 'ifdef' and then used 'color'. Identical task sequences (W1, S1, S2, S3, M1 in phase one; W2, S4, S5, S6, M2 in phase two) were completed by both groups in each phase. Thus, Group A used the 'color' version for tasks W1-M1 and the 'ifdef' version for tasks W2-M2 (and vice versa for Group B). Corresponding tasks across phases (e.g., W1 and W2) were designed for comparability (e.g., requiring the same number of features), enabling within-phase (between-group) and between-phase (within-group) comparisons.
