text: In order to answer RQ1 a quantitative analysis was conducted. In this analysis, we assessed the number of solutions and performed an analysis of the Pareto fronts, in order to evaluate the capability of the algorithms in ﬁnding a great number and diversiﬁed solutions (PLAs). In this sense, we calculated the Error Ratio [40] quality indicator for measuring the ratio between the solutions that are present in the approximated true Pareto front (PFtrueApprox) and the ones that are not. The lower the error ratio value, the better it is and a greater number of solutions are in PFtrueApprox. We used the hypervolume [41] as the main quality indicator and the Kruskal Wallis (signiﬁcance level of 95%) [42] as non-parametric statistic test. Hypervolume measures the coverage area of a known Pareto front (PFknown) on the objective space regarding a nadir (reference) point. The higher the hypervolume, the better the Pareto front. In this work, we normalize the objective values between 0 and 1 and deﬁne the nadir point as the worst possible point (1, 1) with a small oﬀset, thus being (1.1, 1.1). Hypervolume was used because it has the capability to evaluate a set of solutions generated by multi-objective algorithms regarding convergence and diversity, besides being one of the most used indicators in the literature [43]. In addition, hypervolume is ▷-completeness compliant [41], which means that, hypervolume can measure if a Pareto front is better than another in terms of dominance relation [41]. It is a useful indicator for what we are trying to assess, since we want to ﬁnd which resulting Pareto Front is the best one by comparing fronts generated by diﬀerent sets of operators. Furthermore, for calculating the hypervolume, only the objective values of the solutions and the nadir point is needed as entry. Other quality indicators also commonly used in the literature need information that are not available in this kind of problem. For example, IGD and GD [44] require the true Pareto Front, which we do not know. Other widely used quality indicator is R2 [45], which needs a weight vector distributed uniformly in the objective space. In such work, we do not accurately know the objective space landscape. The objective functions have maximum and minimum values, but it is not possible to know if these maximum and minimum will be reached during the optimization process. In order to answer RQ2 and RQ3 a qualitative analysis was conducted. In order to validate the eﬀectiveness of the proposed search operators in preserving the architectural styles, we performed an analysis of the solutions organization and also analyzed the number of PLAs violated. An analysis of the feature modularization (related to FM) was also performed in order to verify the modularity of the PLAs. Taking into account that the architect will choose only one solution from the set of non-dominated solutions, we analyzed, for each experiment, the solutions with the lowest euclidean distance (ED) from the ideal solution. The lower the ED value, the better the trade-oﬀbetween the objectives. In this work, the ideal solution has the ﬁtness values of the objectives CM and FM equal to zero. The statistical test Kruskal Wallis was used in order to determine if the conﬁgurations showed statistical diﬀerences. The conﬁguration with the best signiﬁcant hypervolume value was chosen for each combination of experiment and PLA. When there was not statistical diﬀerence (Kruskal Wallis) among hypervolume values we selected the conﬁguration with the lower number of evaluations (population size ∗ number of generations) in order to decrease the execution time. The ﬁnal experiment conﬁgurations are presented in Table 10.
paraphrases: To address Research Question 1 (RQ1), we conducted a quantitative analysis. This involved evaluating the number of solutions and examining Pareto fronts to determine how effectively the algorithms generated numerous and diverse solutions (PLAs). We specifically used the Error Ratio [40] to quantify the proportion of solutions within the approximated true Pareto front (PFtrueApprox) versus those outside it; a lower error ratio indicates a better outcome with more solutions in PFtrueApprox. Our primary quality metric was hypervolume [41], complemented by the Kruskal Wallis non-parametric statistical test (with a 95% significance level) [42]. Hypervolume quantifies the objective space coverage of a known Pareto front (PFknown) relative to a nadir point, with higher values signifying superior Pareto fronts. For this study, objective values were normalized to a 0-1 range, and the nadir point was set as the worst possible point (1.1, 1.1) with a slight offset. Hypervolume was chosen for its ability to assess both convergence and diversity in multi-objective algorithm solutions and its widespread use in literature [43]. Its ▷-completeness compliance [41] also allows it to measure the dominance relationship between Pareto fronts, making it suitable for identifying the best front among those generated by different operator sets. Crucially, hypervolume calculation only requires objective values and the nadir point, unlike other common indicators like IGD and GD [44] which demand knowledge of the true Pareto Front (unavailable here), or R2 [45] which needs a uniformly distributed weight vector, and we lack precise knowledge of the objective space landscape. While objective functions have maximum and minimum values, reaching these during optimization isn't guaranteed. For RQ2 and RQ3, a qualitative analysis was performed. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed search operators in maintaining architectural styles, we analyzed solution organization and the number of violated PLAs. We also examined feature modularization (related to FM) to verify PLA modularity. Assuming an architect selects a single non-dominated solution, we identified the solution with the lowest Euclidean distance (ED) from the ideal solution for each experiment, as a lower ED represents a better objective trade-off. Our ideal solution in this work has fitness values of zero for both CM and FM objectives. The Kruskal Wallis statistical test determined if configurations had significant differences. The configuration with the highest significant hypervolume value was selected for each experiment and PLA combination. If no statistical difference was found (Kruskal Wallis) in hypervolume values, we prioritized the configuration with fewer evaluations (population size ∗ number of generations) to reduce execution time. Table 10 presents the final experimental configurations.

A quantitative analysis was conducted to answer RQ1. This involved evaluating the number of solutions and analyzing Pareto fronts to gauge the algorithms' ability to generate a large and diverse set of solutions (PLAs). We computed the Error Ratio [40] to quantify the proportion of solutions within the approximated true Pareto front (PFtrueApprox), with a lower ratio indicating a better outcome and more solutions in PFtrueApprox. The primary quality metric employed was hypervolume [41], along with the Kruskal Wallis non-parametric statistical test (at a 95% significance level) [42]. Hypervolume assesses the coverage area of a known Pareto front (PFknown) within the objective space relative to a nadir (reference) point; a higher hypervolume indicates a superior Pareto front. In this study, objective values were normalized between 0 and 1, and the nadir point was defined as the worst possible point (1.1, 1.1) with a small offset. Hypervolume was chosen due to its capacity to evaluate the convergence and diversity of solutions generated by multi-objective algorithms, and its status as a widely used indicator in the literature [43]. Furthermore, hypervolume is ▷-completeness compliant [41], enabling it to measure if one Pareto front is superior to another based on dominance. This makes it a valuable indicator for our goal of identifying the best resulting Pareto Front by comparing fronts from different operator sets. Importantly, hypervolume calculation only requires the objective values of solutions and the nadir point, unlike other common quality indicators such as IGD and GD [44], which require the true Pareto Front (unknown in our case), or R2 [45], which needs a uniformly distributed weight vector and whose objective space landscape is not precisely known in this work. Although objective functions have maximum and minimum values, it is uncertain if these will be achieved during optimization. For RQ2 and RQ3, a qualitative analysis was performed. To confirm the effectiveness of the proposed search operators in maintaining architectural styles, we examined the organization of solutions and the number of violated PLAs. We also analyzed feature modularization (FM) to assess the modularity of the PLAs. Recognizing that an architect will select one non-dominated solution, for each experiment, we focused on solutions with the lowest Euclidean distance (ED) from the ideal solution. A lower ED signifies a better trade-off between objectives. In this work, the ideal solution has zero fitness values for the CM and FM objectives. The Kruskal Wallis statistical test was used to determine if configurations exhibited statistical differences. For each experiment and PLA combination, the configuration with the most significant hypervolume value was chosen. If hypervolume values showed no statistical difference (Kruskal Wallis), we selected the configuration with fewer evaluations (population size ∗ number of generations) to reduce execution time. text: According to the type of study (i.e. repeated measures design), hypotheses (causality-comparative questions), and independent and dependent variables; appropriate tests were identified for the hypotheses. Generally, for repeated measure designs where each participant performs the tasks on all the groups (e.g., the basic tool and visually-enhanced tool groups), the suitable paired test is employed. Since the dependent variables (i.e., completion time, number of correct answers, ease-of-use, and ease-of-learning) are numerical and the independent variable (i.e., visualization technique) is categorical with two levels, we can either use one-tailed paired t-test or Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test. One-tailed paired t-test is a well-known statistical test for comparing the means of two groups of data with normal distribution. It is also suitable for the samples with small sizes. The Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test is a none-parametric statistic test which is an alternative to the paired t-test when the sample is not normally distributed. To identify appropriate test for the hypotheses, we investigated normality of the involved variables: 1) time completion variable is continuous variable and based on the Shapiro W test it has a normal distribution. Therefore, the one-tailed paired t-test was used for comparing the mean of this variable in two groups (Hypotheses 1 and 3); 2) the number of correct answers, based on the Shapiro W test, was not distributed normally, so we used the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test for comparing two samples in terms of accuracy (Hypotheses 2 and 4); 3) the collected data regarding ease-of-use and ease-of-learning also did not have normal distribution, so we used the Wilcoxon Sign-Rank test to compare two tools in terms of these variables (Hypotheses 4 and 6). As mentioned in Section 5.2.1, complexity of a feature model is considered as a confounding variable and we designed two variants for each task—one with simple feature model and one with complex feature model—to handle this variable. As a result, two variant of hypotheses 1–4 were tested—one for simple task (e.g. simple comprehension task) and one for complex task (e.g. complex comprehension task).

text: The Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon-test (U-test) is a nonparametric test, which can be applied on an unknown distribution, instead of only on a normal distribution like the t-test. We used a two-tailed U-test at a signiﬁcance level of 0.05 to get a p-value of the lowest signiﬁcance level for which the null-hypothesis would not be rejected.
paraphrases: The Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon U-test is a nonparametric statistical test applicable to data with an unknown distribution, unlike the t-test which assumes a normal distribution. We employed a two-tailed U-test with a significance level of 0.05 to determine the p-value, representing the lowest significance at which the null hypothesis would not be rejected.

Unlike the t-test, which requires a normal distribution, the Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon U-test is a nonparametric test that can be used with any distribution. We conducted a two-tailed U-test at a 0.05 significance level to find the p-value corresponding to the smallest significance level where the null hypothesis remained accepted.

text: Number of Features: First, we measured how calculation time scales as feature models increase in size. Therefore, we varied the size of the generated feature model between 10 and 10 000 features (which is signiﬁcantly larger than all reported feature models in practice we came across). For each feature model, we performed 10 random edits (not restricted to refactorings or generalizations). As described above, we performed 200 repetitions for each model size, as there is a ﬂuctuation of calculation times depending on the randomly generated models (with the same size) and the randomly performed edits. Kind of Edits: Next, we performed the same measurement varying the feature model size from 10 to 10 000, but now we distinguished between different possible edits. This should determine whether changes that make arbitrary edits are more difﬁcult to detect than those selected from Alves’ set of sound operations. We distinguish between three possible kinds of edits: refactorings from the catalog of sound operations, generalizations from the same catalog, and arbitrary edits as described above. Specializations are not considered as they are the inverse of generalizations. Again we applied 10 random edits of this classiﬁcation (i.e., 10 refactorings, or 10 generalizations, or 10 arbitrary edits) to each feature model. Number of Edits: Finally, we measured the calculation time while varying the number of edits for a ﬁxed feature model size of 1000 features. In this way, we can determine whether more edits require longer calculation times. We again distinguish between the three classiﬁcations refactoring, generalization (which includes specialization), and arbitrary edits. As special cases, we also measured identical feature models (0 edits) and compared completely independently generated feature models with the same feature names (which is roughly similar to an inﬁnite number of edits and can be regarded as upper bound).
paraphrases: **Number of Features:** Initially, we investigated how calculation time changed with increasing feature model size. We varied the generated feature models from 10 to 10,000 features, a range considerably larger than practical feature models typically reported. For each feature model, we applied 10 random modifications (not limited to refactorings or generalizations). As previously mentioned, we conducted 200 repetitions for each model size to account for variations in calculation times due to randomly generated models (of the same size) and randomly applied edits. **Kind of Edits:** Subsequently, we repeated the same measurements, again varying feature model size from 10 to 10,000, but this time differentiating between various types of edits. This allowed us to assess if detecting arbitrary changes is more challenging than detecting changes derived from Alves' set of sound operations. We categorized edits into three types: refactorings from the sound operations catalog, generalizations from the same catalog, and arbitrary edits as previously described. Specializations were excluded as they are the inverse of generalizations. We again applied 10 random edits from each category (e.g., 10 refactorings, 10 generalizations, or 10 arbitrary edits) to each feature model. **Number of Edits:** Finally, we measured calculation time while varying the number of edits for a fixed feature model size of 1000 features. This approach helped determine if a greater number of edits leads to longer calculation times. We again distinguished between refactoring, generalization (including specialization), and arbitrary edits. Additionally, as special cases, we also measured identical feature models (zero edits) and compared independently generated feature models with identical feature names, which approximates an infinite number of edits and serves as an upper bound.

**Feature Count:** Our initial step involved assessing the relationship between calculation time and the increasing size of feature models. We created feature models ranging from 10 to 10,000 features, a scope significantly broader than any reported practical feature models we encountered. For each model, 10 random edits were performed (without limiting them to refactorings or generalizations). As previously noted, we ran 200 repetitions for each model size, acknowledging that calculation times fluctuate based on both the randomly generated models (of identical size) and the random edits. **Edit Types:** Next, we conducted the same measurements across feature model sizes of 10 to 10,000, but this time distinguishing between different categories of edits. The goal was to determine if detecting arbitrary edits is more difficult than detecting those from Alves' established sound operations. We classified edits into three types: refactorings and generalizations (both from the sound operations catalog), and arbitrary edits (as defined earlier). Specializations were not included, being the inverse of generalizations. Once more, we applied 10 random edits from each classification (i.e., 10 refactorings, 10 generalizations, or 10 arbitrary edits) to each feature model. **Edit Quantity:** Lastly, we measured calculation time while varying the number of edits for a consistent feature model size of 1000 features. This allowed us to ascertain if more edits translate to longer calculation times. We again differentiated among refactoring, generalization (encompassing specialization), and arbitrary edits. For specific comparisons, we also measured feature models with no edits (0 edits) and contrasted them with entirely independently generated feature models possessing the same feature names, which roughly represents an infinite number of edits and provides an upper limit.

text: 4.4.1. Direct observations by the mentors The participants were observed personally by the mentors throughout Phase 1. Each team was observed by at least one mentor all the time. Mentors mainly noted qualitative data on the interaction of participants with IVM. In particular, mentors had to observe how participants constructed issue-based argumentation structures, how decisions were made, and how – if at all – rationale was reused. Our mentors noted motivation of the individual participants on the linear ﬁve point scale provided by Q7. In the scale, 1 is the highest motivation and 5 (worst) is the lowest motivation. Mentors assessed the motivation of participants in two stages: (i) during training sessions and (ii) in Phase 1. We computed the overall motivation of a student as the mean of his/her motivation in both phases. Our approach for assessing motivation is a modiﬁed version of Briand’s technique (Briand et al., 2001) that also quantiﬁes motivation using a ﬁve point linear scale. Briand directly asked students to express their motivation after the experiment. We modiﬁed Briand’s technique: We did not ask students directly to express their motivation but used tutors for this task and we did a two stage assessment. Mentors assessed motivation of individual participants during training and during experimentation (in Phase 1). We computed the mean of assessments in both sessions. It is difﬁcult to verbalize motivation. We considered several aspects such as enthusiasm of subjects, attitude to ask good questions during training session, focus during training/project work and team work (or active interaction with other participants). Before the training sessions, the four mentors were given a short training about assessing motivation in order to keep the measurement consistent. At a pragmatic level the mentors had a common understanding of motivation. In Phase 2 motivation was not measured because mentors did not do direct observations. 4.4.2. Analysis of artifacts Artifacts captured were analyzed to measure quality of instantiation, quality of rationale and reuse of rationale. The measurement was done with a linear ﬁve point scale from 1 (best quality) to 5 (worst quality) (see Q8 in Appendix A). To perform these measurements, we captured the rationales from each team and compared them against a reference baseline which contains variability models including justiﬁcation matrices for identiﬁcation, instantiation, and, evolution (e.g. Tables 1–3) that were provided from our industrial partner.3 In other words, the reference baseline contained a version of justiﬁcation matrices that were captured from experts working at the industry. Quality of instantiation, quality of rationale and reuse of rationale refers to the overall quality of justiﬁcation matrices developed/ reused by a team. Each team in Phase 1 was assessed with respect to the quality of instantiation. Similarly, each team in Phase 2 had an assessment for the quality of rationale and reuse of rationale. Unlike Phase 2, the rationale was captured and reused in the same team while instantiating variability models. Therefore, we did not quantify reuse of rationale in Phase 1. Moreover, we collected qualitative evidence on reuse of rationale during product instantiation (see R4). Assessing quality of rationale and quality of instantiation. To assess the quality of the rationale we initially checked if the assessments of the stakeholders as well as their arguments of stakeholders (++, +, 0, − and −−) were realistic and made sense. Then we checked if the decisions were logical, for example, we checked if a decision considered the assessments in the justiﬁcation matrix. Rationale which passed these initial checks, it was given the assessment value Fair (level 3). If a justiﬁcation matrix failed these initial checks, rationale was graded with Low or Very low depending on the information documented. To get a positive assessment, the justiﬁcation matrix had to have information close to information from the reference baseline information. To grade the overall assessments of a team, the mean was computed. For example, if a team documented three justiﬁcation matrices during variability instantiation shown in Table 3, then the overall quality of instantiation for the team is the mean of the individual quality of instantiations for the three justiﬁcation matrices. Measuring reuse of rationale. Let us consider two versions of a justiﬁcation matrix: an old justiﬁcation matrix captured during variability identiﬁcation and a new justiﬁcation matrix from variability evolution. Reuse of rationale corresponds to a direct reuse of information between justiﬁcation matrices, the old and new justiﬁcation matrices have common information (e.g. assessments or criteria). We measured Reuse of rationale as follows: As a ﬁrst step, rationale information reused was identiﬁed. For this purpose, commonalities between old (captured during variability identiﬁcation of Phase 1) and new justiﬁcation matrices (variability evolution of Phase 2) were extracted. Later, it was checked whether reuse makes sense (arguments of participants for the reuse of assessments were considered). A pair of justiﬁcation matrices passing this check received at least a fair (or above) assessment. The pair of matrices failing the test obtained Low or Very low. High and Very high assessments were given if the reuse was consistent with the reference justiﬁcation matrices obtained from our industrial partners. 4.4.3. Questionnaire to the sample At the end of Phase 2, the participants were given a set of questions (see Appendix A, Q1–Q6) and were asked to ﬁll the questionnaire. The questions were mostly open, that is, respondents were given a possibility to express their views verbally. Therefore, data collection using the questionnaire was mainly qualitative. Q6 was modeled as a closed question.
paraphrases: **4.4.1. Mentor Direct Observations**

Throughout Phase 1, mentors personally observed all participants. At least one mentor consistently watched each team, primarily documenting qualitative data on participant interactions with IVM. Specifically, mentors focused on how participants constructed issue-based argumentation structures, made decisions, and reused (or did not reuse) rationale. Individual participant motivation was rated by mentors on a linear five-point scale (Q7), where 1 represented the highest motivation and 5 the lowest. Motivation assessments occurred in two stages: (i) during training and (ii) during Phase 1. A student's overall motivation was calculated as the average of their scores from both phases. Our method for evaluating motivation is a modified version of Briand's technique (Briand et al., 2001), which also uses a five-point scale. Unlike Briand, who directly asked students about their motivation post-experiment, we employed tutors for this assessment and used a two-stage process. Mentors assessed individual participants' motivation during training and during Phase 1 experimentation, with the mean of these assessments forming the final score. Recognizing the difficulty in verbally expressing motivation, we considered factors such as enthusiasm, quality of questions during training, focus during training/project work, and teamwork/interaction. Before training, the four mentors received brief instruction on consistent motivation assessment to ensure a shared understanding. Motivation was not measured in Phase 2 due to the absence of direct mentor observations.
**4.4.2. Artifact Analysis**

Captured artifacts were analyzed to determine the quality of instantiation, rationale, and rationale reuse. These assessments were made using a linear five-point scale, from 1 (best) to 5 (worst) (see Q8 in Appendix A). To do this, we collected each team's rationales and compared them against a reference baseline. This baseline, provided by our industrial partner, contained variability models with justification matrices for identification, instantiation, and evolution (e.g., Tables 1–3); essentially, it comprised expert-derived justification matrices. "Quality of instantiation," "quality of rationale," and "reuse of rationale" collectively refer to the overall quality of justification matrices developed or reused by a team. Phase 1 teams were assessed on instantiation quality, while Phase 2 teams were assessed on rationale quality and rationale reuse. Unlike Phase 2, rationale in Phase 1 was captured and reused within the same team during variability model instantiation, so reuse of rationale was not quantitatively measured for Phase 1. We also gathered qualitative evidence on rationale reuse during product instantiation (see R4).

**Assessing quality of rationale and quality of instantiation:** To assess rationale quality, we first verified if stakeholder assessments and arguments (++, +, 0, −, −−) were realistic and logical (e.g., if decisions aligned with justification matrix assessments). Rationale passing these initial checks received a "Fair" (level 3) assessment. Justification matrices failing these checks were graded "Low" or "Very low" based on documented information. A positive assessment required the justification matrix to closely resemble the reference baseline information. Overall team assessments were calculated as a mean. For example, if a team documented three justification matrices during variability instantiation (Table 3), their overall instantiation quality was the average of the individual qualities of those three matrices.

**Measuring reuse of rationale:** Considering an "old" justification matrix from variability identification and a "new" one from variability evolution, rationale reuse signifies direct information overlap (e.g., common assessments or criteria) between them. We measured reuse as follows: First, reused rationale information was identified by extracting commonalities between old (Phase 1 variability identification) and new (Phase 2 variability evolution) justification matrices. Then, the meaningfulness of this reuse was checked (considering participant arguments for assessment reuse). Pairs of justification matrices passing this check received at least a "Fair" (or higher) assessment, while failing pairs received "Low" or "Very low." "High" and "Very high" assessments were awarded for reuse consistent with our industrial partners' reference justification matrices.
**4.4.3. Participant Questionnaire**

At the conclusion of Phase 2, participants completed a questionnaire (see Appendix A, Q1–Q6). Most questions were open-ended, allowing verbal expression of views, thus making the questionnaire data primarily qualitative. Q6 was a closed question.
**4.4.1. Mentor-Led Direct Observations**

Mentors directly observed participants throughout Phase 1, with at least one mentor present for each team at all times. Their primary focus was collecting qualitative data on how participants interacted with the IVM system. Specifically, mentors noted how participants constructed issue-based argumentation structures, made decisions, and whether (and how) they reused rationale. Individual participant motivation was assessed by mentors using a five-point linear scale from Q7, where 1 indicated the highest motivation and 5 the lowest. These motivation evaluations were conducted in two phases: during training sessions and again during Phase 1. A student's overall motivation score was the average of these two phase assessments. Our method for gauging motivation is a modified version of Briand's technique (Briand et al., 2001), which also uses a five-point linear scale. Unlike Briand, who directly solicited student motivation after the experiment, we opted for a two-stage assessment using tutors for this task. Mentors evaluated individual participants' motivation during both training and Phase 1 experimentation, and the mean of these scores was computed. Recognizing the challenge in articulating motivation, we considered various aspects, including participant enthusiasm, their propensity to ask insightful questions during training, their focus during training/project work, and their level of teamwork or active interaction with others. To ensure consistent measurement, the four mentors received a brief training on motivation assessment before the training sessions, thereby establishing a shared understanding of motivation. Motivation was not assessed in Phase 2 due to the absence of direct mentor observations.
**4.4.2. Analysis of Produced Artifacts**

The collected artifacts were analyzed to determine the quality of instantiation, the quality of rationale, and the reuse of rationale. These measurements were performed using a linear five-point scale, where 1 represented the highest quality and 5 the lowest (refer to Q8 in Appendix A). To conduct these evaluations, we gathered the rationales from each team and compared them against a reference baseline. This baseline, provided by our industrial partner, contained variability models that included justification matrices for identification, instantiation, and evolution (e.g., Tables 1–3). In essence, this reference baseline consisted of justification matrices created by industry experts. The terms "Quality of instantiation," "quality of rationale," and "reuse of rationale" all refer to the overall quality of the justification matrices a team developed or reused. Each team in Phase 1 was evaluated on its quality of instantiation. Similarly, each team in Phase 2 underwent an assessment for the quality of rationale and the reuse of rationale. Unlike Phase 2, where rationale was captured and reused within the same team during variability model instantiation, we did not quantitatively assess the reuse of rationale in Phase 1. Additionally, we gathered qualitative evidence regarding the reuse of rationale during product instantiation (see R4).

**Assessing quality of rationale and quality of instantiation:** To evaluate the quality of the rationale, we initially checked whether stakeholder assessments and arguments (++, +, 0, −, and −−) were realistic and logical. For instance, we verified if decisions were consistent with the assessments recorded in the justification matrix. Rationale that passed these initial checks was assigned a "Fair" (level 3) assessment. If a justification matrix failed these preliminary checks, the rationale was graded "Low" or "Very low," depending on the completeness of the documented information. For a positive assessment, the justification matrix needed to contain information closely aligned with the reference baseline. To determine a team's overall assessment, the mean was computed. For example, if a team documented three justification matrices during variability instantiation, as shown in Table 3, their overall quality of instantiation would be the average of the individual quality scores for those three matrices.

**Measuring reuse of rationale:** Consider two versions of a justification matrix: an older one from variability identification and a newer one from variability evolution. Reuse of rationale implies a direct sharing of information (e.g., common assessments or criteria) between these old and new justification matrices. Our measurement of rationale reuse proceeded as follows: First, we identified the rationale information that was reused. This involved extracting commonalities between the old justification matrices (captured during Phase 1 variability identification) and the new justification matrices (from Phase 2 variability evolution). Subsequently, we assessed whether the reuse was logical and appropriate (considering participant arguments for the reuse of assessments). A pair of justification matrices that passed this check received at least a "Fair" (or higher) assessment, whereas those that failed received a "Low" or "Very low" grade. "High" and "Very high" assessments were assigned if the reuse was consistent with the reference justification matrices provided by our industrial partners.
**4.4.3. Questionnaire for Participants**

At the end of Phase 2, participants were given a set of questions (see Appendix A, Q1–Q6) and asked to complete the questionnaire. The questions were predominantly open-ended, allowing respondents to articulate their views freely. Consequently, the data collected via the questionnaire was primarily qualitative. Q6 was structured as a closed question.

text: We evaluate the performance of our techniques based on two types of metrics, following Wang et al. [61] practical guide for selecting quality indicators: (i) quality metrics: how good is the obtained Pareto front? and (ii) diversity metrics: how large/representative are its solutions? In order to validate the signiﬁcance of our comparison, we per- form a statistical test using a non-parametric test: the two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (MWU). On every target, MWU takes in the different performance values obtained by both eSATiBEA and SAT- IBEA on a given metric from each run (in our case 30). MWU re- turns the p-value that one of the algorithms obtains different val- ues than the other. We consider tests signiﬁcant when they are be- low a signiﬁcance level of 0.05. Moreover, given the small number of runs in our experiment, and in order to lower the risk of having incorrect rejection of true null hypothesis, we use a conservative but safe adjustment (i.e., the standard Bonferroni adjustment [4] ) which reduces the chances of their erroneous rejection. Further- more, following the advice in the practical guide proposed by Ar- curi and Briand [4] , we also use the non-parametric Â12 [59] effect size measure which evaluates the ratio of runs from the ﬁrst al- gorithm that outperform the second one. It is considered in the literature that when Â12 is above 0.71, differences between the al- gorithms are large.
paraphrases: Following Wang et al.'s [61] guidance on selecting quality indicators, we assessed our techniques using two metric categories: (i) quality metrics, evaluating the effectiveness of the Pareto front, and (ii) diversity metrics, examining the breadth and representativeness of solutions. To ensure the statistical validity of our comparisons, we employed the non-parametric two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (MWU). For each target, MWU processed the performance values of both eSATiBEA and SAT-IBEA for a specific metric across 30 runs, yielding a p-value indicating differences between algorithms. A p-value below 0.05 was deemed statistically significant. Due to the limited number of experimental runs, we incorporated the conservative Bonferroni adjustment [4] to mitigate the risk of incorrectly rejecting true null hypotheses. Additionally, as recommended by Arcuri and Briand [4], we utilized the non-parametric Â12 [59] effect size measure, which quantifies the proportion of times the first algorithm outperformed the second; an Â12 value exceeding 0.71 suggests substantial algorithmic differences.

Our techniques were evaluated using two metric types, aligning with the practical guide by Wang et al. [61] for quality indicator selection: (i) quality metrics, which gauge the effectiveness of the generated Pareto front, and (ii) diversity metrics, which assess the extent and representativeness of the solutions. To establish the statistical significance of our comparisons, we conducted a non-parametric two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (MWU). For each target, the MWU test analyzed the performance values from 30 runs of both eSATiBEA and SAT-IBEA for a given metric, producing a p-value to indicate if one algorithm yielded significantly different results from the other. We considered tests statistically significant when the p-value was less than 0.05. Given the small number of runs in our experiment, and to reduce the likelihood of Type I errors, we applied the standard Bonferroni adjustment [4]. Furthermore, guided by Arcuri and Briand [4], we also employed the non-parametric Â12 [59] effect size measure, which determines the proportion of runs where the first algorithm outperformed the second. In the literature, an Â12 value greater than 0.71 is typically interpreted as indicating large differences between algorithms.

Subsequently, the coordinator correlates participants' existing variability knowledge with the effectiveness achieved in each study. As illustrated in Figure 4, Shapiro-Wilk normality tests were performed in our experiment to check for normal distribution of samples; if confirmed, a parametric T-Test hypothesis test was then conducted.

Upon completion of the experimental sessions, the experiment coordinator undertakes data preparation, involving tabulation and descriptive statistics calculation, to derive the effectiveness of each variability management approach (VMApp Effectiv) sample. This effectiveness is subsequently correlated with the variability knowledge (VarKnowledge) acquired in each study. The effectiveness formula is defined as: effectiveness(z) = nVarC - nVarI, where 'z' denotes a particular variability management approach, 'nVarC' signifies the number of correctly identified and represented variabilities using approach 'z', and 'nVarI' indicates the number of incorrectly identified and represented variabilities by approach 'z'. To guide the selection of an appropriate hypothesis test, normality tests were conducted on the effectiveness samples. Following this, the coordinator established a correlation between participants' prior variability knowledge and the observed effectiveness in each study. Figure 4 provides an overview of the experimental analysis procedure, showing that for our experiment, Shapiro-Wilk normality tests were used to determine if samples were normally distributed, leading to the application of a parametric T-Test hypothesis test if normality was affirmed.

text: While data from the pre-questionnaire (e.g., age, interview experience, etc.) were directly entered into the statistical tool SPSS, the data gathered during observation (e.g., number of asked relevant questions, etc.) were recounted first in order to reduce the risk of measurement errors. The subjective ratings based on the Likert-scale in the post-questionnaire were collected in MS Excel. Additional qualitative comments were listed in MS Word. All data was processed anonymously and confidentially. For the quantitative observation data, descriptive statistics were then calculated. Further, the data distributions were analyzed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. This was done to determine a suitable hypothesis test based on the different tests’ assumptions regarding data distribution in an independent sample setting. For most hypotheses, we used the t-test for equality of means accordingly, except for those for which the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test had not confirmed equal distribution between the groups. As this was the case for H12, H13, H22, we used the suitable independent samples median test instead. However, as the t-test is valid even under violation of its assumptions [15], we also used this test for non-parametric (but same) distributions. A cross-check with Mann-Whitney U confirmed that the application of the t-test led to the same results. As all hypotheses were directional, we used one-tailed results with α=0.05.

Data from the pre-questionnaire (e.g., age, interview experience) was directly entered into the SPSS statistical software. Exceptions included H12, H13, and H22, where the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test did not confirm equal distribution between groups, leading to the use of an independent samples median test. Nevertheless, acknowledging the t-test's robustness even with assumption violations [15], it was also applied to non-parametric (but similarly distributed) datasets. A validation using the Mann-Whitney U test confirmed that the t-test produced identical results. As all hypotheses were directional, one-tailed results with an alpha level of 0.05 were utilized.

Recall measures coverage and is the ratio of the correct composition found to the total number of all correct composition.

text: The replication of the quasi-experiment adopted the following mechanisms for analyzing the collected data: Comparison between results of ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections to test the hypotheses. Calculation of the time spent on the inspections to check efficiency. Calculation of variance of the defects and standard deviation in a view to comparing effectiveness/ effectiveness between ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections. Elimination of outliers and verification of data normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (Levene). Application of a nonparametric test (Wilcoxon) or a parametric test (Student’s t), according to each case.
paraphrases: For the quasi-experiment's replication, data analysis involved several steps: comparing ad-hoc and FMCheck inspection results to test hypotheses, determining inspection time for efficiency, and calculating defect variance and standard deviation to assess effectiveness differences between ad-hoc and FMCheck. Additionally, outliers were removed, and data normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (Levene) were checked before applying appropriate nonparametric (Wilcoxon) or parametric (Student's t) tests.

To analyze the data from the repeated quasi-experiment, we used these methods: First, we compared the outcomes of ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections to validate our hypotheses. Second, we measured the time taken for each inspection type to evaluate their efficiency. Third, we computed the variance and standard deviation of defects to contrast the effectiveness of ad-hoc versus FMCheck inspections. Fourth, we processed the data by removing outliers and confirming its normality (using Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (using Levene). Finally, we applied either a Wilcoxon nonparametric test or a Student's t-test, depending on the data characteristics.

text: Our quantitative analysis strategy, illustrated in Fig. 5, aims to build a reliable set of evidence based on the application of statistical methods. The results for each dependent variable constitute a sample, therefore, the first analysis step consists of identifying the statistical distribution for each sample through the Shapiro and Wilk (1965) method. Its null hypothesis claims the population as normally distributed. The Shapiro-Wilk test determines which set of methods must be applied in the steps: hypothesis testing, strength of association between variables, two-sample analysis, and effect size estimation (meta-analysis). The set of parametric methods is applied in samples following the normal distribution, and non-parametric methods for the other ones. The hypothesis testing focuses on investigating differences between quality in the IR methods related to precision, recall, F-measure or execution time. This step is divided into analysis of variance, which analyzes the existence of any difference between methods, and the pairwise comparison, analyzing and indicating the eventual pairs of methods that lead to such result discrepancies. The parametric analysis of variance is addressed by ANOVA (Gelman 2005), complemented with results provided by the pairwise Student’s t test with Hochberg correction (Hochberg 1988) and Tukey’s honest significance difference (HSD) test (Tukey 1949). The non-parametric set comprises the Kruskal and Wallis (1952) method to analyze variances, and the Wilcoxon non-parametric test (Wilcoxon 1945) for pairwise comparison. The analysis of variance reveals differences between IR methods for any dependent variable. Aiming to characterize such differences, an additional hypothesis testing is applied to investigate which methods present greater (or lower) results when compared to others. The Welch’s t-test (Welch 1947) and Wilcoxon test realize it for parametric and non-parametric sets, respectively. Strength of association between experiment variables is the third step of the quantitative analysis. For numerical variables, the association is analyzed through the calculation of the Pearson’s or Spearman’s correlation coefficients (DeGroot and Schervish 2002). The Pearson’s coefficient holds for normally distributed samples, and Spearman’s coefficient is applied in samples following other distributions. On the other hand, the linear regression model (Montgomery et al. 2007) investigates the association between categorical variables, independent from sample distribution. The fourth step is the two-sample analysis, which aims to compare results from different experiment samples. Suitable statistical tests in this scenario are Welch’s t-test, used in the normally distributed samples, and Mann-Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney 1947), which does not require assumption of normal distributions. The first method proposes an adaptation of the Student’s t-test by analyzing two samples which have unequal variances and unequal sample size. The second one indicates whether a randomly selected value from one sample will be greater (or lower) than a randomly selected value from the another sample, both of them with any sample distribution. This experiment design not only seeks the eventual differences between experiment methods, but also intends to characterize eventual behavior differences of a method when applied into different experiment contexts. To achieve it, the last data analysis step is the effect size estimation (or meta-analysis). This is a statistical procedure that allows to integrate the results of a set of studies related to the matter of interest, as an attempt to reach a conclusion about the parameters of interest used in the studies. Meta-analysis is frequently realized by the effective size estimation, quantifying the effects of an experimental method (Kampenes et al. 2007). We adopted the Hedges’ g (Hedges et al. 1985) as a measure of effect size.
paraphrases: Our quantitative analysis strategy, depicted in Fig. 5, uses statistical methods to establish strong evidence. Initially, we identify the statistical distribution of each dependent variable's sample using the Shapiro-Wilk method (1965), which tests for normal distribution. This test then dictates the appropriate statistical methods for subsequent steps: hypothesis testing, assessing variable association, two-sample analysis, and meta-analysis (effect size estimation). Parametric methods are employed for normally distributed data, while non-parametric methods are used otherwise. Hypothesis testing investigates differences in IR method quality across precision, recall, F-measure, or execution time. This involves both variance analysis to detect overall differences and pairwise comparisons to pinpoint specific discrepancies. Parametric variance analysis uses ANOVA (Gelman 2005), supplemented by Student’s t-tests with Hochberg correction (Hochberg 1988) and Tukey’s HSD test (Tukey 1949) for pairwise comparisons. For non-parametric data, Kruskal-Wallis (1952) handles variance, and Wilcoxon (1945) performs pairwise comparisons. To further clarify observed differences, an additional hypothesis test (Welch’s t-test for parametric, Wilcoxon for non-parametric) determines which methods yield superior or inferior results. The third step, analyzing the strength of association between variables, uses Pearson's or Spearman's correlation coefficients for numerical data (DeGroot and Schervish 2002), depending on normality. For categorical variables, linear regression (Montgomery et al. 2007) assesses association regardless of distribution. The fourth step, two-sample analysis, compares results from different experimental samples using Welch’s t-test for normal distributions (accommodating unequal variances and sample sizes) and the Mann-Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney 1947) for non-normal data, which determines if values from one sample tend to be greater or smaller than those from another. Finally, to understand how method behavior changes across contexts and integrate findings, we perform effect size estimation (meta-analysis) using Hedges’ g (Hedges et al. 1985).

As illustrated in Fig. 5, our quantitative analysis approach aims to develop a robust evidence base through statistical methods. The initial step involves determining the statistical distribution of each dependent variable's sample using the Shapiro-Wilk test (1965), which assesses for normality. The outcome of this test guides the selection of methods for subsequent analyses, including hypothesis testing, measuring variable association, conducting two-sample analyses, and estimating effect size (meta-analysis). Parametric methods are applied to normally distributed samples, while non-parametric methods are used for others. Hypothesis testing specifically examines quality differences among IR methods concerning precision, recall, F-measure, or execution time. This step is divided into analysis of variance, which identifies any general differences, and pairwise comparisons, which pinpoint specific method pairs causing discrepancies. For parametric analysis of variance, we use ANOVA (Gelman 2005), complemented by pairwise Student’s t-tests with Hochberg correction (Hochberg 1988) and Tukey’s HSD test (Tukey 1949). The non-parametric equivalent uses Kruskal-Wallis (1952) for variance analysis and the Wilcoxon non-parametric test (Wilcoxon 1945) for pairwise comparisons. To detail the observed differences, we apply additional hypothesis tests – Welch’s t-test (Welch 1947) for parametric data and the Wilcoxon test for non-parametric data – to ascertain which methods yield superior or inferior results. The third analytical step involves assessing the strength of association between experimental variables. For numerical variables, Pearson’s or Spearman’s correlation coefficients (DeGroot and Schervish 2002) are calculated, depending on the sample's distribution. For categorical variables, linear regression (Montgomery et al. 2007) investigates associations irrespective of distribution. The fourth step, two-sample analysis, compares results across different experimental samples. Here, Welch’s t-test is employed for normally distributed samples (accounting for unequal variances and sample sizes), and the Mann-Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney 1947) is used for non-normally distributed data, indicating whether values from one sample are generally higher or lower than those from another. The final step is effect size estimation (meta-analysis), employing Hedges’ g (Hedges etal. 1985), which helps integrate findings from multiple studies and characterize how method behaviors might vary across different experimental contexts.

text: For this purpose, we employ intra-class correlation (ICC). ICC is used to measure the degree of resemblance between the quantitative traits of a group of individuals, i.e., the subjective opinions of the participants with regard to the subcharacteristics of maintainability in our case. ... As the ﬁrst step of our analysis, we hypothesize that a meaningful correlation between the deﬁned metrics and maintainability can be found (H1). In order to test this hypothesis, we ﬁrst applied the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test that revealed that our collected data did not have a normal distribution. Therefore, a non-parametric test statistic, the Spearman’s Rho correlation coefﬁcient (signiﬁcance level of 0.05) was used to investigate any signiﬁcance relationships. ... The next hypothesis is that the proposed structural metrics are able to serve as discriminatory references for indicating maintainability (H2). We further employ the concept of entropy (Fenton and Neil 1999) to see how these proposed metrics are able to reduce the uncertainty associated with the correct level of maintainability of a feature model. ... The amount of reduced entropy as a result of revealing the correct value for a given metric is known as information gain (Kent 1983). ... The last two hypotheses (H3 and H4) are related to the predictive power of the deﬁned metrics for maintainability and also the issue that a small set of metrics would be sufﬁcient to accurately evaluate the maintainability of a feature model. To evaluate these hypotheses, we build four learning machines for predicting the three subcharacteristics of maintainability using the proposed metrics. ... In our experiments, we have developed four learning machines to predict the maintainability of a feature model from the decision tree and logistic regression family of learning machines. These learning machines are commonly used in the domain of software engineering for tasks such as software quality analysis and effort prediction.
paraphrases: To assess the similarity in subjective opinions regarding maintainability's subcharacteristics among participants, we use intra-class correlation (ICC). Our first hypothesis (H1) postulates a significant correlation between our metrics and maintainability. Since the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test showed our data isn't normally distributed, we used Spearman's Rho correlation coefficient (p < 0.05), a non-parametric test, to check for significant relationships. The second hypothesis (H2) suggests that our structural metrics can effectively differentiate maintainability levels. We then apply the concept of entropy (Fenton and Neil 1999) and information gain (Kent 1983) to determine how these metrics reduce uncertainty about a feature model's maintainability. Hypotheses H3 and H4 explore the metrics' predictive capability for maintainability and whether a small subset of metrics suffices for accurate evaluation. To test these, we developed four machine learning models, specifically from the decision tree and logistic regression families—common in software engineering for quality analysis and effort prediction—to predict the three maintainability subcharacteristics.

We utilize intra-class correlation (ICC) to gauge the agreement among participants' subjective assessments of maintainability's subcharacteristics. Our initial hypothesis (H1) posits a significant relationship between our defined metrics and maintainability. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test indicated that our data lacked a normal distribution, leading us to employ the non-parametric Spearman's Rho correlation coefficient (with a significance level of 0.05) to investigate any meaningful connections. Our next hypothesis (H2) proposes that the structural metrics we've developed can serve as distinguishing indicators of maintainability. We further explore the concept of entropy (Fenton and Neil 1999) to understand how these metrics reduce the inherent uncertainty in determining a feature model's true maintainability level, with the reduction in entropy from revealing a metric's correct value being termed information gain (Kent 1983). The final two hypotheses (H3 and H4) concern the predictive power of our metrics for maintainability and the possibility that a limited set of metrics could accurately assess a feature model's maintainability. To evaluate these, we constructed four learning machines, drawn from the decision tree and logistic regression families—frequently used in software engineering for tasks like quality analysis and effort estimation—to predict the three subcharacteristics of maintainability.

text: To answer RQ1 and RQ2, we ﬁrst report mean difference (MD) between Automated and Manual indicating the direction in which the results are signiﬁcant. We further check whether the differences between Automated and Manual are statistically signiﬁcant such that we can reject the null hypotheses [21]. As a ﬁrst step to test the normality of distributions (i.e., Sel-Time, NCF, FC, NST, PST, Eff_F and Eff_TC) of the obtained samples, we used the Shapiro–Wilk test. We choose the signiﬁcance level of 0.05; i.e., a sample is normally distributed if the p value is greater than 0.05. The results of the Shapiro–Wilk test showed that the distributions do not strongly depart from normality; i.e., all the obtained samples for dependent variables are normally distributed. Based on these results, we chose the t test as this test requires a distribution from a normal distribution. The signiﬁcant level for t test was chosen as 0.05 to compare Automated and Manual for the dependent variables discussed in Sect. 7.2. In addition, we also double-checked the results of the t test with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which is an equivalent, nonparametric test [21]. We report the results for both tests, and the results of the tests turned out to be consistent. We also report the mean differences between Automated and Manual indicating the direction in which the result is statistically signiﬁcant. To answer RQ4, we choose the Spearman’s rank correlation coefﬁcient (ρ) to measure the relations between the results of dependent variables and complexity of VCS products [21]. The value of ρ ranges from −1 to 1; i.e., there is a positive correlation if ρ is closer to 1 and a negative correlation when ρ is closer to −1. A ρ close to 0 shows that there is no correlation between the two sets of data. Moreover, we also report signiﬁcance of correlation using Prob > |p|, a value lower than 0.05 means the correlation is statistically signiﬁcant. Moreover, to address RQ5, one-sample t test is performed to compare the results obtained by experts and graduate students when using Automated. The reason is that we compare results of a sample of students with exactly one value obtained for the industrial case study (Sect. 6).
paraphrases: To address RQ1 and RQ2, we first present the mean difference (MD) between Automated and Manual methods, indicating the direction of significant results. We then verify if these differences are statistically significant enough to reject the null hypotheses [21]. Initially, we applied the Shapiro-Wilk test to assess the normality of distributions for sample variables like Sel-Time, NCF, FC, NST, PST, Eff_F, and Eff_TC. With a significance level of 0.05, the test indicated that these distributions did not significantly deviate from normality, meaning all dependent variable samples were normally distributed. Consequently, we selected the t-test, which assumes normal distribution, with a 0.05 significance level to compare Automated and Manual methods for the dependent variables mentioned in Section 7.2. As a cross-check, we also performed a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, a non-parametric equivalent [21], and found consistent results across both tests. We additionally report mean differences between Automated and Manual, specifying the direction of statistical significance. For RQ4, we used Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ) to quantify the relationship between dependent variables and VCS product complexity [21]. A ρ value between -1 and 1 indicates positive correlation if close to 1, negative correlation if close to -1, and no correlation if near 0. We also report the significance of this correlation using Prob > |p|, where a value below 0.05 signifies statistical significance. Lastly, to answer RQ5, a one-sample t-test was conducted to compare expert results with those from graduate students using the Automated method, as we are comparing a student sample to a single industrial case study value (Section 6).

For RQ1 and RQ2, we begin by detailing the mean difference (MD) between Automated and Manual approaches, highlighting where results are significantly directional. We then statistically examine these differences to determine if they are robust enough to dismiss the null hypotheses [21]. Our preliminary step involved using the Shapiro-Wilk test to confirm the normality of distributions for our collected samples (including Sel-Time, NCF, FC, NST, PST, Eff_F, and Eff_TC). Setting the significance level at 0.05, the Shapiro-Wilk test demonstrated that the distributions closely adhered to normality, confirming all dependent variable samples were normally distributed. This finding led us to employ the t-test, given its requirement for normally distributed data, with a 0.05 significance level to compare the Automated and Manual methods across the dependent variables discussed in Section 7.2. To ensure robustness, we also cross-verified the t-test outcomes with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, a non-parametric alternative [21], and observed consistent results. We further present the mean differences between Automated and Manual, specifying the direction of statistical significance. Addressing RQ4, we applied Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (ρ) to quantify the relationship between dependent variable results and the complexity of VCS products [21]. A ρ value ranging from -1 to 1 signifies positive correlation if approaching 1, negative correlation if approaching -1, and no correlation if near 0. We also indicate the correlation's significance using Prob > |p|, where a value less than 0.05 denotes a statistically significant correlation. Finally, to tackle RQ5, a one-sample t-test was performed to contrast the results from experts with those from graduate students using the Automated system, primarily because we are comparing a student sample against a single data point from an industrial case study (Section 6).

text: Composition and measurement stage: In total, 180 compositions were performed, being 60 in the Mobile Media, 60 in the Shogi Game and 60 in the Checkers Game. The compositions were performed manually using the IBM RSA [19,35]. The result of this phase was a document of composition descriptions, including the gathered data from the application of our metrics suite and all design models created. We used a well-validated suite of inconsistency metrics applied in previous work [14] focused on quantifying syntactic and semantic inconsistencies. The syntactic inconsistencies were quantified using the IBM RSA’s model validation mechanism. The semantic inconsistencies were quantified using the SDMetrics tool [46]. In addition, we also check both syntactic and semantic inconsistencies manually because some metrics, e.g., “the number of non-meaningful model elements” depends on the meaning of the model elements and the current modeling tools are unable to compute this metric. The identification of the inconsistencies was performed in three review cycles in order to avoid false positives and false negatives. We also consulted the developers as needed, such as checking and confirming specific cases of semantic inconsistencies. On the other hand, the well-formedness (syntactic and semantic) rules defined in the UML metamodel were automatically checked by the IBM RAS’s model validation mechanism. Effort assessment stage: The goal of the third phase was to assess the effort to resolve the inconsistencies using the quantification method described in Sect. 3.4. The composition heuristics were used to generate the evolved models, so that we could evaluate the effect of stability on the model composition effort. In order to support a detailed data analysis, the assessment phase was further decomposed in two main stages. The first stage is concerned with pinpointing the inconsistency rates produced by the compositions (H1). The second stage aims at assessing the effort to resolve a set of previously identified inconsistencies (H2).

text: We analyze the fault rate visually using box plots [23] and Quantile–Quantile (Q–Q) plots. A box plot plots the median as a line within the box and the quartiles as lines as the boundary of the box, so that 50% of all measurements are inside the box. Whiskers describe the distribution of the remaining measure-ments (see Table 4). A Q–Q plot is often used to compare two data distributions by plotting their quantiles against each other. That is, a point (xi,yi) on the plot refers to the ith data point of ﬁrst distribution (x-coor-dinate) and to the ith data point of the second distribution (y-coor-dinate). If both distributions are similar then x is equal to y and the point lies on the diagonal line y = x. We use this plot to compare for the same conﬁgurations predicted versus measured properties. For a perfect prediction, all dots would lie on the diagonal line. We visualize each conﬁguration as a dot on the plot. In addition to the visual analysis, we compute the average fault rate (arithmetic mean) per SPL and per measurement technique (i.e., feature-wise, interaction-wise, and pair-wise). To this end, we compute for each sample product P the fault rate, sum them up, and divide the result by the number of measurements: AvgFaultRate ¼ 1 n X n i¼1 jmeasurementðPiÞ predictionðPiÞj measurementðPiÞ 100 ð1Þ Furthermore, we compute the standard deviation in percent of all measurements per SPL and per measurement approach to quantify the scattering of predictions around the average fault rate.
paraphrases: We visually inspect the fault rate using box plots [23] and Quantile–Quantile (Q–Q) plots. Box plots show the median, quartiles (enclosing 50% of data), and whiskers illustrating the remaining data distribution (see Table 4). Q–Q plots compare two distributions by plotting their quantiles; similar distributions result in points aligning with the y = x diagonal. We use Q–Q plots to compare predicted versus measured properties for identical configurations, where perfect predictions would fall on the diagonal. Each configuration is represented as a dot. Beyond visual analysis, we calculate the average fault rate (arithmetic mean) for each SPL and measurement technique (feature-wise, interaction-wise, pair-wise) using the formula: AvgFaultRate = (1/n) * Σ |(measurement(Pi) - prediction(Pi)) / measurement(Pi)| * 100 (1). Additionally, we determine the percentage standard deviation of all measurements per SPL and measurement approach to quantify prediction variability around the average fault rate.

Our analysis of fault rates involves visual examination using box plots [23] and Quantile–Quantile (Q–Q) plots. Box plots delineate the median, quartiles (bounding the central 50% of measurements), and whiskers that depict the spread of the remaining data (refer to Table 4). A Q–Q plot is employed to compare two data distributions by mapping their respective quantiles. In this plot, a point (xi, yi) indicates the ith data point from the first distribution (x-coordinate) and the ith data point from the second (y-coordinate); if the distributions are alike, these points align along the y = x diagonal. We use this plot to compare predicted versus measured properties for identical configurations, with perfect predictions forming a straight diagonal line. Each configuration is represented as a distinct dot. Complementing this visual assessment, we calculate the average fault rate (arithmetic mean) for each SPL and for each measurement technique (i.e., feature-wise, interaction-wise, and pair-wise). This is done by computing the fault rate for each sample product P, summing these rates, and then dividing by the total number of measurements, as per Equation (1): AvgFaultRate ¼ 1 n X n i¼1 jmeasurementðPiÞ predictionðPiÞj measurementðPiÞ 100 ð1Þ. Furthermore, to quantify the dispersion of predictions around the average fault rate, we determine the standard deviation, expressed as a percentage of all measurements, for each SPL and measurement approach.

text: We employed statistical tests to assess the RQs. More speciﬁcally, we compared the results of the di↵erent algo-rithms with the Mann-Whitney U-test. In the results table for RQ1 and RQ2, three numbers are shown separated by a slash for each pair of algorithms and each test level. The ﬁrst number refers to the number of artiﬁcial problems for which the algorithm in the left has shown signiﬁcantly better performance than the algorithm in the right. The second number refers to the number of artiﬁcial problems for which the algorithm in the right has shown signiﬁcantly better performance than the algorithm in the left. Finally, the last number refers to the number of artiﬁcial problems for which there was no signiﬁcant di↵erence between both algorithms.

text: Quantitative and qualitative analysis were carried out to evaluate the results obtained with this experiment.
