text: To undertake the quasi-experiment, the following analysis mechanisms for the collected data were adopted: Comparison between results from ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections. Comparison between the performance of each participant in both rounds. Calculation of defects’ variance and standard deviation. Calculation of the time spent with the inspections. Elimination of outliers and verification of data normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (Levene). Application of a nonparametric test (Wilcoxon) or a parametric test (Student’s t), according to each case.
paraphrases: For the quasi-experiment, the collected data was analyzed using several methods: comparing results from ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections, evaluating participant performance across two rounds, calculating the variance and standard deviation of defects, and determining the time spent on inspections. Outliers were removed, and data normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (Levene) were checked. Depending on the specific case, either a nonparametric test (Wilcoxon) or a parametric test (Student’s t) was applied.

To conduct the quasi-experiment, we used the following analytical approaches for the gathered data: We compared the outcomes of ad-hoc and FMCheck inspections, assessed each participant's performance in both phases, computed the variance and standard deviation of defects, and measured the time dedicated to inspections. We also removed any outliers and confirmed the data's normality (using Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (using Levene). Finally, either a nonparametric test (Wilcoxon) or a parametric test (Student’s t) was applied, depending on the specific characteristics of the data.

text: In order to investigate their predictive power, we ﬁrst use the measures described in Section 4.2 to assess the modularity of the three product lines used as our target cases. Wefocus on quantifying the crosscutting properties of the different features of these systems. In that sense, we compute the Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting metrics for the features and the Degree of tangling for the use cases. As a result of the analysis: (i) the features with poor modularity, i.e. those with higher degree of scattering and crosscutting, are obtained; and (ii) use cases addressing more features, i.e. with more tangled concerns, are identiﬁed. Moreover, the analysis is used to extract important conclusions, such as the need for a spe-ciﬁc metric for crosscutting aiming to help developers to identify some crosscutting situations that scattering and tangling metrics do not capture. Second, once modularity has been assessed, it is compared with different maintainability attributes in Section 6. Then, this section computes all the values needed for the empirical comparison between modularity and maintainability. This section addresses RQ1 testing whether the features with higher impact of changes (no matter whether they are variable or mandatory) are those with higher Degree of crosscutting (Hypothesis 1). In order to have a way to assess the change impact of a feature, we use the idea presented in Ref. [23]. This work is also based on the crosscutting pattern introduced in Section 2 and it deﬁnes change impact in terms of the elements involved in the change of a source element. Assuming there are two related domains (source and target), the change impact of a source ele-ment is deﬁned as the addition of the number of trace links that must be changed and the number of trace links that must be pre-served. In Fig. 9 an example of several source and target elements related is shown. A change in the source element s2 implies to change target elements t1, t2 and t3. There are three trace links from s2 to these target elements. However, since s1 and s3 are also addressed by two of the target elements changed, the trace links from s1 to t1 and from s3 to t3 must be also preserved, so that s1 and s3 are also affected by the change of s2: impact (s2) = change ((s2, t1), (s2, t2), (s2, t3)) + preserve ((s1, t1), (s3, t3)). Using this assumption, the change impact of a source element can be quantiﬁed using our dependency matrix (dm). In particular, the number of trace links affected by a change of a source element sk is calculated counting the number of 1 values of row k and the number of 1 values in the columns where there are 1’s in row k. This may be formally deﬁned as: Impact Set ðskÞ ¼ X jTj i¼1 dmki X jSj j¼1 dmij ! ! ð11Þ Applying formula (11), the impact set of a change in each fea-ture in the different releases of MobileMedia has been calculated. Table 17 shows these results. The table shows, for each feature, the number of trace links affected by a change in the feature. These trace links include both the links to be changed and the links to be preserved. Since we are focusing on changes in features, in this analysis we consider modiﬁcations to accomplish changes in func-tional speciﬁcations or, in general, requirements of the system. An M, V, or O has been added to the feature’s name indicating whether the feature is mandatory, variable or optional, respectively. Note also that the Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting for each feature are also shown in the table in order to be compared with the Impact Set metric. Finally, taking the results obtained by the change impact analysis, the Impact Set metric has been correlated with both Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting metrics. The results are shown in Figs. 10 and 11 where we can see the cor-relations for the eight different releases. We have used the least squares criterion to estimate the linear regression between the variables assessed. Finally, in order to study how tangling affects changeability, the Impact set has been also compared with the Degree of tangling. Note that, the former is a metric deﬁned in terms of source elements whilst the latter is deﬁned based on target elements. Then, in order to compare both measurements, the Concern degree of tangling metric for each concern has been deﬁned. This new metric is calcu-lated by the addition of the Degree of tangling of each use case that addresses the corresponding concern. Then, this metric was com-puted by using the dependency matrix for each release. This matrix was modiﬁed to show the Degree of tangling of the different use cases instead of just representing the mappings existing between source and target elements. For the sake of simplicity, the depen-dency matrix for release 7 is the only one shown. This matrix is de-picted in Table 18. As an example, observe that the cells of the ﬁrst column have been changed by values of 0.28 which is the Degree of tangling of the Add Album use case. The Concern degree of tangling for each concern is shown in the last column of the table. Then, once the Concern degree of tangling have been calculated for each release, these values are compared with the impact set metric previously calculated. Table 19 shows the values obtained for both metrics and for each release. Based on these values, both metrics have been also correlated. The correlation between Impact set and Concern degree of tangling for each release is presented in Fig. 12, from a to h. Regarding to our second analyzed system, the HealthWatcher, Fig. 13 shows the correlation of the Impact Set metric with Degree of Crosscutting in the ﬁve releases of the system. Similarly, Fig. 14 shows the correlations between the metrics Impact Set and Concern Degree of Tangling for the same system. The same correlations are also shown for the SmartHome system in Figs. 15 and 16, respectively. To date, there is no empirical study that investigates whether scattering and crosscutting negatively affect software stability at requirements level. This section addresses RQ2 by analysing whether the concerns with a higher degree of scattering and cross-cutting are addressed by more unstable use cases than concerns with lower degree of scattering and crosscutting (Hypothesis 2). It also compares the degree of tangling of the use cases in order to study whether those with higher values are more unstable. Sta-bility is highly related to change management so that the more unstable a system is, the more complicated the change management becomes [23]. Unstable models gradually lead to the degeneration of the design maintainability and its quality in gen-eral [23]. Then, we can infer that early crosscutting is likely to have a negative effect on software quality. In this analysis we mainly fo-cus on changes in the functionality of the system, i.e. modiﬁcations to accomplish changes in requirements or functional speciﬁcations [10]. It is important to highlight that our focus is not on corrective changes performed to remove bugs or on perfective modiﬁcations. However, we do not rule out this kind of changes in future analyses and they should be the target of further studies. In order to perform our empirical study, Table 20 shows the use cases (rows) which are modiﬁed in the different releases (columns) of the MobileMedia. A modiﬁcation in a use case is mainly due to: either (i) the concerns, which it addresses, have evolved or (ii) it has been affected by the addition, modiﬁcation or removal of a concern to the system. In this table, a ‘1’ in a cell represents that the corresponding use case has been modiﬁed in that release. As an example, in release 1 (r1) all the cells in the column present the value 1. This is due to the fact that Error Handling is added in this release, and this concern affects all use cases. An ‘‘a’’ in a cell represents that the use case is added in that release. There are also some use cases whose names are modiﬁed in a release. These use cases are marked in the ‘‘Renaming’’ column, where the release which introduces the modiﬁcation in the name is shown (e.g. Add Photo use case modiﬁes its name to Add Media in release 6). Finally, use cases with a number of modiﬁcations higher than a threshold value (higher than 1 in our analysis) are marked as unstable. To study how crosscutting properties affect to stability, once the changes affecting each use case are known, these values are used to compare with our metrics. First, we observe the Degree of tangling for each use case in order to analyse if those use cases with a higher number of changes (unstable) are also more tangled (whole data in Ref. [48]). Then, in Table 21 the Degree of tangling for each use case is compared with the number of changes. In order to relate stabil-ity with metrics for source elements, the dependency matrix for re-lease 7 of the MobileMedia was observed to calculate the number of unstable use cases which realise each concern. The results ob-tained are presented in Table 22. In this table, the columns show the unstable use cases, in particular, those with two modiﬁcations or more. The concerns are shown in the rows. A cell with 1 repre-sents that the use case addresses the corresponding concern. The last column of the table shows the total number of unstable use cases contributing to each concern. Then, the number of unstable use cases for each concern is related with the degree of scattering and crosscutting for such con-cerns. In particular, Fig. 17 shows the linear regression between the number of unstable use cases and the Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting metrics, respectively. Again, the least squares criteria to estimate the linear regression between the variables as-sessed was used. At a ﬁrst glance, we may anticipate that use cases addressing scattered or crosscutting concerns are more prone to be unstable. This ﬁrst intuition is later conﬁrmed by the computation of Pearson’s coefﬁcient, as it is explained in next section. The selec-tion of scattering and tangling metrics is inﬂuenced by our purpose of comparing modularity with stability. Then, this is why we select the metrics quantifying crosscutting properties (closely related to modularity). The process to compare modularity and stability was replicated for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems. We do not show here all the data calculated in the process but just show the corre-lations between instability and both Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting metrics. These correlations may be observed in Figs. 18 and 19 for both systems, respectively. It has been already observed that feature dependencies are harmful for maintainability of software assets [17,20,35,39]. How-ever, to date there is no empirical study analysing whether the presence of crosscutting features at requirements level increments dependencies between features, making thus, their maintainability difﬁcult. This section addresses RQ3 investigating whether the presence of crosscutting introduces dependencies between fea-tures (Hypothesis 3.1). This hypothesis is tested by using our con-cern metrics to infer information about the feature dependencies existing in the product line. Moreover, since crosscutting has been compared with change impact and stability in previous sections, we also compare these two maintainability attributes with feature dependencies showing their relation (Hypothesis 3.2). In Ref. [17], the authors introduce the concepts of feature inter-lacing in order to assess feature dependencies in a product line. Interlacing denotes the situation where the implementations of two features, F1 and F2, have one or more components (or operations) in common [17]. The authors introduce the metric Component-level Interlacing Between Concerns (CIBC) which counts the number of components shared by two different features. This metric, among others deﬁned in Refs. [17,18,27,37], have been previously used to assess dependencies at the programming, detailed design or archi-tectural levels. However, to date, they have not been applied to measure dependencies at an earlier stage, i.e. in requirements docu-ments. In this section, the metrics have been applied to the require-ments of the three product lines used in our analyses. In particular we have deﬁned and calculated a new Use Case-level Interlacing Between Concerns (UCIBC) metric, which measures the number of use cases shared by the implementation of two features. Moreover, we have deﬁned a new metric, called Concern Interlacing (CI), as the total number of feature dependencies of a particular feature. The Concern Interlacing metric is calculated by the addition of the UCIBC values for a feature with respect to the rest of features. As an example, in a system where three features (A, B and C) are consid-ered, if feature A shares 2 use cases with feature B and 4 uses cases with feature C, then the Concern Interlacing metric for A is 6. Note that a use case may be computed twice if feature A shares this use case with two different features. Both metrics, UCIBC and CI are calculated using our dependency matrix. In particular, the cal-culation of UCIBC metric is obtained by counting the number of col-umns of the dependency matrix where two particular features have a 1. In other words, this metric can be calculated for all the features by performing the product of the dependency matrix and its trans-pose. The matrix resulting of this product is called the Concern interlacing matrix. CI metric is calculated by counting the values obtained for each row of this matrix (discarding the values obtained in the diagonal). The formalization of Concern Interlacing Matrix and CI metric are as follows: Concern interlacing matrix ðcimÞ ¼ DM DMT ð12Þ Concern Interlacing ðskÞ ¼ X jTj i¼1 cimki ! cimkk ð13Þ where DM and cimki represent the Dependency matrix and the cell [k, i] of the Concern interlacing matrix, respectively. In order to illustrate the calculation of the UCIBC metric, Table 23 shows the dependency matrix obtained for release 3 of the MobileMedia system. By applying the product of this matrix and its transpose, the Concern Interlacing Matrix shown in Table 24 is obtained. In this matrix, a cell denotes the value of the UCIBC metric for the feature represented in the row with respect to the feature of the corresponding column. The values of the CI metric for each feature are also shown in the last column of this matrix. As an example, observe that the UCIBC metric for Photo and Label features is 2 since these features share the implementation of the AddPhoto and ViewAlbum use cases. However, Photo shares the implementation of DeleteAlbum, AddPhoto and ViewAlbum use cases with the Album concern, thus the metric is 3 for these two features. Finally, the resulting CI metric for photo is 18 since the feature has 18 occurrences of use cases shared with other features or NFCs. Using the dependency matrix for each release, we have calcu-lated the CI metric for the 8 releases of the MobileMedia. The gathered data are shown in Table 25. For each release the degree of crosscutting for each feature has been also shown in order to have a way of comparing both metrics. The last column of the table shows the average of both metrics taking into account the eight re-leases. In this case, we do not show the Degree of scattering metric since, like with the previous analyses, the results obtained are very similar to those obtained for the Degree of crosscutting metric. Anal-ogously, Concern degree of tangling metric is not shown since the results are also consistent and similar to the shown for the Degree of crosscutting metric. Based on the data presented in Table 25, Concern Interlacing and Degree of crosscutting metrics have been compared in order to observe the correlation that exists between both metrics. The corre-lations for each release are shown in Fig. 20, from a to h. Since the Degree of crosscutting metric has been compared with the Concern Interlacing and Change Impact Set metrics, we compare now these two metrics. Intuitively, since Degree of crosscutting is cor-related with Concern Interlacing and Change Impact, these two last metrics should be also correlated. However, in order to check this conclusion, we have empirically compared the two metrics. The re-sults are used to check whether the features with higher concern interlacing (more dependencies) are those with a bigger change impact set. The graphics that show the correlation between Change Impact and Concern Interlacing for each release are shown in Fig. 21. Finally, once Concern Interlacing has been compared with Degree of crosscutting and Change Impact Set metrics, we may also compare it with the stability of the different features. The results allow us to check whether the features with more dependencies are those implemented by more unstable use cases. Fig. 22 shows the corre-lation existing between these two measurements. The data to ob-tain this graphic are extracted from Table 22 (unstable use cases) and Table 25 (concern interlacing average). As we did with the previous studies, we replicated the process for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems in order to check whether the results obtained for the product lines are consistent. The results obtained are shown in the next ﬁgures: Figs. 23 and 24 show the correlations between Concern Interlacing and Degree of crosscutting for HealthWatcher and SmartHome, respectively; Fig. 25 does the same for Concern interlacing and Instability. The correlations between Concern Interlacing and Impact Set for these systems are not shown as the results are similar to those presented for Concern Interlacing and Degree of Crosscutting.
paraphrases: To evaluate their predictive ability, we first used the metrics from Section 4.2 to assess the modularity of three product lines, our case studies. Our focus was on quantifying the crosscutting characteristics of these systems' various features. Specifically, we calculated the Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting for features, and the Degree of tangling for use cases. This analysis revealed: (i) features with poor modularity (high scattering and crosscutting) and (ii) use cases addressing multiple features (more tangled concerns). The analysis also highlighted the need for a specialized crosscutting metric to identify situations missed by scattering and tangling metrics. Next, we compared modularity with various maintainability attributes in Section 6, calculating all necessary values for an empirical comparison. This section addresses RQ1, testing Hypothesis 1: whether features with a greater change impact (variable or mandatory) also have a higher Degree of crosscutting. To assess change impact, we adopted the approach from Ref. [23], which is based on the crosscutting pattern in Section 2 and defines change impact by the elements involved when a source element changes. Assuming related source and target domains, a source element's change impact is the sum of trace links that must be changed and those that must be preserved. Figure 9 illustrates this: a change in s2 affects t1, t2, and t3 (three trace links from s2), but also s1 and s3 due to shared target elements, requiring preservation of their trace links to t1 and t3. Thus, impact(s2) = change((s2,t1),(s2,t2),(s2,t3)) + preserve((s1,t1),(s3,t3)). We quantify a source element's change impact using our dependency matrix (dm), where the number of affected trace links for source element sk is the sum of 1s in row k and 1s in columns containing 1s in row k (formally given by Equation 11). Applying this, we calculated the change impact set for each MobileMedia feature across different releases, with Table 17 showing the number of affected trace links (both to be changed and preserved). Our analysis focuses on functional changes (modifications to requirements or specifications), not bug fixes or perfective changes, though future studies may include these. Features are labeled M, V, or O for mandatory, variable, or optional. Table 17 also includes Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting for comparison with the Impact Set. The change impact analysis results were correlated with both scattering and crosscutting, as shown in Figures 10 and 11 for the eight releases, using least squares for linear regression. To examine tangling's effect on changeability, Impact Set was also compared with Degree of tangling. Since Impact Set focuses on source elements and Degree of tangling on target elements, we defined a new "Concern degree of tangling" metric for each concern, calculated by summing the Degree of tangling of all use cases addressing that concern. This metric was computed for each release using a modified dependency matrix (Table 18 shows release 7), which displays use case tangling degrees instead of just source-target mappings. For example, the "Add Album" use case has a tangling degree of 0.28. The Concern degree of tangling for each concern is in the last column of Table 18. These values were then compared with the previously calculated Impact Set metric for each release (Table 19) and correlated, with Figure 12 showing these correlations. For HealthWatcher, Figure 13 shows Impact Set correlation with Degree of Crosscutting, and Figure 14 with Concern Degree of Tangling. Figures 15 and 16 show similar correlations for SmartHome. To date, no empirical study has explored whether scattering and crosscutting negatively affect software stability at the requirements level. This section addresses RQ2 by examining if concerns with higher scattering and crosscutting are linked to more unstable use cases (Hypothesis 2), and if use cases with higher tangling are more unstable. Stability is crucial for change management; unstable models degrade design maintainability and overall quality [23], implying early crosscutting may harm software quality. Our analysis primarily focuses on functional changes (modifications to requirements [10]), not corrective or perfective changes, though these may be considered in future work. For our empirical study, Table 20 shows MobileMedia use cases modified across releases. A '1' indicates modification (e.g., in release 1, all use cases are '1' due to the addition of Error Handling), and an 'a' indicates addition. Renamed use cases are noted, with their renaming release. Use cases with more than one modification are deemed unstable. To analyze crosscutting properties' effect on stability, we compared use case changes with our metrics. First, we checked if unstable use cases also exhibit higher Degree of tangling (Table 21 compares Degree of tangling with the number of changes). To link stability with source element metrics, we used MobileMedia's release 7 dependency matrix to find the number of unstable use cases for each concern (Table 22), where columns represent unstable use cases (two or more modifications) and rows represent concerns; a '1' signifies a use case addresses a concern, and the last column shows the total unstable use cases per concern. We then related these unstable use case counts to the Degree of scattering and Degree of crosscutting for each concern. Figure 17 shows linear regressions between unstable use cases and scattering/crosscutting, estimated using least squares. We initially anticipated that use cases addressing scattered or crosscutting concerns would be more unstable, which Pearson's coefficient later confirmed. We chose scattering and tangling metrics to compare modularity with stability, as they quantify crosscutting properties related to modularity. This modularity-stability comparison process was repeated for HealthWatcher and SmartHome, with correlations between instability and scattering/crosscutting shown in Figures 18 and 19. Feature dependencies are known to hinder software maintainability [17,20,35,39], but no empirical study has yet investigated if crosscutting features at the requirements level increase these dependencies, complicating maintainability. This section addresses RQ3, testing Hypothesis 3.1: whether crosscutting introduces feature dependencies. We use our concern metrics to infer feature dependencies within product lines. Furthermore, having compared crosscutting with change impact and stability, we also compare these two maintainability attributes with feature dependencies, showing their relationship (Hypothesis 3.2). Ref. [17] introduces feature interlacing concepts to assess dependencies, defining interlacing as shared components/operations between two features (F1, F2). They proposed Component-level Interlacing Between Concerns (CIBC) to count shared components. While CIBC and similar metrics [17,18,27,37] have been used at later development stages (programming, design, architecture), they haven't been applied to requirements. Here, we apply these metrics to the requirements of our three product lines. We define a new Use Case-level Interlacing Between Concerns (UCIBC) metric, measuring shared use cases between two feature implementations, and "Concern Interlacing" (CI) as the total feature dependencies for a specific feature, calculated by summing UCIBC values for that feature against all others. For example, if feature A shares 2 use cases with B and 4 with C, its CI is 6 (a use case might be counted twice if shared with two features). Both UCIBC and CI are calculated using our dependency matrix. UCIBC is derived by counting columns in the dependency matrix where two features both have a '1', effectively the product of the dependency matrix and its transpose, which yields the Concern interlacing matrix. CI is then calculated by summing values in each row of this matrix, excluding the diagonal. Equations 12 and 13 formally define the Concern interlacing matrix (cim = DM * DM^T) and Concern Interlacing (CI(sk) = sum(cimki) - cimkk). To illustrate UCIBC, Table 23 shows MobileMedia release 3's dependency matrix. Its product with its transpose gives the Concern Interlacing Matrix (Table 24), where cells indicate UCIBC values between row and column features. The CI values for each feature are in the last column. For instance, Photo and Label features have a UCIBC of 2 (sharing AddPhoto, ViewAlbum), while Photo and Album have a UCIBC of 3 (sharing DeleteAlbum, AddPhoto, ViewAlbum). The CI for Photo is 18 (18 use case occurrences shared with other features or NFCs). We calculated CI for all 8 MobileMedia releases using their respective dependency matrices (Table 25). Table 25 also includes Degree of crosscutting for each feature, allowing comparison. The last column shows the average of both metrics across releases. Scattering and tangling metrics are omitted as their results were consistent with crosscutting. Based on Table 25, we compared Concern Interlacing and Degree of crosscutting, showing their correlations for each release in Figure 20. Next, we compared Concern Interlacing with Change Impact Set, reasoning that their intuitive correlation with Degree of crosscutting should extend to each other. Figure 21 displays the empirical correlations between Change Impact and Concern Interlacing for each release, confirming that features with higher interlacing (more dependencies) tend to have a larger change impact. Finally, we compared Concern Interlacing with feature stability to see if more dependent features are implemented by more unstable use cases. Figure 22 shows this correlation, using data from Table 22 (unstable use cases) and Table 25 (average concern interlacing). This entire process was replicated for HealthWatcher and SmartHome to ensure consistency. Figures 23 and 24 show correlations between Concern Interlacing and Degree of crosscutting for HealthWatcher and SmartHome, respectively. Figure 25 shows Concern Interlacing and Instability correlations for these systems. Correlations between Concern Interlacing and Impact Set are not explicitly shown for these systems as they mirrored those with Degree of Crosscutting.

We first evaluated the predictive power of modularity measures (from Section 4.2) on three product lines, our chosen target cases. Our primary objective was to quantify the crosscutting nature of these systems' features. This involved calculating the "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" for features, and the "Degree of tangling" for use cases. The analysis yielded two main results: (i) identification of features with poor modularity, characterized by high scattering and crosscutting degrees, and (ii) detection of use cases that address multiple features, indicating more tangled concerns. Furthermore, this analysis led to important insights, such as the need for a dedicated crosscutting metric to capture situations that scattering and tangling metrics do not adequately address. Second, after assessing modularity, we compared it with various maintainability attributes in Section 6. This section details the computation of all necessary values for an empirical comparison between modularity and maintainability. It also addresses Research Question 1 (RQ1) by testing Hypothesis 1, which posits that features with a higher impact of changes (regardless of being variable or mandatory) will also exhibit a higher "Degree of crosscutting." To quantify the change impact of a feature, we adopted the approach described in Ref. [23]. This approach, building on the crosscutting pattern from Section 2, defines change impact based on the elements affected when a source element changes. Assuming two related domains (source and target), the change impact of a source element is the sum of trace links that must be modified and those that must be preserved. Figure 9 illustrates this with an example where changing source element s2 necessitates changes to target elements t1, t2, and t3 (three trace links). Additionally, since s1 and s3 are also connected to two of the affected target elements, their trace links to t1 and t3 must be preserved. Thus, the impact of s2 is calculated as: impact (s2) = change ((s2, t1), (s2, t2), (s2, t3)) + preserve ((s1, t1), (s3, t3)). Based on this principle, the change impact of a source element can be quantitatively determined using our dependency matrix (dm). Specifically, the number of trace links affected by a change in source element sk is found by summing the '1' values in row k and the '1' values in the columns that also contain '1's in row k. This is formally expressed by formula (11). Applying formula (11), we calculated the "Impact Set" for changes in each feature across different releases of MobileMedia. Table 17 presents these results, showing for each feature the total number of affected trace links, encompassing both those to be changed and those to be preserved. Our analysis here focuses on changes to functional specifications or system requirements, deliberately excluding corrective changes (bug fixes) or perfective modifications, though these are considered for future research. Each feature's name is augmented with M, V, or O to denote whether it is mandatory, variable, or optional. For comparative purposes with the "Impact Set" metric, the "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" for each feature are also included in Table 17. Finally, the "Impact Set" metric was correlated with both the "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" metrics, based on the change impact analysis results. Figures 10 and 11 display these correlations for the eight different releases, with linear regression estimated using the least squares criterion. To further understand how tangling influences changeability, the "Impact Set" was also compared with the "Degree of tangling." Given that "Impact Set" is defined for source elements and "Degree of tangling" for target elements, we introduced a "Concern degree of tangling" metric for each concern to enable their comparison. This new metric is computed by summing the "Degree of tangling" of all use cases associated with the corresponding concern. This metric was then calculated for each release using the dependency matrix, which was modified to represent the "Degree of tangling" of different use cases rather than just source-target mappings. For brevity, only the dependency matrix for release 7 is shown (Table 18). As an illustration, the cells in the first column of Table 18 are updated with a value of 0.28, representing the "Degree of tangling" for the "Add Album" use case. The "Concern degree of tangling" for each concern is presented in the last column of this table. Once the "Concern degree of tangling" was computed for each release, these values were compared with the previously calculated "Impact Set" metric. Table 19 shows the obtained values for both metrics across all releases, and based on these, both metrics were correlated. Figure 12 (panels a to h) illustrates the correlation between "Impact Set" and "Concern degree of tangling" for each release. For the HealthWatcher system, our second analyzed system, Figure 13 displays the correlation between the "Impact Set" metric and "Degree of Crosscutting" across its five releases. Similarly, Figure 14 shows the correlations between "Impact Set" and "Concern Degree of Tangling" for the same system. Identical correlations are presented for the SmartHome system in Figures 15 and 16. Currently, there is a lack of empirical research investigating whether scattering and crosscutting negatively impact software stability at the requirements level. This section addresses Research Question 2 (RQ2) by analyzing whether concerns with higher scattering and crosscutting are associated with more unstable use cases compared to concerns with lower scattering and crosscutting (Hypothesis 2). It also compares the "Degree of tangling" of use cases to determine if those with higher values are more unstable. System stability is closely linked to change management, with less stable systems making change management more complex [23]. Unstable models can lead to a decline in design maintainability and overall quality [23]. Therefore, we infer that early crosscutting likely has a detrimental effect on software quality. In this analysis, we primarily focus on changes to system functionality, i.e., modifications made to align with changes in requirements or functional specifications [10]. It is crucial to note that our focus is not on corrective changes (bug fixes) or perfective modifications, though these types of changes are not excluded from future analyses and warrant further study. To conduct our empirical study, Table 20 details the use cases (rows) modified across different releases (columns) of MobileMedia. A use case modification typically arises from either: (i) the evolution of the concerns it addresses, or (ii) being affected by the addition, modification, or removal of a concern from the system. In Table 20, a '1' in a cell indicates that the corresponding use case was modified in that release. For example, in release 1 (r1), all cells in the column show '1' because "Error Handling" was added, affecting all use cases. An 'a' in a cell signifies that the use case was added in that particular release. Some use cases also underwent name changes, indicated in the "Renaming" column along with the release introducing the modification (e.g., "Add Photo" became "Add Media" in release 6). Finally, use cases with a number of modifications exceeding a threshold (greater than 1 in our analysis) are labeled as unstable. To investigate how crosscutting properties influence stability, once the changes affecting each use case are known, these values are compared with our metrics. First, we examine the "Degree of tangling" for each use case to determine if unstable use cases (those with more changes) are also more tangled (refer to data in Ref. [48]). Table 21 then compares the "Degree of tangling" for each use case with the number of changes it underwent. To connect stability with metrics for source elements, the dependency matrix for release 7 of MobileMedia was used to calculate the number of unstable use cases that implement each concern. Table 22 presents these results, where columns denote unstable use cases (those with two or more modifications) and rows represent concerns. A '1' in a cell indicates that the use case addresses the corresponding concern. The last column of the table displays the total number of unstable use cases contributing to each concern. Subsequently, the number of unstable use cases for each concern is related to its "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting." Specifically, Figure 17 illustrates the linear regression between the number of unstable use cases and both "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" metrics, respectively. Again, the least squares criterion was used for linear regression estimation. Initially, we hypothesized that use cases addressing scattered or crosscutting concerns would be more prone to instability. This intuition is later confirmed by the computation of Pearson’s coefficient, as detailed in the subsequent section. The choice of scattering and tangling metrics is guided by our objective to compare modularity with stability, hence our focus on metrics quantifying crosscutting properties (which are closely related to modularity). The process of comparing modularity and stability was replicated for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems. We do not present all intermediate data here, but rather focus on the correlations between instability and both "Degree of scattering" and "Degree of crosscutting" metrics, shown in Figures 18 and 19 for both systems, respectively. It has long been recognized that feature dependencies negatively impact the maintainability of software assets [17,20,35,39]. However, there is currently no empirical study examining whether the presence of crosscutting features at the requirements level increases these inter-feature dependencies, thereby complicating their maintainability. This section addresses Research Question 3 (RQ3) by investigating whether crosscutting introduces dependencies between features (Hypothesis 3.1). This hypothesis is tested using our concern metrics to infer information about the feature dependencies within the product line. Furthermore, having compared crosscutting with change impact and stability in previous sections, we also compare these two maintainability attributes with feature dependencies to illustrate their relationship (Hypothesis 3.2). In Ref. [17], the authors introduced "feature interlacing" to assess feature dependencies in a product line, where interlacing signifies that two features (F1 and F2) share one or more common components or operations. They proposed the "Component-level Interlacing Between Concerns (CIBC)" metric, which counts the number of components shared by two distinct features. This metric, along with others defined in Refs. [17,18,27,37], has previously been used to assess dependencies at programming, detailed design, or architectural levels. However, to date, these metrics have not been applied to measure dependencies at an earlier stage, specifically within requirements documents. In this section, we apply these metrics to the requirements of the three product lines under analysis. Specifically, we define and calculate a new "Use Case-level Interlacing Between Concerns (UCIBC)" metric, which quantifies the number of use cases shared by the implementation of two features. Additionally, we define another new metric, "Concern Interlacing (CI)," as the total number of feature dependencies for a particular feature. The "Concern Interlacing" metric is computed by summing the UCIBC values for a given feature with respect to all other features. For example, in a system with three features (A, B, and C), if feature A shares 2 use cases with feature B and 4 use cases with feature C, its "Concern Interlacing" metric is 6. It's important to note that a use case might be counted twice if feature A shares it with two different features. Both UCIBC and CI metrics are calculated using our dependency matrix. The UCIBC metric is obtained by counting the number of columns in the dependency matrix where two specific features both have a '1'. More formally, this metric can be calculated for all features by multiplying the dependency matrix by its transpose, resulting in the "Concern interlacing matrix." The CI metric is then calculated by summing the values obtained for each row of this matrix, excluding the diagonal elements. The formal definitions of the "Concern interlacing matrix" and "CI metric" are given by equations (12) and (13), respectively, where DM represents the Dependency matrix and cimki denotes the cell [k, i] of the Concern interlacing matrix. To demonstrate the calculation of the UCIBC metric, Table 23 presents the dependency matrix for release 3 of the MobileMedia system. By performing the product of this matrix and its transpose, the "Concern Interlacing Matrix" shown in Table 24 is derived. In this matrix, each cell represents the UCIBC value between the feature in the row and the feature in the corresponding column. The CI metric values for each feature are also included in the last column of this matrix. As an example, the UCIBC metric for the "Photo" and "Label" features is 2, as they share the implementation of the "AddPhoto" and "ViewAlbum" use cases. However, "Photo" shares the implementation of "DeleteAlbum," "AddPhoto," and "ViewAlbum" use cases with the "Album" concern, resulting in a metric value of 3 for these two features. Finally, the resulting CI metric for "Photo" is 18, indicating that this feature has 18 occurrences of use cases shared with other features or NFCs. Using the dependency matrix for each release, we calculated the CI metric for all 8 releases of MobileMedia. The collected data are presented in Table 25. For each release, the "Degree of crosscutting" for each feature is also shown, allowing for a direct comparison between the two metrics. The last column of the table shows the average of both metrics across all eight releases. In this particular analysis, we omit the "Degree of scattering" metric because, similar to previous analyses, its results were highly consistent with those obtained for the "Degree of crosscutting" metric. Similarly, the "Concern degree of tangling" metric is not shown as its results were also consistent and comparable to the "Degree of crosscutting" metric. Based on the data in Table 25, the "Concern Interlacing" and "Degree of crosscutting" metrics were compared to observe their correlation. Figures 20 (a to h) display these correlations for each release. Since the "Degree of crosscutting" metric has been compared with both "Concern Interlacing" and "Change Impact Set" metrics, we now compare these latter two metrics. Intuitively, given the correlation between "Degree of crosscutting" and both "Concern Interlacing" and "Change Impact," these two metrics should also exhibit a correlation. To verify this, we empirically compared them. The results are used to determine if features with higher "concern interlacing" (i.e., more dependencies) also have a larger "change impact set." Figure 21 presents graphs showing the correlation between "Change Impact" and "Concern Interlacing" for each release. Finally, having compared "Concern Interlacing" with "Degree of crosscutting" and "Change Impact Set" metrics, we also compare it with the stability of different features. These results enable us to check whether features with more dependencies are implemented by more unstable use cases. Figure 22 illustrates the correlation between these two measurements, using data extracted from Table 22 (unstable use cases) and Table 25 (average concern interlacing). As in our previous studies, we replicated this entire process for the HealthWatcher and SmartHome systems to confirm the consistency of the results across product lines. The obtained results are presented in the following figures: Figures 23 and 24 show the correlations between "Concern Interlacing" and "Degree of crosscutting" for HealthWatcher and SmartHome, respectively. Figure 25 shows the correlations between "Concern interlacing" and "Instability" for these systems. The correlations between "Concern Interlacing" and "Impact Set" for these systems are not shown, as their results were found to be similar to those presented for "Concern Interlacing" and "Degree of Crosscutting."

text: Dependent Variable - FM Quality: According to the MUSiC method, quality is a measure of the degree to which the output achieves the task goals. For the purpose of this experiment, quality is expressed in terms of a ﬁnal FM quality. Dependent Variable - User Eﬀectiveness: To assess user eﬀectiveness, we deﬁned a quantity that is a measure of the amount of a task completed by a user. Finally, the user eﬀectiveness is given as a percentage, and is calculated using the following formula: UserEffectiveness = (FMQuantity ∗FMQuality)%. Dependent Variable - User Eﬃciency: The user eﬃciency calculation does include the time component. The user eﬃciency is calculated using the following formula: UserEfficiency = UserEffectiveness / ScenarioT ime.

text: Quality criterion 1 (from Section I-C) is fulﬁlled by the distribution of the tree width measures in our experiments, as shown in Tables II–IV. The tables show the number of models with a tree width value in a given interval. For example, Table II shows in row 1 that for twG(PP )+ – short for the upper bound of the Gaifman tree-width of the parallel binary counter encoding PP – there are 40 models for which the computed value is within [0, 1] (column 1), 28 models with a tree width in [2, 4], etc. Because the lower and upper bound approximations delivered by the tree width approximation algorithm differ slightly, we computed all correlations for the set of lower and the set of upper bounds separately. We use x−to refer to the lower bound, x+ to refer to the upper bound. Because of the complexity of computing the incidence graph for the models with 1000 features, we were restricted to conduct the analysis on the Gaifman graph for these models. To analyze quality criterion 2, we used the solver-speciﬁc execution times in addition to the tree width measures to conduct a Spearman’s rank correlation analysis (see [37] for details). We applied a post-hoc signiﬁcance test to the resulting correlation coefﬁcient. Spearman’s rank correlation is non-parametric and thus we do not need to make assumptions on the distribution of the base data (e.g. normality). A general observation on the solver execution times of the BDD-based solvers is that these solvers were incapable of processing models with cardinality constraints as they ran out of memory. This might be due to our decision to connect BDD solvers directly to the LT n,k P AR encoder without using BDD-speciﬁc heuristics, as described in the previous section. Tables V–XIII describe signiﬁcant correlations between graph width measures and solver execution time revealed by the post-hoc signiﬁcance test at the 5% signiﬁcance level. In the four columns, correlations are shown for the lower (-) and upper (+) bound heuristics of the tree width applied to the Gaifman (twG) and the incidence graph (twI). The results of each experiment are grouped according to the analyzed encoding. We describe the correlation between the tree width of the analyzed encoding and the execution time of the solvers that are run on this particular type of encoding. These are highlighted grey in the following tables. In addition, for each encoding, we describe correlations between the tree width of the encoding and the execution time of the solvers on the according models that are not being run on the encoding (but that were run on the other encodings). This allows us to evaluate the suitability of measures to approximate the structural complexity of more than one type of encoding.

text: The authors utilized Average Percentage of Fault Detected (APFD) as an evaluation metric in order to investigate the rate of faults detected by similarity measures [27]. APFD metric evaluates the effectiveness of prioritization by calculating the average number of faults exposed based on their index position in a prioritized test suite. A higher APFD indicates a more effective similarity measure in detecting faults.
paraphrases: To assess how well similarity measures detect faults, the authors employed the Average Percentage of Fault Detected (APFD) as an evaluation metric [27]. The APFD metric gauges prioritization effectiveness by determining the average number of faults uncovered, considering their order within a prioritized test suite. A greater APFD value signifies that a similarity measure is more proficient at identifying faults.

The Average Percentage of Fault Detected (APFD) was used by the authors as a metric to study how quickly similarity measures uncover faults [27]. This APFD metric assesses the efficiency of prioritization by computing the average number of faults revealed according to their placement in a ranked test suite. A higher APFD score suggests that a similarity measure is more successful in detecting faults.

text: To make fair comparisons, we adopted the same techniques suggested by the state-of-the-art [5, 32] for statistical testing. Based on the experimental results of 30 executions per algorithm, we conducted a statistical test at the significance level of 5%. We performed the Mann-Whitney U test, which is a non-parametric test and makes fewer assumptions regarding the underlying populations. We calculated the estimated probability, i.e., p-value, that an algorithm produces different results than the other. Furthermore, we reported the non-parametric effect size measure Â12 [70]. It indicates the performance superiority, and it measures the extent to which an algorithm outperforms the other. The superiority between algorithms are considered as small, medium and large when Â12 value is over 0.56, 0.64 and 0.71, respectively
paraphrases: For unbiased comparisons, we utilized state-of-the-art statistical testing methods [5, 32]. After 30 executions per algorithm, we conducted a statistical test at a 5% significance level. We employed the Mann-Whitney U test, a non-parametric test that requires fewer assumptions about the populations. We determined the p-value, which estimates the probability that algorithms produce different results. Additionally, we reported Â12 [70], a non-parametric effect size measure indicating performance superiority and quantifying how much one algorithm surpasses another. Algorithm superiority is categorized as small, medium, or large for Â12 values exceeding 0.56, 0.64, and 0.71, respectively.

To ensure equitable comparisons, we implemented statistical testing techniques consistent with current best practices [5, 32]. Following 30 runs for each algorithm, we performed a statistical test using a 5% significance level. We opted for the Mann-Whitney U test, a non-parametric method known for its minimal assumptions about the underlying data distributions. We then computed the p-value, representing the estimated likelihood that an algorithm yields results distinct from another. Furthermore, we presented Â12 [70], a non-parametric measure of effect size. This metric quantifies the degree to which one algorithm outperforms another, with Â12 values above 0.56, 0.64, and 0.71 signifying small, medium, and large performance superiorities, respectively.

text: We performed a power analysis using the G*Power 3 software [22] to approximate sample size requirements for a subsequent ANCOVA (analysis of covariance) with one covariate across two groups (modeling style) and expecting medium effect sizes of f(U) > .30 with type-1 error probability of α < .05. A sample size of n = 90 was required to reach sufficient statistical power (> .80). We performed t-tests and Χ² tests to screen for possible differences between the experimental groups. Results did not suggest significant differences between groups. Data analysis was carried out with SPSS 20.0.
paraphrases: Using G*Power 3 software [22], we conducted a power analysis to estimate the necessary sample size for a future ANCOVA. This analysis anticipated a medium effect size (f(U) > .30), a type-1 error probability (α) less than .05, and involved two groups based on modeling style with one covariate. A sample size of n = 90 was determined to achieve adequate statistical power (greater than .80). To identify potential differences between the experimental groups, t-tests and Χ² tests were performed, but their results indicated no significant differences. SPSS 20.0 was used for all data analysis.

A power analysis, conducted with G*Power 3 software [22], helped us determine the approximate sample size needed for a planned ANCOVA. This analysis, designed for two modeling style groups with a single covariate, assumed a medium effect size (f(U) > .30) and a type-1 error probability (α) below .05. The findings indicated that a sample size of n = 90 would provide sufficient statistical power (exceeding .80). To check for initial differences between the experimental groups, we ran t-tests and Χ² tests, neither of which revealed any statistically significant distinctions. All data analysis was executed using SPSS 20.0.

text: The quantitative analysis takes into account the fitness values of the solutions of each experiment. First we plotted the obtained fronts, and then we used the hypervolume [47] and the Euclidean distance to the ideal solution (ED) [23] indicators to evaluate the quality of these fronts. After this, we present the execution time of each algorithm. ... text: The analysis on the collected data was carried out employing SPSS PASW Statistics software, release 18.0.0. At ﬁrst, a Shapiro-Wilks W test [27] was run on the dataset to test if they are normally distributed. This test is used when the number of data points is between 3 and 2 000 [27] and is performed because the prerequisite for a lot of statistical tests is knowing whether the data points are normally distributed or not. The test, with a conﬁdence level of 95%, failed to reject the null hypothesis that the data was normally distributed. In other words, we are not assured about the normal distribution of the data points, and therefore, non-parametric statistical tests were appropriate to test our hypotheses. The statistical test that we used for both hypotheses was the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test (also known as Wilcoxon Rank Sum test and Mann-Whitney U test) [27]. This test is a non-parametric equivalent of the well-known T-Test, used for comparing two independent variables to test the null hypothesis that the two variables are from the same population and have the same mean values [27]. Therefore, it is most suitable when the research hypothesis is that the two variables are different (the mean of data points of one variable is less than, greater than or just different from that of the other). Moreover, a signiﬁcance level (α) must be set. α is the probability of a statistical error known as “Type I Error”, which happens when a null hypothesis is rejected while it is actually true. When the test is run, values called “p-values” are obtained that represent the signiﬁcance probability. The p-values are compared against α to test the null hypotheses. When p-value is less than α, the null hypothesis is rejected [27]. In this research, we set α to 0.05, which is a commonly-used level in scientiﬁc works [27].

Specifically, the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test [27] was employed for both hypotheses. This test, a non-parametric alternative to the T-test, is ideal for comparing two independent variables to see if their means differ. We established a significance level (α) of 0.05, a standard practice [27], to determine if observed p-values warrant rejecting the null hypothesis (p < α).

Data analysis was performed using SPSS PASW Statistics, release 18.0.0. This test is suitable for comparing two independent variables to see if they originate from different populations or have different mean values. We set our significance level (α) at 0.05, a standard in scientific research [27], where a p-value below this threshold indicates rejection of the null hypothesis, thereby minimizing Type I error.

text: All measurements were performed on the same Windows 7 Machine with Intel Core i5 CPU 3.5 GHz and 16 GB RAM. The algorithms are compute-bound and not memory inten- sive. Since Henard et at. reported that SATIBEA stabilizes on its ultimate solutions in 15min [26], we performed each studied algorithm 15min to compute the approximate Pareto front for each subject. To reduce measurement ﬂuctuations caused by random- ness (e.g., the randomness of performing crossover and mutation), we independently executed each algorithm 30 times for each subject to support inferential statistical test- ing for signiﬁcance and assessment of effect size. We took both the median and mean values of the measurements for analysis. Based on the experimental results of 30 executions per algo- rithm, we conducted a statistical test at the signiﬁcance level of 5%. We performed the Mann–Whitney U test, which is a nonparametric test and makes fewer assumptions regard- ing the underlying populations. We calculated the estimated probability, i.e., p-value, that an algorithm produces different results than the other. As suggested by Arcuri and Briand [2], we reported the nonparametric effect size measure ˆA12, introduced by Vargha and Delaney [53]. It indicates the performance superiority, and it measures the extent to which an algorithm outperforms the other. Moreover, the superiority between algorithms is considered as small, medium and large when ˆA12 value is over 0.56, 0.64 and 0.71, respectively.

All measurements were taken on a consistent hardware setup: a Windows 7 machine equipped with an Intel Core i5 CPU (3.5 GHz) and 16 GB of RAM. The algorithms are primarily compute-bound and do not demand extensive memory. Given Henard et al.'s observation that SATIBEA converges to its optimal solutions within 15 minutes [26], each algorithm studied was allotted 15 minutes to compute the approximate Pareto front for each subject. This approach facilitated robust inferential statistical testing for significance and effect size, with both median and mean values being analyzed. Based on these 30 executions per algorithm, we applied a statistical test with a 5% significance level. The Mann–Whitney U test, a non-parametric method with minimal assumptions about population distributions, was used to calculate the p-value, indicating the likelihood of an algorithm producing results statistically different from others. Furthermore, adhering to Arcuri and Briand's guidance [2], we included the nonparametric effect size measure ˆA12, proposed by Vargha and Delaney [53]. This metric quantifies an algorithm's superior performance, with ˆA12 values above 0.56, 0.64, and 0.71 signifying small, medium, and large performance advantages, respectively.

text: To address RQ1, a set of thresholds for TMP, FPC, FDC and OET are selected showing the minimum acceptable values for a partic-ular context. Notice that these thresholds are set through the do-main analysis, discussion with test engineers and a test manager at Cisco, and test execution history. Meanwhile, there is no speciﬁc threshold provided for AEF since the test engineers think that it is not meaningful for them to propose such threshold. In our context, these thresholds values are: TMP := 0.8; FPC := 0.8; FDC := 0.85 and OET := 2 (h). Notice the purpose of these pre-deﬁned thresholds is to assess the performance of the selected search algorithms and the obtained solutions are independent of the availability of these thresh-old values. In other contexts, experts can provide such thresholds if required. As discussed in Section 2, NSGA-II, MOCell, SPEA2, PAES, SMPSO, CellDE may produce more than one solutions. Our evaluation mecha-nism is to choose the best solution with the highest value of objective functions for TMP, FPC, FDC and OET and compare the values of ob-jective functions with provided thresholds separately. For instance, for TMP using NSGA-II, the highest value of objective function for the best solution is ﬁrst chosen from the obtained ones. The value of the objective function is then compared with the threshold for TMP. No-tice that for each objective, the chosen solution may be different so that it is essential to seek a mechanism to evaluate the overall per-formance of obtained solutions by the algorithms considering all the objectives together. Our mechanism is to calculate the average value to combine the ﬁve provided thresholds and the values of objective functions for the solutions obtained by all the search algorithms. The formula for combining is shown as below and the combined value is called as Overall Fitness Value (OFV). OFV = (nor(TMP)+ nor(FPC)+ nor(FDC)+ (1 −nor(OET))+ nor(AEF)) 5 Afterwards, we can evaluate the overall performance for all the selected search algorithms using the values of OFV. Such mechanism makes sense since we deﬁne the same objective functions, and use the same formula to combine the values of objective functions for all the algorithms. Notice that higher the OFV value is, better the performance of a speciﬁc algorithm is. To answer RQ2, RQ3 and RQ4, the same mechanisms are adapted as above when comparing all the algorithms. Notice that for the industrial case study, we ﬁrst compare and analyze the results ob-tained by the selected algorithms for each objective separately and then evaluate the OFV considering the ﬁve objectives together. As for artiﬁcial problems, we only evaluate the values of OFV to as-sess the performance and scalability for the ten algorithms. More-over, for artiﬁcial problems, Mean Fitness Value for each problem (MFVi,j, i refers to the number of features and j means the number of associated test cases, i.e., 10 ≤i ≤1000 with an increment of 10 and 5 ≤j ≤45 with an increment of 10) is deﬁned to measure the mean overall ﬁtness value for a certain number of runs nr as below (in our case, nr = 100). OFVi,j,r is the ﬁtness value of the 25,000th generation after the rth run with i features and j associated test cases. MFVi,j = nr r=1OFVi,j,r nr Moreover, Mean Fitness Value for Features (MFVFi) is deﬁned for RQ4 to measure how the increment of the number of fea-tures impacts the performance of the selected search algorithms as below. MFVFi = 45 j=5,j=j+10MFVi,j 5 where 10 ≤i ≤1000 with an increment of 10, i.e., a set of hundred MFV_F values can be obtained for various numbers of features. Similarly, Mean Fitness Value for associated Test Cases (MFVTCj) is also deﬁned for RQ4 to measure how the increment of the number of associated test cases impacts the performance of the selected multi-objective search algorithms as follows. MFVTCj = 1000 i=10,i=i+10MFVi,j 100 where 5 ≤i ≤45 with an increment of 10, i.e., a set of ﬁve MFV_TC values can be obtained for different number of associated test cases.
paraphrases: To address Research Question 1 (RQ1), we established minimum acceptable thresholds for TMP, FPC, FDC, and OET, derived from domain analysis, discussions with Cisco test engineers and a test manager, and historical test execution data. AEF, however, lacked a specific threshold as engineers found it irrelevant to propose one. Our chosen thresholds are: TMP = 0.8; FPC = 0.8; FDC = 0.85; and OET = 2 hours. These thresholds serve to evaluate search algorithm performance, and the generated solutions are not dependent on their presence. Experts in other contexts could provide such thresholds if needed. As outlined in Section 2, algorithms like NSGA-II, MOCell, SPEA2, PAES, SMPSO, and CellDE can yield multiple solutions. Our evaluation approach involves selecting the best solution for each of TMP, FPC, FDC, and OET (based on the highest objective function value) and individually comparing these values against their respective thresholds. For instance, with NSGA-II for TMP, the highest objective function value from the obtained solutions is chosen and then compared to the TMP threshold. Recognizing that the "best" solution might differ across objectives, we developed a mechanism to assess the overall performance of an algorithm's solutions across all objectives simultaneously. This mechanism calculates an average value by combining the five provided thresholds and the objective function values from all search algorithms, resulting in an Overall Fitness Value (OFV) using the formula provided. A higher OFV indicates better algorithm performance. This method is consistent because all algorithms share the same objective functions and combination formula. For RQ2, RQ3, and RQ4, we applied similar evaluation mechanisms. In the industrial case study, we first analyzed results for each objective individually before combining them into OFV. For artificial problems, we solely used OFV to assess performance and scalability across the ten algorithms. Additionally, for artificial problems, we defined Mean Fitness Value per problem (MFVi,j, where i is features and j is test cases, ranging from 10-1000 and 5-45 respectively) as the average OFV over nr runs (nr=100), using the given formula. For RQ4, Mean Fitness Value for Features (MFVFi) quantifies the impact of increasing feature count on algorithm performance, calculated by averaging MFVi,j over all j, producing 100 MFV_F values. Similarly, Mean Fitness Value for associated Test Cases (MFVTCj) measures the impact of increasing test case count, calculated by averaging MFVi,j over all i, yielding five MFV_TC values.

To address RQ1, we established contextual minimum acceptable thresholds for TMP, FPC, FDC, and OET through domain analysis, consultations with Cisco test engineers and a test manager, and historical test execution data. No specific threshold was set for AEF, as test engineers found it impractical. Our defined thresholds are: TMP = 0.8; FPC = 0.8; FDC = 0.85; and OET = 2 (h). These thresholds are intended for evaluating search algorithm performance, and the solutions themselves are not reliant on their existence. In other contexts, experts could supply such thresholds. As mentioned in Section 2, multi-objective algorithms like NSGA-II, MOCell, SPEA2, PAES, SMPSO, and CellDE can generate multiple solutions. Our evaluation strategy is to select the solution with the highest objective function value for each of TMP, FPC, FDC, and OET, and then compare these individual objective values against their respective thresholds. For example, for TMP with NSGA-II, we pick the highest objective function value from the generated solutions and compare it to the TMP threshold. Since the optimal solution might vary for different objectives, we devised a mechanism to evaluate the algorithms' overall performance by considering all objectives simultaneously. This involves calculating an "Overall Fitness Value" (OFV) by averaging the normalized values of the five objectives, as shown in the provided formula: OFV = (nor(TMP)+ nor(FPC)+ nor(FDC)+ (1 −nor(OET))+ nor(AEF)) / 5. A higher OFV signifies better algorithm performance. This approach is consistent as all algorithms utilize the same objective functions and combination formula. For RQ2, RQ3, and RQ4, the same evaluation mechanisms are employed. In the industrial case study, we initially compare and analyze algorithm results for each objective independently before calculating the OFV across all five objectives. For artificial problems, we exclusively use OFV to assess the performance and scalability of the ten algorithms. Furthermore, for artificial problems, we define a Mean Fitness Value for each problem (MFVi,j, where 'i' is features (10-1000, increment 10) and 'j' is test cases (5-45, increment 10)) as the average OFV over a specific number of runs (nr=100). Here, OFVi,j,r represents the fitness value of the 25,000th generation after the r-th run. Additionally, for RQ4, Mean Fitness Value for Features (MFVFi) is defined to assess how increasing features affects algorithm performance, calculated by averaging MFVi,j over 'j' (yielding 100 MFV_F values). Similarly, Mean Fitness Value for associated Test Cases (MFVTCj) is defined to measure the impact of increasing test cases, calculated by averaging MFVi,j over 'i' (yielding five MFV_TC values).

text: The approach gives an extraction method that guides the extraction process, With the approach, different kinds of product line artifacts (like Features, Use Cases elements, functional and nonfunctional requirements) can be identified in user documentations by a non-expert and can later be approved and used for modeling by domain experts. the main advantage of this pattern based approach can be seen in the expert load reduction and therefore in the support of product line introduction in practice by avoiding the bottleneck of the workload of the domain experts. In this chapter we have described the elements of the approach and its evaluation in a controlled experiment and a case study. Our general experiences are that the approach with its process steps and the patterns support the finding of relevant elements that can be used for modeling. In the industrial case study, with the help of the approach, more than 90% of a product feature matrix, an artifact that is often used in product line scoping, could be built.

text: In future work, ﬁrst, we plan to extend PACOGEN to N-wise fea- ture coverage, allowing the generation of test conﬁgurations with higher or lower interaction strength (e.g., N = 3 and N = 1). This involves the development of an algorithm to generate N-tuples in addition to a special additional constraint to enforce the coverage of N-wise interactions. Second, we plan to analyse the correlation between pairwise-coverage and error-detection effectiveness of a test suite. Third, we will analyse the performance of PACOGEN using problems in the transition phase (in between under-constrained and over- constrained problems), as this is the area where the hardest problems lie. Finally, we plan to integrate PACOGEN with the industry-strength variability management technology we are currently developing. We envision to fully integrate PACOGEN in our industrial partner’s testing framework that runs in a continuous integration environment. However, this process is challenging, as it requires not only technical adoption, but also organisational and cultural changes at different levels in the company.

Second, we will investigate the relationship between pairwise coverage and a test suite's ability to detect errors. Third, we'll assess PACOGEN's performance on problems in the transition phase, which are typically the most difficult. Lastly, we aim to integrate PACOGEN with our robust variability management technology, specifically within our industrial partner's continuous integration testing framework. This integration presents significant challenges, demanding not only technical adjustments but also organizational and cultural shifts throughout the company.

Another promising avenue is identifying service variability models across multiple domains, simultaneously using the variability models of various business processes to inform service identification, thus enabling suitable assessments of both spatial and temporal reusability for the identified services.

text: As a future work, we will improve the efficiency of our algorithms. For doing so, we plan to study additional data structures for representing states in FTA. In our current implementation, such states are represented by triplets composed of an explicit location, a binary decision diagram, and a difference bound matrix. As alternatives, we plan to use either Multi-Terminal BDD or a data structure that combines zone and binary variables representations. For the latter, Clock Restriction Diagrams [20] and appear as promising candidates. Also, we plan to extend FTA modelling to non-Boolean features. This would allow to directly express real-time constraints in terms of a feature attributes. As an example, the running speed of a processor may drastically influence the execution time of a software. Considering this extension would definitively impact on our model-checking procedure. Indeed, in this context we would not be able to use binary decision diagrams or SAT solver to reason on sets of products. Second, we may not be able to translate the FTA into an infinite FTS anymore.
paraphrases: In future work, we aim to enhance our algorithms' efficiency by exploring new data structures for representing states in FTA. Currently, states are defined by an explicit location, a binary decision diagram, and a difference bound matrix; alternatively, we plan to investigate Multi-Terminal BDDs or a combination of zone and binary variable representations, with Clock Restriction Diagrams [20] showing promise for the latter. Additionally, we intend to expand FTA modeling to include non-Boolean features, enabling direct expression of real-time constraints as feature attributes (e.g., a processor's speed impacting software execution time). This extension would significantly alter our model-checking process, as it would preclude the use of binary decision diagrams or SAT solvers for reasoning about product sets, and potentially prevent the translation of FTA into an infinite FTS.

text: Several challenges remain for our future work in two main directions, namely: We intend to extend our suite with new operations and testing techniques. We also plan to evaluate our suite with other tools and in development scenarios using FaMa and report our experiences to the community; and We also plan to explore the benefits obtained when combining our suite with other automated testing methods. In a previous work [30], we presented an automated test data generator for the analysis of feature models with promising results. It generates random follow-up test cases based on the relations between inputs feature models and theirs expected outputs (so-called metamorphic testing). However, it is known that metamorphic testing produce better results when combined with other test case selection strategies that generate the initial set of test cases. We intend to use our suite to guide the generation of test cases in our automated test data generator and study the gains in efficiency and efficacy.
paraphrases: Our future work addresses two primary areas: First, we aim to enhance our testing suite with new operations and techniques. We also plan to assess its performance against other tools and within development environments utilizing FaMa, sharing our findings with the community. Second, we will investigate the advantages of integrating our suite with other automated testing methods. While our previous work [30] introduced a promising automated test data generator for feature model analysis, which uses metamorphic testing to create random follow-up test cases based on input-output relationships, metamorphic testing is known to improve when combined with strategies for generating initial test cases. Therefore, we plan to leverage our suite to guide the test case generation in our automated generator, thereby analyzing improvements in efficiency and efficacy.

text: To evaluate the efﬁciency of these three approaches, we carried out experiments on the medical domain. The results show a time-space tradeoff: FABS always produces smaller formulas, but the compositional technique computes the for-mula faster. This observation is useful for practitioners to choose an approach depending on how they value time and space. In our experiments, the parametric approach alone never obtained the best results, but we should keep in mind that the compositional technique requires that the model has a special form, and that the execution time of FABS increases more steeply with the number of features. However, all these methods outperform, in terms of practical time and space complexity, the baseline product-based approach that analyses each Markov model corresponding to a product individually.
paraphrases: We tested the effectiveness of three methods within the medical field. Our findings reveal a time-space compromise: FABS consistently generates more compact formulas, while the compositional method offers faster computation. This insight helps practitioners select an approach based on their priorities for time and space. Although the parametric approach on its own didn't yield optimal results in our tests, it's important to remember that the compositional technique needs a specific model structure, and FABS's execution time escalates more rapidly with more features. Nevertheless, all these methods surpass the traditional product-based approach, which individually analyzes each Markov model, in terms of real-world time and space efficiency.
